query: I'm looking for a mount that allows me to use both open sights and a scope effectively on my Marlin 22 LR. I want to ensure that I can easily mount a laser, night light, and regular light while maintaining visibility through the scope and the laser dot. How can I achieve the right height for mounting these accessories so that they work well together, especially for distances around 25 to 50 yards? Any recommendations for a versatile riser mount that can help with this setup would be appreciated.
ori_review:
I put this on a Marlin 22 LR. It works great. I can use my open sights. Plus I mounted my scope, Laser, Night light, and a regular light. The night light works great. It puts out a green light that lets you see through a scope just like daytime use. I can see the laser dot through the 1 inch opening to. The laser is mounted at the front of the rail in front of the scope. The scope sits high enough above the laser and can still see the laser dot very easy.
My laser is 2-1/8 inch above center of barrel. Cross hair of scope is 2-7/8 inch above center of barrel. I can lower this some by using a lower profile mount than the one I have the 1" rail mounted to. The lower mount converts the dovetail on the Marlin to a Picatinny mount. If you like to use nice open sights and a scope this is a must have for me. Any thing closer than 25 yards. I use the open sight.

I keep the laser and scope set parallel to center of barrel. Once you learn how to work the up and down of the scope for different yardage it works great. I keep the laser always parallel with center of barrel. Makes adjusting the scope easy. At 50 yards I have no problem hitting a circle the size of a quarter. At 25 yards I hit within a dime easy. Wind will affect left and right at 50 yards.

query: I'm considering upgrading my ebike controller to a more powerful option and I'm curious about the benefits of moving from a 48v 22ah to a 48v 30ah controller. Is it really worth the investment, and how much of a difference in speed and performance can I expect? Also, how does the upgrade process work if I want to get the 48v 30ah controller since it's not listed on Amazon? Any insights would be appreciated!
ori_review:
So, this was kinda expensive, but well worth the investment.
Upgraded my Super73 Z1 from its original controller 36v 11ah
Purchased this set 48v 22ah as upgrade. Purchased 48v 20ah battery to match controller voltage, too.

Controller and display are great but….I ended up burning out a MOSFET.
I contacted company for replacement since I was still under warranty.

Company did not have a 48v 22ah in stock at time so they offered to UPGRADE my replacement with a 48v 30ah controller. Only had to pay $20 shipping.

I don’t think I will ever go back to anything less than 48v 30ah for a controller. I thought 48v 22ah was powerful.
The speed and takeoff are even more amazing with 48v 30ah controller.

You can see the difference in size of controller with just a few more amp hours added. But boy what a difference!
(Pic bottom image 22ah controller; top image 30ah controller)

They don’t sell the 48v 30ah controller on Amazon, but if you email them when u make your purchase, you can upgrade. And I strongly urge you to.
48v 30ah has to be experienced to believe!!

Matter of fact, 48v 30ah controller is so much better than 48v 22 ah that comes with order (which definitely ain’t bad) that I ordered a second set and paid full price for upgraded controller and display ($139 + $20 upgrade fee) to have when I build/mod my next ebike.

Well worth the money, imo. Hope this review helps.

/Bklyn👑

I like this way better than the Hydroflask water bottle.

- hydroflask kid bottle comes with a silicone sleeve that guarantees your water bottle tips over if you accidentally knock it rather than it sliding a little. If you take the silicone sleeve off then the paint starts to chip off. The Yeti unpainted stainless steel on the bottom, so no paint to chip.

- hydroflask handle is just big enough to skip one finger in and then inevitably catch on something and twist your finger off. Not really, but it’s awkward. The Yeti handle is big. Easy for little kids to hold. Easy to clip on to something. And if it falls right can keep the nozzle from touching the ground if you drop it.

- on the hydroflask the bottom part of the nozzle is difficult to access to clean. On the Yeti the side of the bottom of the nozzle is exposed so I’m not worried about anything growing there that I can’t see.

- the hydroflask lid has to be lined up just right or it won’t thread on right. My 5 year old certainly can’t do it. On the Yeti the threads are on the inside of the bottle so everything always gets lined up properly and is easy to put on.

- the plastic on the yeti lid seems more durable. We have damaged the hydroflask lids but the yeti still looks like brand new.

- the nubbin on the nozzle that plugs the air hole when closed is higher on the hydroflask than in the yeti. My friend’s kid chipped her tooth on that nubbin. So the lower the better.

12 oz is a good size too. I think I’m going to get one for myself.

query: I'm looking for a carry case that can accommodate my Umarex Legends full-auto MP40 airgun. ori_review:
Love it! It's nice heavy fabric and seems to be strongly stitched. I own an Umarex Legends full-auto MP40 airgun (which is AWESOME!) and there are two things specific to the Umarex MP40 you should know about if you're buying this for it.

First, the bolt handle doesn't go all the way forward, which was the Lock position on the original. The reinforcement patch on the side thus doesn't quite cover the bolt handle. Won't be an issue for me, it's always treated nicely. Second, the Legends BB magazine is 1/2" inch longer than the 9mm original. The lower three mag pouches fit the mags fine and look good. The top two mag pouches won't close over the Legends magazine, too short. You could punch a new hole in the strap, but the flap would ride up too far and look weird. No problem unless you have four or more magazines.

IT'S PERFECT ANYWAY! I stash my two magazines in the lower pouches, and one holds a tube of BBs. The top two slots store my CO2 carts (6-8 each). The square pouch holds my C02 wrench and the loading-assist tool I made. The gun is stored protected with all ammo, gas, and tools needed for a long session of machine pistol goodness. It also looks like I stole it from a Wehrmacht officer's luggage, a level of realism needed for such a nice replica gun.

If you have a genuine MP40 (lucky bastard) it will probably fit perfectly. It works fine for the Legends replica with the caveats above.

query: I'm looking for a solution to prevent flats while riding, especially from goathead thorns. I've heard about tire liners that can block thorns and provide a good ride quality. ori_review: I've been using Mr Tuffys for years and now I won't ride without them. Where I live, goathead thorns (Tribulus terrestris) are the most common cause of flats. The bigger ones can get right through the toughest tires (even mountain bike knobbies) and yes they can go through a Mr. Tuffy liner if you hit the thorn dead on. But that happens only rarely, and these strips block 95 percent of thorns from the tire center in my experience. Thorns can still get through from the sides sometimes, but again, not often. When used with a regular tube, Mr Tuffy's are much lighter than a thorn-proof tube, and offer better ride quality and performance. I use competition level tires on my Pinarello Dogma racing bike, which are light and supple but also more easily punctured than heavier tires. The liners do add some weight, but I have not noticed any decline in suppleness, cornering stability, or overall ride quality. And I get a lot fewer flats with these!

query: I'm looking for an air mattress that is suitable for occasional use, as I've recently experienced some issues with one I purchased. It deflated unexpectedly, and after trying to locate a leak, I found a tear. I was pleased with the customer service response, but I want to ensure I choose a mattress that is durable enough for my needs. Can you recommend an inflatable mattress that is reliable for short-term stays and has good customer support in case of issues?
ori_review:
I am a minister from Florida visiting and helping a family on their ranch in Missouri.

The family didn’t have a bed so I purchased a queen size mattress from Amazon on August 21, 2017 and delivered on the 23rd. The mattress was working good until two nights ago (Friday September 29, 2017) the mattress deflated in the middle of the night needless to say I had a frustrating night.

Unfortunately, I needed to get up very early Saturday morning to help do work for the family I am visiting. We didn’t get home until late in the day. When we got home and after doing chores we inflated the mattress looking and listening for leaks. We were not able to find anything yet we definitely could notice the mattress deflating pretty quickly. The following day we took a spray bottle with water and sprayed all around the outside of the mattress looking for bubbles/leaks but couldn’t find any.

So after two nights of somewhat sleeping in a chair I am half awake writing this to you.

This morning (Monday October 02) I wrote two emails one was from the Amazon site and the other I went to the SoundAsleep website, found their customer service email and sent an email from my email address. Both emails were answered very quickly and had a phone number to call.

While awaiting the email I wanted to recheck the mattress to see if I could find the leak. I reinflated the mattress and took a rag with some soapy water and started rubbing along one edge of the mattress. While doing so I felt some air escaping from the top of it and spotted the tear. I thought to myself that is why I didn’t spot the leak to begin with and besides I had a mattress cover on top and didn’t even think the leak could have originated from the top. Anyway lesson learned...

As soon as possible I called the number and talked to a customer service rep who was very courteous. I gave him my order number and told him I found the leak. He asked how long I had been sleeping on the mattress and I said at least 30 days. He said the mattress isn’t meant for long term use but they would replace the mattress this one time. So I anticipate that it will arrive in a couple of days.

I wanted to point this out. As I mentioned above this is not a long term mattress and is only supposed to be used on occasion. When I first bought the mattress I didn’t know how long I was staying here and I didn’t think about the longevity of the mattress. As it turns out I didn’t think about that nor catch that when I was looking for a sleeping solution. So keep that in mind.

On another note I really love the mattress and has worked well for me while here. I am very thankful that the company is replacing it.

query: I'm looking for a camping stove that ignites easily, even in windy conditions, and boils water quickly. I've had issues with my previous stove being hard to light and taking too long to boil water. I also want something that can handle freeze-dried food packs effectively. Additionally, it would be great if the cooking container had better volume indicators for measuring in low light. Does the Jetboil MiniMo fit these needs?
ori_review:
I don't know about you, but I camp with my girls, and when they say they are "getting a little bit hungry," that's code for "You had better put something warm in my belly in twenty nanoseconds or there's going to be hell to pay."

Knowing that the slightest hunger pangs constitute a five-alarm emergency, I could not be more pleased with my Jetboil MiniMo. I had an older style unit made by a different brand before buying this unit. It was one of those where you use a match to light a little cube. That unit was itself a big improvement over what we had decades ago, but if the weather stinks those kind of units are hard to light, depending on weather and altitude they take forever to boil if they will boil the quantity you want at all, the little cubes sometimes make a little mess wherever they burn, and the residue turns sticky if it rains. Long story short, with my old unit, I spent half my time trying to prepare the meal, and the other half watching my back to make sure I didn't get shived.

I cannot describe to you how much better the Jetboil MiniMo is compared to my old unit. Push a button and it ignites (even in high winds), control the flow at your leisure, and whatever you do, don't blink - the darn thing boils water so fast you won't believe it. It's really, really awesome, and the girls are always happy.

A couple of quick notes - Although the title says "Mini," if you mostly or entirely live off typical freeze dried food packs you may find this unit to be a little bigger than you need. And a note for the product development team - it would be nice if there were more than two indents to indicate volumes on the cooking container. Ideally, you could estimate to the quarter cup or so and equivalent liters. In a perfect world, you would be able to measure in the dark. That's really my only critical feedback.

query: I'm looking for a golf swing analyzer that can help me improve my swing while practicing into a net. I need a device that provides detailed feedback like club head speed and can record my swings effectively. I've heard that some devices require hitting a ball to get data, and I'm also interested in how to interpret the data for improvement. Additionally, I want to know if the associated app functions well and if it has any issues, like crashing or not recording swings due to interruptions. Can this product meet those needs?
ori_review:
This is a must-have product if you a lot of hitting into a net, where you can not see the ultimate result of your golf shot. For $150 (the price I paid), this is the best swing analyzing tool you can get before you start looking into launch monitors (good launch monitors START at around $1000!).

The Good
This device is rugged, and simple to use. Simply charge it up, download the app to your smart phone or tablet, pair the SwingTalk to your smart device, and insert into the back of your selected club, making sure the index mark is aligned to the face of your club. The SwingTalk does not get in the way of your swing, and accurately provides a whole host of detail, including the club head speed. The battery lasts long enough for two hours of practice, and the app keeps track of ALL of your swings, separated by date. You can easily go back to any swing on any date and look at a 3D model of your swing.

The Bad
In order to record your swing, you must actually hit a ball; you cannot simply take practice swings and expect to see any data. I suspect this is because it uses the 'feel' of the impact to record data such as the angle of the club head on impact, and from that it calculates a whole host of other data. The other issue with this device is that it doesn't come with any information about how to interpret the data and use it to improve your swing. Fortunately, there are several Youtube videos that actually do this. Just do a search on Youtube for "SwingTalk" and they should be the top or near the top results.

The Ugly
The associated smart phone app is pretty good, but still could use some more work. It crashes on occasion, and if you receive a call or text in the middle of your swing, it will not record the data for that swing. Also, the 3D graphic of your swing is not an accurate representation of your whole swing. Rather, it shows the position of the club head throughout the swing and attempts to extrapolate your body position from that. There is another app that you can download and use with the SwingTalk called the SwingTalkDR for driving range. This app attempts to show how far the ball would travel and in what direction. However, there is basically no documentation on this app, and the data it provides is a rough estimate at best. Still, considering the price and how it works, I wouldn't expect it to be able to replicate the results of a $1000+ launch monitor.

Can anyone share their experiences with models that offer good sizing options, especially for larger boot sizes? I need something that fits well around the leg and is versatile for both winter and spring/fall use. Any tips on choosing the right size would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Gaiters in general:
It's important to keep the bottom of your pants dry (and of course the dreaded wicking upwards); it's apparent when you go hiking with your friends and they all end up with wet pants (whether walking in the [well below freezing temp] snow or wet brush). Thick (and durable) and breathable gaiters help with versatility for both winter and wet spring/fall.

Thoughts on (Outdoor Research) models:
These "crocodiles" have the extra weight fabric, wider velcro seam, and an extra velcro tab at the front base, which totally helps to keep the velco seam from unraveling; and, comes in an XXL size--over their "verglas" counterpart. The "expedition crocodiles" would just be a heavier step up (fabric wise).

Thoughts on sizing:
XXL fits 12-15 boot size (or euro 46-50), as opposed to XL, which fits 10-13 or euro 43-47--I bought the XXL for my size 13 (or euro 47)--could be a bit snugger in the leg area, especially the top closure that I seem to have fully tightened and the leg area seems just a tad baggy (which I could use the wide velco seem for adjustments: over lapping the seam a bit, but don't want to have that non-battened edge that could get opened by snow build-up; i.e. perhaps your choice of sizing would be better influenced by your perception of your leg size, and I would suggest *NOT* oversizing as you can always give slack in the underbelt and under lap the wide velco seam and have the bottom wrap higher on your boot (assuming you are using boots and not hiking shoes)).

Bottom line:
LOVE THEM!

OVERFILL the sandbags to the point where the sand is just pouring out the top.

Watch a few videos on Youtube and practice tent setup and breakdown before you travel so you get the hang of it. -I'm 6'5" and 225lbs. I fit in this thing, but barely in length. My head rests up against one end, and the ends of my toes touch the other end. If you sleep a little curled up (and I do), this thing will be long enough. If you sleep straight like a board and like to really stretch out all night long and not have anything touching you, and you're 6'3" or above, this may be a deal breaker. Again, I'm 6'5" and it didn't bother me. But if you don't like things touching your toes, and you're a huge person, this may be bothersome. Also, the idea of this isn't to be a huge tent around you. It's more like a casket, meant to be snug.
-I was able to put my sleeping pad, sleep sack, and Thermarest pillow inside the tent. There was plenty of width in the tent, and I'm a pretty wide person. When I got back home my small dog crawled in it and I think we could almost sleep in there together if we got real snuggly.
-The tent also goes on top of things, like crappy bug infested third world mattresses. I did this in Haiti too. I was worried I would wake up others around me if I moved a lot, but the floor of the tent isn't too crinkly or loud on top of mattresses. I didn't test the waterproofness of the floor but trust that it would hold up to a little water if it needed to.
-This is not a true tent. If you're outside and it rains, you'll get wet. If you add a ground floor or tarp underneath and rig up a rain fly, you could get by with it as a summer tent. While the bottom does appear to be waterproof, the fabric is relatively thin. If I used this outside on rocky ground or gravel, I'd definitely want a tarp underneath it!
-The zippers allow you to get in on either side of this, which was really nice depending on how my sleep setup was arranged. The zippers grabs themselves are a little loud, especially in a quiet room at night. The zipper grabs meet on a certain point of the zipper line, and when you move they bang against each other a little. They make some noise as you move around. It never bothered anyone else that slept around me, but if a roommate was a super light sleeper, it might wake them up. This was really the only negative I could find at all. And it wasn't really that bad at all. If you're mostly sleeping by yourself, or with some space between you and roommates, this isn't a concern.
-The mosquito netting is really effective. I don't know technical specs, but the netting is fine mesh, and it kept out literally everything, including no-see-ums or whatever those tiny little bugs are. Not sure about fleas, but I didn't have any bites overnight of any kind when I was in this thing. I'm confident it'll keep out anything that poses a threat to me while sleeping.
-It was hot in Haiti, and this tent really didn't retain heat at all. It did knock down a little bit of the fan speed overhead, but I didn't feel like it affected the warmth around me. This was really important for me as I mostly travel to developing countries closer to the equator. I did NOT want to add heat to my sleeping arrangement and was thrilled this tent did not.
-This traveled well in my checked bag. It has some flexibility, even in it's most compact size. If this even makes it through a year of my travels, I'll keep replacing it. (I hate taking anti-malarial tablets). I'm headed to Sri Lanka, Togo, and Peru in the coming months, and if this tent breaks or poles snap expect me to write an update and change my review!
-When I store this, I think I'll not fold it up into the most compact size. I'll probably store this in the larger, circular size. I'm worried in the most compact form long-term storage might bend the poles over time. Just a hunch.

My overall recommendation is to purchase this. I travel to countries with zika, chikungunya, malaria, and other mosquito-borne illnesses. This takes up little room in my checked bag (I think it would fit in a carry on too), sets up quick, and lets me sleep with confidence. No more setting up mosquito nets at midnight in dark rooms. Or getting tore up with bites when I sleep in large rooms on concrete. When I hit purchase on Amazon I was a little concerned about price. But honestly, after using in Haiti during Hurricane Matthew response, boy am I glad I had this with me. Great piece of kit that I'll keep traveling with for a long time. Buy with confidence.

query: What are some tips for assembling the darts for my blowgun, and how can I improve my shooting technique for better accuracy? I’ve found the assembly process to be a bit challenging, and I want to ensure I'm using it effectively to hit my targets consistently.
ori_review:
I love this blowgun. For what it is, it's capable of surprising accuracy. My only complaint is that it was unnecessarily hard to assemble the darts. The trick is as follows:

1) Grasp the shaft of a dart about an inch from the sharp end with a pair of pliers.

2) Allow the cup to sit upright on a piece of scrap wood, and slowly press the sharp end of the dart all the way through the cup to the other side. Try to go in as straight as you can.

3) Pull the cup free, reverse the shaft so your pliers are now an inch or so from the dull end, and force the dull end into the hole you just made until you are just short of coming through the other side. It won't come apart now under normal use, don't be too worried if it's not perfectly straight, it matters less than you probably think.

My current shooting technique is to hold the mid shaft of the blowgun with my right hand, and the mouthpiece with my left. When I stand square to the target and focus on it, I see two images of the front sight. The dart will strike exactly in the middle of those two images. (I've noticed that if I reverse my hand positions, the dart will not longer strike in the middle - I suspect it has to do with eye dominance but I really have no idea).

The first trick is to not move the shaft after blowing the air in. The second trick is to continue to provide breath until the dart exits the muzzle. The third trick is to deliver the same amount of air for each shot. It's fun, but it's not easy. It feels kind of like archery.

A cardboard box is all the target you need. My best five-shot group so far was about the size of a fifty cent piece, from 20 feet away. I think it's capable of even more than that.

query: I'm curious about the battery life of these heated socks. How long can I expect them to last on a single charge, especially when using the highest setting? The heating pads are thin and you can definitely feel them when you walk but it's the kind of presence that you can get used to after a while. The top cuff has a deep pocket on the side in which to stuff the battery and wire. It bulges out a bit but is not a problem to cover with your pant leg. How long do the batteries last on one charge? Setting 1 (highest, 55°C) lasts 4-5 hours; setting 2 (45°C) lasts 6-7 hours; setting 3 (38°C) lasts 9-10 hours. I tested it on the max setting (#1) and got around 5 hours of warmth during mixed usage indoors and outdoors (35°F, 2°C). This was consistent with the claimed duration in the owners manual. How hot does it feel? 55°C (131°F) merely feels warm but that is how these heated foot devices work. I've used heated insoles in ski boots for decades and they work by taking the edge off the cold though gentle warmth. These socks work the same way. I have not run an extended test on these yet so I won't comment on how they hold up through many wash cycles and many charge cycles; I'll update later as appropriate. But my initial reaction to these socks is very positive. They are made well and work as designed. Nice!

query: I'm looking for a mini pedal exerciser that I can use while watching TV to stay active. I want something affordable, preferably with a display to track my calories and time, and I appreciate it being already assembled. Are there options that are simple, quiet, and won't slide around on the floor? ori_review:
I wanted a mini pedal exerciser for a few months now; something that I could use while I'm watching TV, so I don't feel like I'm being so lazy and so I could get some exercise and multitask.

I was initially looking at the more expensive types that were over $100 and had a lot more plastic. But then I noticed these less expensive and simpler ones that seemed like there weren't as many plastic parts that could potentially break. Some of the less expensive models didn't have displays / counters, but this one did, it was cheap enough and the reviews were good enough so I took a chance and bought one. I've only had it for 4 or 5 days but I'm so happy with it!

The display tracks calories burned, revolutions and time pedaled and I couldn't be happier. It works well, it came already assembled (battery included), it has adjustable tension, and it folds up. It comes with a strap to attach to a chair so it doesn't slide, but I put mine on the floor in front of the couch on my living room carpet and it doesn't slide at all.

It's pretty quiet and the sound from the TV covers up any small noises that it does make. One of the pedal straps (stirrups) is a little bit bent and hits the metal bar that the pedal is attached to, so it makes a tiny tapping sound, but I'm sure I can get the stirrup eventually to bend away so that doesn't happen. That noise is not a deal-breaker for me though. It's very quiet. The stirrups can be adjusted so if I move it to a different hole, that tapping would probably stop, but I haven't tried to move the stirrup yet because I'm afraid I'll break it since the stirrup plastic is a bit rigid.

All in all, I am completely happy with this purchase and if anything does eventually go wrong with the exerciser, I will update my review at that time. But right now I would say to definitely buy one if you want a simple way to exercise while watching TV!

ori_review: These blanks are awesome for anyone who wants to make their own honing set. They have leather stops available but I prefer to use something a little more rigid to help prevent rolling the edge of the blade, especially if it's a low angle. I built mine with MDF, carefully measuring the thickness to ensure it matches that of the other wicked edge stones, otherwise the angle would be slightly off and if you're spending the money on a wicked edge then you obviously want your angles perfect. Don't use an adhesive that's too permanent as you will likely wear the medium out and if it's permanently affixed you'll need a new set of blanks. I used hot glue for mine and they hold perfectly well and yet can be removed easily enough when the time comes. You'll be amazed at the mirror shine you can produce using MDF or balsa blanks and a bit of polish. W. E.  would kill me for saying this but you don't need the expensive diamond paste to get amazing results, Truth be told Ive been using the same polish I use for buffing out clear coat after wet sanding. query: I'm looking for a switch that has a bright indicator light but I need it to have consistent brightness across multiple units. I've noticed some switches have varying brightness due to the resistor placement, and I want to ensure that all my switches can be adjusted to match in brightness. Additionally, I want to modify the wiring so that the indicator light only turns on during the momentary on position, rather than when the switch is in the steady on position. Can you help me find a waterproof option that can withstand salt spray, especially for the internal components? I need it to pass inspection as well.
ori_review: Nice bright indicator light. I bought eight of these and in some of them the resistor was inside the switch on the negative side of the LED and strangely that made those ones brighter. I was able to move the spring and resistor matching the rest so that all of my switches were the same brightness. I also had to move the positive wire of the LED to only the momentary terminal so that my light only lit up when the pump had power.  The way they have the switch lit is so the light is on when it's in the on position and the light is also on when you're holding the switch in the momentary on position. But because of the way my system is wired I had to open the switch and move the positive leg of the LED so the light only came on when it was in the momentary on position, this way when it is in the steady on position the light was back fed through the system so the light would only come on when the automatic float came up that way we knew when the automatic system was pumping due to high water.  After this alteration it passes Coast Guard inspection. Only the outside of the switch is waterproof and actually has a o-ring on The Rocker to prevent water entry. The switch body underneath the dash and the terminals are not waterproof so if you have salt spray back there it will rot out the internals of the switch.

We bought the XL Sun Ninja Beach Tent to use for our family vacation at Nags Head on the NC Outer Banks. We’ve been vacationing here every summer for over 30 years and have tried more than a dozen types of beach tents from a variety of manufacturers. Every single one was eventually destroyed by the strong blustery winds that are common on the Outer Banks. To our delight and surprise our new Sun Ninja tent performed flawlessly! An unexpected thunderstorm (with wind gusts of over 35 mph according to the National Weather Service) did cause the tent to come down but the poles simply fell over gently with no damage whatsoever to the tent. When the storm passed we put the poles back in place and had the tent back up in less than a minute. This tent performs even BETTER than advertised and I recommend it it highly with no reservations.

Keith W., Durham, NC

The lure casts incredibly far which is why I believe it is one of the most effective surfcasting plugs for striper, it’s pretty much the ideal one size fits all type profile, as it’s not TOO big to completely alienate smaller schoolies, but it is a large enough profile to primarily target the bigger fish. query: I'm looking for a power tower that's great for the price. I need something that is easy to assemble and sturdy, especially for dips, pull-ups, and leg raises. I'm particularly interested in options that allow for adjustable pull-up bar height since my ceilings are not very high. I've seen some reviews mentioning issues with wobbling and the quality of the instruction manual. Can you tell me if this model has addressed those concerns, particularly regarding the dip bars and overall stability during workouts? I also wonder if the leg raise handles are suitable for taller users like myself. Thanks!
ori_review:
Definitely do recommend, especially for the money. There may be better options out there which cost more, but I'd buy this brand/model again if I needed another power tower. Below is my general write-up, plus final notes after my first workout with it.

*note: I'd add pics, and might later, but my phone won't allow it right now for some reason*

pros: - fairly easy to assemble - looks as advertised - all pieces including small pieces were accounted for (some reviews mentioned screws or larger pieces missing) - after my first workout, nothing bent out of place, there are no horrible wobbles or imbalances, it does what it was advertised to do - biggest thing for me was the ability to modify the pull-up bar height since I don't have high ceilings

Cons: - the English in the instruction manual is sketchy, but the illustrations were enough to allow easy assembly - the dip bars had some definite wiggle problems both horizontally and vertically when assembled and tightened (I was able to fix the horizontal wiggle with some extra washers which I'll explain later, and the vertical wiggle isn't a true issue since all your weight goes one direction) - the dip bars' vertical handles for leg/knee raises are pretty far forward. I have long arms and can see how shorter people would have issues grasping them while also having their backs on the backrest. However, I've done raises without handles to grasp at all before, so possibly it's not a make or break problem for people; also, you don't HAVE to have your back on the backrest to do those exercises, and I prefer not to [though that arguably makes the backrest worthless]. Newer versions of this power tower should include modifiable vertical handle lengths, but it's passable in my mind) - the wide grip part of the pull-up bar seems a little oddly placed to me, but I typically do closer, shoulder-width pull-ups anyway. I'll try some in my first workout and leave a review down below

Receiving and putting it together: I have to admit I was skeptical buying this especially after looking at 1 star and 2 star reviews of the various power towers out there. I've wanted a power tower for a little over a year mostly for dips but also pull-ups and leg raises. After a lot of researching, I decided to give this one a try (I had been using my door-frame pull-up bar before this [which is ok, but I wanted something I could use with the rest of my gym equipment outdoors]). It took a little while to be delivered, but that was understandable for something coming halfway around the world and during the pandemic. The box was pretty beat up when it did arrive, but all the pieces were in there and nothing had been damaged thankfully; everything was wrapped in individual plastic. I put this together within a couple of hours by myself. A few notes on that: 1) I definitely recommend putting the push-up bars on first instead of last. 2) the dip bars were super wobbly/wiggly when it was all put together. I took those back off and figured out a decent fix: I found 4 extra washers of the same approximate size and put them on the INSIDE of the dip bar screw areas (4 in total; I taped them into position with clear tape and then cut a small slit in the centers to allow the screw to pass through when re-assembling). Doing this stopped the horizontal wobbling completely and after tightening everything at the end of full assembly, it feels pretty sturdy. 3) if you lose a screw or some other small piece, you're going to have to replace it yourself as there are no extras in the box. I imagine you could if you had to, but it would be better if the makers included an extra bolt, washer, nut, etc. (I wouldn't mind paying another dollar or two for piece of mind).

1st workout with it: I weigh about 165-170 and am 5'11". I did 5 sets of back-to-back pull-ups, leg raises, push-ups, and dips. Pull-ups: I did a couple of sets holding out wide and it more or less felt fine. I'll probably stick with the shoulder-width ones I'm used to, but it wasn't really uncomfortable holding out wide. No wobbling from tower. Leg raises: definitely cannot both put my back on the backrest AND hold the vertical handles. I opted to hold the vertical handles without my back on the backrest and it was fine for me, but it does mean the backrest is mostly worthless in this scenario. I tried putting my back on the backrest and not holding h handles, but without the forearm pads canted inwards, I couldn't comfortably do the exercise. *This doesn't mean I find it unusable by any means; in fact, I'd rather keep my back off the back rest as that's how I learned how to do the exercise anyway years ago.* I still think future versions need to either have the handles recessed back a few inches or for them to be modifiable to be users' arm length. Push-ups: the handles didn't bend under my weight even though I was worried they might. The fit between the handle and the bar beneath it isn't quite snug though, so they tend to push out a couple centimeters, but it definitely doesn't make them unusable. A little padding in the gap would clear that up and I might try a couple layers of athletic tape later. They work just fine for me now though. Dips: same as with the pull-ups, I was hoping the dip handles would hold during the exercise...and they did without fail. No wobbling, wiggling; I'm happy that one of the main reasons I bought this power tower came through. Note: my wife weighs a bit more than me and it held her weight as well (about 200). I plan to do my future workouts with a 20 lb weight vest.

Final thoughts: I might tighten a couple screws after my first workout, but that was to be expected with some movement during its first-ever use. I might take the forearm pads apart and re-pad them so they bow upwards on the outside to give them some cant inwards (so my elbows/forearms don't want to try and slip off when they get sweaty.) The rubber grips will probably fall apart with repeated use over time (as anything rubbery does with sweat and use), but I'll probably end up re-gripping them with athletic tape and maybe some tennis racquet grip when that happens. Besides a couple things I've mentioned (which can be fixed in later versions and doesn't make the current version unusable), this is everything I was hoping for in a power tower.

I'm really happy for what I paid and received. I'll purchase this again, or recommend it to others, in a heartbeat.

I'll update this review if anything detrimental happens

ori_review:
I purchased this pack a few months ago and have taken it on about 20 mountain bike rides ranging between 8 and 42 miles in southern AZ (cross-country riding). Most rides have been in the 10-15 mile range. I researched this pack before purchasing it and one of the complaints was that it didn't hold enough water for longer rides. I agree that if you were relying only on the bladder it comes with, you would certainly need more water for longer rides; however, you can fit two more water bottles in the outer carriers of the pack and two more in bottle cages on your frame. With this combination, I ended up with nearly a gallon of water on the 42-mile epic. There was enough room in the pack to carry tire repair tools including 2 co2 cartridges, a portable hand pump, an extra tube, a few snacks, and a burrito.

I went from a using a traditional backpack to this one because I wanted to keep the weight off my back due to lower back issues. The pack has worked great for this and I've been able to use my hardtail more! The pack is comfortable to the point it's easy to forget it's even there. I've hit a few extended bumpy downhill sections where the pack has flopped up and down a bit, but have found that's a pretty rare occurrence. In all fairness, I have not messed with the adjustable pull straps to make the pack tighter for going downhill. My only complaint about this pack is similar to other reviews I read in that the water straw is not easy to re-secure while riding. Like others, I resolved this problem by purchasing a retractable ID Badge/Key holder. I've had no issues accessing the straw or securing it since then. The magnet that secures the straw to the pack is pretty much useless if you ride twisty trails and you drink water while pedaling. I'm very happy with this pack and it's my go-to for the type of riding I do.

query: I'm looking for a stable and easy-to-install bike rack for my car that can securely hold two bikes during long trips. What steps should I take to ensure proper installation and adjustment of the straps? Are there any tips for preventing the bikes from moving or spinning while driving, especially during windy conditions? Also, how might I manage access to my trunk while using the rack for longer journeys? Lastly, I'm considering investing in a hitch rack for added convenience—would this setup still be useful for other vehicles like rentals or zip cars?
ori_review:
So the first install is something you should do before you and your family / friends are standing around the car ready to load and go. Take your time to first get the two top straps to the right length and figure out how it all goes together. Then the side and bottom straps fall into place.
Many talk of taping the clips but the fabric loop keeps all but the contact area away from the paintwork.
I took this on 2200 miles of interstates with two bikes attached firmly throughout. I checked the straps at each rest stop, the sway ones can loosen slightly in strong crosswinds (so a quick tug retightened them) but the top ones and bottom ones did not budge.
I also added bungees between the bike frame and front wheel to stop it spinning and keep the handlebars straight, on one of my bikes if I did not do that the wheel turned until the car trunk stopped it.
Alternating bikes so the front wheels point left right and similarly looking to have the pedals horizontal then vertical can make getting bikes back to back on the frame much easier.
With this on don't expect to open your trunk or use your rear wash wipe (on a SUV/hatch), not such a big deal for a short trip but for a longer journey this can be awkward.
I'll probably invest in a hitch now as they are fairly easy to do yourself and $100-200 to give more convenience (no need to add the electrical connections). Even though that is the plan this will hang around for other peoples cars, zip cars etc.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable double sleeping bag that I can use for car camping with my family. I want to know how spacious it really is for two adults and a baby, and if it's easy to pack back into the stuff sack after use. Are there any tips for rolling it up efficiently? I read mixed reviews about that, but I want to ensure it's manageable. Also, I'm curious if it holds up well in colder temperatures like 32 degrees. Can anyone share their experience?
ori_review: So there I was excited to use my new Teton Mammoth sleeping back with my wife and daughter. We get the bag out, fluff it a little to let it reach it's maximum "fluff status" and add in the sleeping bag liner(which I'd give 4 stars, needs a way to anchor in at the bag so it doesn't get tangled). The three of us get in to test it out and see how roomy it is.. and might I say.. it's roomy! Granted I'm only 5'8" 165, my wife is only 5'3" 115 and my daughter is only 1 year old but we could fit baby number 2 when it comes and still be comfortable. When the fun is all had, I was mentally prepared to wrestle this sleeping for the next hour to get it back in the bag after reading several reviews stating how difficult it is to get back in. My wife is pregnant so she took care of the insert while I single handedly slew the Mammoth. I folded it in half hot dog style and flattened it to let out the air and kept all the corners together and then I started rolling the sleeping bag using my hands and knees keeping the air out as I rolled. I grabbed the stuff sack it came with and guess what???? It slid right in! 5 minutes...  5 minutes! I was blown away at how easy it was, and I did it myself... I wonder if some of these people on here have ever rolled a sleeping bag before? I wonder if they've even rolled their own socks, I'm sorry for those it took an hour and a half to get this back in the bag, I'm surprised you even found the campsite. The sleeping bag is great, it's comfy and we are excited to try it out this weekend in 32 degree weather. I'll update this if I find that the wild somehow changes the sleeping bag, or perhaps my intelligence. If you are looking for a relatively inexpensive sleeping bag to cuddle with your significant other while in the great outdoors, this a great purchase(car camping only, I would never attempt to backpack with this beast). Please, take a moment and come up with a game plan before attempting, perhaps practice rolling empty garbage bags if you must, it's not that hard.

query: I'm looking for brake pads that perform well and offer great value, especially with a focus on the Sintered Metal version. I've previously used Copper-Based pads, but they wore out quickly and caused rotor wear. I want pads that provide more mileage and maintain performance without fading or making noise. Can you recommend pads that meet these criteria and are compatible with hydraulic Tektro HD-E 350s on an e-bike?
ori_review:
Updated 3/30/2023 for Sintered Metal version
The new compound is fantastic! There were minor things on the Copper-Based that were easy to live with for the performance. First, the brake material was thinner and backing plate was thicker than OEM. Overall they were under 4mm total. You got less mileage. Also, the Copper-Based did take their toll on rotors. My rear stock TR-24 (180-24) rotor lasted just over 2,000 miles before it was approaching the 1.5mm replacement point (1.55mm at thinnest point).

The Sintered Metal have more braking material, a backing plate closer to OEM, and an overall thickness just the tiniest bit over 4mm. Significantly more mileage (over 900 versus 500-600) with all the things we loved about the Copper-Based. The edges do seem a little more brittle, so go easy on wheel changes! Still, I have to say the Sintered Metal are my choice now for this pad form factor.

Full disclosure: I was provided a set (4 pads) of Sintered by Corki when I inquired about the compound change. I have since purchased a set (4 pads) as well.

Original review of Copper-Based:
Purchased the Copper-Based pads to replace A10.11 OEM pads for hyraulic Tektro HD-E 350s on an Ariel Rider Kepler ebike. I had used 0.2mm of the original pads and had enough of their turkey gobbler call when heated up.

These Corki Copper-Based pads perform superbly. No more fade and odd sounds by heat buildup. They bring my 26" x 4" wheels, on 90lbs of bike with super grippy slicks, and 225lbs of me, to a quick, controlled stop from 32mph.

Whisper quiet stopping with no fade. Do not wait to replace cheap OEM pads. Put these in now!

ori_review:
Folks don't buy this without an air pump. This tube is fun, but it is BIG!!!!. About 13 feet or so when inflated. It is also pretty heavy when it's dry, and really heavy when it is wet. We have a 27 foot boat and it is a small feat of engineering to inflate and deflate the tube out on the water. It is three separate air chambers. the main chamber uses a Boston valve. The two side chambers have built in one way valves, so you will need multiple attachments for the pump.

The quality is very high and the materials are very robust. It'll last a long time with some basic TLC. It is surprisingly stable with three of fewer riders, but becomes less so when you tack on 5. query: I'm looking for a portable umbrella that has a solid construction and performs well in light rain and wind. I noticed that some umbrellas can be a bit small, so I'm curious about the size and whether it can keep my legs and shoes dry in windy conditions. How does this umbrella handle wind and rain? Also, does it have any features that help it shed water easily, like a hydrophobic coating?
ori_review:
Disclaimer: I haven't been able to use the umbrella under very rainy conditions.

I got to pull out the umbrella for the first time today in a light drizzle with some fair wind. The umbrella is definitely a bit smaller than my previous one; I hadn't taken measurements of it but it was probably more so the 60'' ones. This one for me at 5'9" meant my shins and shoes would get slightly wet if there was any wind. Not a big deal, but just letting people know.

The construction feels extremely solid. The action is smooth, and especially when pushing the umbrella back in, you can feel the pole being a snug, well-lubricated fit, i.e. when you push down on the umbrella to fold it back up it slides very smoothly. My old umbrella's pole would noticeably wobble back and forth when folding it back up, so this was a welcome change.

It definitely does very well in wind. I intentionally turned it to catch the wind and see how it did, and the legs all flexed but did not give! The wind was pretty gentle but gives me hope. Its ability to do this without the flaps that let the wind pass is particularly impressive.

Definitely deflected rain itself pretty well, and seemed to have come home drier than I expected, probably meaning the rain slid off of it more easily than it did my old umbrella. Seems to suggest at either a smoother surface that doesn't let water collect or a hydrophobic coating that lets water slide off more easily. In any case great there too!

query: I'm looking for a trim tab system that can enhance the performance of my boat, particularly in terms of getting on plane easily and improving handling. I've heard that certain models can eliminate bow lift and increase top speed, even in rough conditions. Can anyone share their experiences with trim tabs that have transformed their boat's handling and overall ride quality? I'm particularly interested in how they perform in choppy water and whether they truly deliver on claims of improved speed and comfort.
ori_review: Ordered smart tab sx from Trim Tab Girl on amazon. Arrived in a flash from those gals. About an hour to install on an Alumacraft Trophy 17. The nylon bolts used in the pivot locations seem inadequate at first but turn out to be fairly tough, I guess I am used to stainless hardware around boats and will change them out at the first sign of fatigue. I used quick set 3m 5200 to seal the screws and injected some into the screw holes before installation. I let everything cure for 24 hours then off to the lake to test. First I want to point out that my Alumacraft was no dog when it came to handling and is as fine and predictable little craft that ever made the waterway.  BUT, I could not get over how effortless I got on plane and how well the boat handled. In fact when I slowed down to around 14 mph I was still planing!  Bow lift was pretty much eliminated as well. I admit I was skeptical about the claims of increased top end speed but there it was on the gps. 3 mph over my former top speed in a 2 ft. chop. Impressive.  The overall feel of the boat changed as well. Cushy is how I would describe it. Like a luxury car sort of thing.  My hull is on the rounded side of things and would roll with the waves taken side-on while drift fishing. I was hoping the smart tabs would dampen this effect and they did to a degree. So few things I have bought in the past lived up to the hype that I have become the ultimate product skeptic. In my opinion the manufacturer downplayed the effect the Smart Tabs would have on my boat, for they proved out or exceeded every claim made...in spades. Are these the cure-all/end-all for a poor handling craft? Probably not. But I will go on the record and say they are the best money I have ever spent on any accessory for a boat. There is a huge bang for your buck here.

query: I'm looking for a blowup mattress that is easy to set up and stow away. I need one that distributes air evenly to prevent bulging and that allows for comfortable sleeping alongside another person without feeling every movement. I also want to know how it compares to regular blowup mattresses. Can you recommend a product that meets these criteria, especially for camping or hosting guests?
ori_review:
If you're looking for a sign, this is the one! This is the most incredible blowup mattress I have every owned. Setting it up and stowing it away is truly a breeze. Once I laid it out flat I was able to pump it up with my foot is less and 60 seconds. The first night we took this for a spin we joined another couple who brought a tall, queen size blowup mattress. But what is the difference in this product and a regular blowup mattress? The design! The "drawstring" design to be exact. Blowup mattresses are notorious for being completely flat, so when pressure is applied to one side, it makes the opposite side swell as the air distributes to that end. Because this mattress is a bunch of mini-cushions separated by these little ripples, it allows air to be distributed evenly around where pressure is applied. This prevents any other part of the mattress from bulging. This designs makes sleeping next to someone less annoying bc you aren't feeling every single movement the other person makes. We think this is such a great mattress that we will use it in the event we have company but not enough spots to sleep. Put this on the floor and pair it with a pillow and a blanket and this thing is better than 30% of bed mattresses on the market today.

We paired this with Amazon's sleeping bag, "MEREZA Double Sleeping Bag for Adults" and experienced luxury camping for an exceptionally affordable price. As an avid reviewer, this product receives my highest recommend, and is in the top 5 best products I purchased from Amazon in 2022.

ori_review:
I only recently got into surf fishing, and needed a good knife after the more expensive knife I had didn't fair to well trying to process a 5 foot blacktip last year. I don't remember the name of the knife I was using but it cost me around $75. It didn't hold an edge, and had to be sharpened at least 5 times while processing the shark.

So with another family beach trip looming, and the hope of catching something worthwhile, I started hunting for what would hopefully be a better replacement. Knowing my propensity for tearing up or losing gear, and the fact that in a year I maybe get to make 2 or 3 trips to to the beach, I was looking to spend as little as possible.

I read several positive reviews of this knife, and the price was very reasonable if it performed as well as the reviews would lead one to believe. The knife came pretty sharp, but not quite shaving sharp. When it comes to my work knives I'm very particular about having a razor edge, as my life and others could depend on it (LEO). I gave it a run it over one of my finer whet stones, and then gave it a nice stropping. It took the edge very quickly, and after that it would shave the hair off my arm with only the weight of the knife.

So off to the beach I went. Let me tell you I was not disappointed. Caught a 37 inch bull red and as you can see in the picture I was thrilled. Other than shark this is the biggest game fish I've taken surf fishing. The knife performed great. Even after processing the fish. The knife still had a razor sharp edge. I processed several other smaller fish including 2 smaller bonnet head sharks and it still has a decent edge that only needed to be retouched after I got home.

I also really like the sheath. it has nice belt slots on it that work great with a web belt. The sheath has a positive click to tell you it's in and a solid retention. The handle it very soft and comfortable with a positive grip surface that doesn't fatigue your hands. I plan on getting several other KastKing products to try out.

query: I'm looking for a saddle that can provide comfort for riders with wider sit bones, as my current saddle is causing pain and numbness. I was initially attracted to this saddle because it is one of the few saddles available that seems to keep riders with wider sit bones comfortable. I bought this saddle to replace the Specialized 'Body Geometry' saddle that came that came with my new Rockhopper, that was causing me to have pain and some numbness. This saddle instantly eliminated all of the pain and numbness that came as a result of the old saddles rounded top profile that was putting pressure between my sit bones. The Purve V has a very flat profile that hence its name has a consistent V taper from front to back. This allows the Pure V, with proper adjustment, to hit the sit bones correctly for a much broader range of riders than the rounded racing style saddles that are meant to hinder the legs less. Yet, chaffing and leg pressure has not been an issue for me on 60+ mile rides.

As a bonus the Pure V is padded with a firm and supportive material that is neither too thick nor thin, that provides just the right amount of padding to make this saddle very comfortable to ride long distances even without a chamois. This is the only saddle Ive ridden to date that has made effective use of the "love channel" that alleviates pressure between the sit bones that might be caused by the slight cushiness of this saddle. I would definitely recommend this saddle to anyone looking for a solid versatile and comfortable saddle.

query: I'm looking for a power cage for my home garage gym that can accommodate various workouts, including cable exercises. I want to ensure it has enough space for my adjustable bench and Olympic weight plates. Additionally, I'm concerned about the stability when racking heavy weights and whether I need to secure it to the ground. Are there any recommendations for products that offer versatility and durability while addressing these concerns?
ori_review:
I am very satisfied with this purchase and cannot express how great having a rack at home in my garage feels. I researched quite a bit of racks and went between two that I really liked. Both had the same specs and attachments. An added bonus for my indecisiveness was that the orange rack became available and now I have the orange cage with lat cable attachment. I purchased additional cable accessories to go with the cable attachment and it has increased the amount of accessory exercises I can do to accommodate my daily workouts.
It took my son and I about an hour to put it together using the whole garage while it was raining outside with no issues.
I currently use a separate adjustable bench from my old setup with plenty of room inside the cage. Using the 2” Olympic weight plate adapter on the weight holders do not have enough spacing vertically to be able to slide them off quickly without having to remove the top or bottom. I am considering building a platform to secure the cage to and limit the amount of movement I get when I have to rack the weight a little more aggressively when it’s heavy.
Everything I mentioned is pretty minor and doesn’t stop me from performing what I want, when I want, and without having to tailor my workouts at a local gym.

Good things to note:
Color: Orange
Versatility: Use of cable attachment adds extra advantages of muscle building
Durability: Metal components are lightweight and can hold up to the amount advertised
Structure: Many of the load bearing components interlock and give peace of mind to safety and security of the cage
Setup: 1 hr build time; all components came in two separate shipments within an hour of each other, no missing or damaged pieces, shipment time was 2 weeks

Things to be aware of:
Olympic Weight Holder: Does not have enough vertical spacing between the large 45lb bumpers and smaller weight dimensions
Structure: Cage will shift when racking moderate (225lbs) to heavy weight if not secured to the ground; is not a cause for concern if you rack weights with control
Durability: The steel used is light weight and soft, meaning when you tighten the bolts it tends to warp or dent the steel if you over tighten
Lat Machine attachment: Did not come with any lubrication; consider using mechanics grease to help the weight sled slide freely. The sled can handle heavy weight as advertised however you have to keep the weight proportional on both sides to allow the weights to slide properly or else you get an offset feel of the weight as you pull
Paint: Will scrape off as you slide the safety bars through the insert holes or if you rack above the J Hook, but not an issue if you are okay letting everyone see how much you actually use your equipment
Attachments: Very light having a plastic feel; instead ordered a new metal set; worth it!

query: I'm looking for rechargeable hand warmers that are effective and easy to use. I want to know if they come with a USB power supply or if I need to purchase one separately. Also, can you provide clear instructions on how to charge them and adjust the heat settings? I need something that will work well for both me and my elderly mother.
ori_review:
These Really Do Work Well. Solidly built. Stick one in each jacket pocket and my bony hands become happy fast. Got my 96 year old mom a pair too. The instructions are poor but adequate; obviously originated in a different language. Comes with 'Y" style double ended power cord but DOES NOT COME with the USB power supply! You need at least a 1.2A USB power supply. 2A is better. Many phone chargers will do the job. I wrote these instructions (but with photos) for mom:

Charging
With the Hand-Warmer turned off,
Plug-in the small connectors into each hand-warmer as shown.
Next, plug-in the power supply into the wall outlet.
When the unit is charging you will see 3 blue lights blinking and streaming forward. When the unit is fully charged, all three lights are lit and remain steady.

Turn On
Turn-ON by pressing the orange button and holding for about 3 seconds until a small red light comes on. I find it works best if I press directly in the middle of the button with a fingernail.

Adjust Heat Low Medium High
Press the button briefly (about a second) to change the temperature. Each press will advance the temperature one step
1 red light means LOW
2 red lights mean Medium
3 red lights mean High

Turn Off
Turn-OFF by pressing the orange button and holding for about 2 seconds until the small red lights disappear. I find it works best if I press directly in the middle of the button with a fingernail.

query: I'm looking for a pedal exerciser that can fit under my desk, ideally something easy to assemble and heavy enough to stay in place while I use it. I need it to have adjustable tension settings for a comfortable workout while I'm working on my computer, and it would be great if it has a digital display to track my progress. Also, I'm concerned about the design—does it slide around easily, and how do I manage the battery life for the digital display? Any tips or advice would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Assembly of this unit was simple. There is a wrench tool included to tighten the bolts. This unit is kind of heavy, which is great because if it were too light, it would slide around too easily. I spend so much time in front of the computer that it had affected my health because I wasn't getting any exercise in. With this device, there is no excuse. It fits perfectly under my desk (make sure to compare dimensions of the height of this item to your desk). I have a clearance of 23 1/2" and it has been just enough height for me to use this comfortably. I have roller chairs so purchasing something like [[ASIN:B000X8X58S Slipstick CB840 3-1/4 Inch Bed Roller / Furniture Wheel Gripper Caster Cups (Set of 4) Caramel Color]] was essential for securing my chair in place while using this exercise bike under my table without my chair rolling all over the place.

The different tension resistances are nice and click into place easily. Even at the highest setting, the resistance does not seem too bad and I can easily cycle if I'm pedaling slowly. If I pedal quickly at the highest tension setting, I'll start to build up a sweat after not too long, but if you're in the workplace using this, you probably don't want to go all out and smell like you just got out of the gym around your co-workers. At home alone, I can get in my workout in the morning while working on the computer and then just shower before heading to work. It's perfect for my needs. The non-slip feet seem to hold it securely in place on my chairmat with the edge of the unit against the wall. If I did not have it against the wall, it might slide around a little more than I'd probably like. A simple solution would be to place some strong double-sided tape along the bottom of the rubber feet. The digital display is powered by 2 AAA batteries and it is attached to the cycle so it is not removable. Also, there doesn't seem to be an on/off switch to the LED display so you'll have to remove your batteries when it's not in use to save on your battery life. However, if you leave the batteries in, it'll turn off by itself after about 5 minutes of inactivity. Likewise, if you leave the batteries in and the unit is off, the digital reader will turn on by itself and start measuring your activity if you start cycling. If I'm just cycling and don't care about the stats, I just leave the digital display alone with the batteries out. The foot straps securely hold your feet in place. Overall, the many benefits of this outweigh the minor design drawbacks. This is easily one of the best investments I've made.

Pros
-Adjustable tension easily clicks into place
-Digital device measures progress
-Easy assembly
-Footstraps hold feet in securely
-Quiet

Cons
-Must remove batteries to turn off digital device
-May slide around if not secured with tape or backed against wall

query: I'm looking for a kick scooter that offers a very smooth ride and good shocks for going over curbs and pavement cracks. I've used several adult scooters before, and I want one that's lightweight, easy to fold, and durable. It would also be ideal if it has good push efficiency and reliable brakes, although I’m aware that some scooters may have better braking systems. Can you recommend a scooter that meets these criteria, even if it's a bit more expensive than basic models?
ori_review:
I have ridden many scooters built for adults over the years. In particular, I owned the adult Razor (with big wheels), two xootr scooters and this one. I rode each regularly (at least two trips per week and at least a distance of 3/4 mile per trip) for over a year. I would have to say this one is my favorite.

Pro:
- Very smooth ride. I love the shocks for going up and down curbs and across pavement cracks that litter the ground where I live. They take a lot of pressure off the knees, especially relative to the adult razor. This is by far my favorite attribute of the scooter.
- fast. the wheels spin very well and you will find you get quite far per push. I would say its push efficiency is better than the razors though maybe not quite as good as the xootrs, but close. they are all pretty efficient, though
- light weight. it is very easy to pick up and put down. This is especially important relative to the heavy xootr scooters I rode. I usually use scooters in combination with public transportation and something clunky
- durability. This one is much more durable than the razor scooters, which always seem to become V-shaped after you hit enough curbs; The locking mechanism on the razors is not as sturdy as the locking mechanism on this scooter. I am quite satisfied
- Ease of fold: it is very easy to fold. Even easier than the razor, because you just have to step on something rather than reach down and fold it. Also easier than the xootr.

Con:
- It is a little more expensive than the razor. But, I think the difference is well worth it (at time of purchase, adult razors ~ 70-80 vs this was 110-120.) It is much, much cheaper than the xootrs.
- Brakes are better on the xootr, especially if you get the front squeeze brake installed for xootr. I would say this scooter can sometimes go too fast for its own good. You do have to be careful to slow down around hidden driveways and intersections, because at full speed this scooter does take a little bit to stop. But, it's never been a problem for me. Just be safe and pay attention to your surroundings.

All-in-all its a great buy at a very reasonable price point for what you get relative to other scooters on market

query: I'm looking for an exercise solution that allows me to stay active while working or gaming at my computer. I spend a lot of time sitting, and I need something compact that can fit under my desk. It has limitations in that it is pretty low to the ground and it's not a full size exercise bike, but the limitations haven't prevented it from giving me a good workout.  I was very concerned with the short crank arms (the arms the pedals are connected to), but it seems fine.  The motion is very smooth, and also very quiet. One of the limitations is that it's very low to the ground and compact, so there isn't much room between the pedal and the floor.  To get around this I usually take off my shoes and then it's not an issue.  I'm using it at home, so that's no big deal for me.  I am also pretty tall ~6'2" and have ~12 size feet, so your mileage may vary.  Another gripe I have is that the resistance between 2 and 3 seems pretty big, but I'm also out of shape, so I dunno.  This may also vary slightly from unit to unit.  As it is though, there are 8 settings and I have only used the first 3 so far.  It really gives a good workout though, like my old recumbent stationary bike I used to use (which I don't have room for right now). It is actually like a compact, high quality stationary bike without the seat--great! I also tried some of the cheap ones, and I'm glad I invested the money for this one--like I said--it's really like having a proper stationary bike, I just use my office chair with a towel on it when I use the desk cycle.  Overall I would say it's worth the money, although the foot clearance is a bit of an issue (so I take my shoes off), and the resistance settings are not as fine tuned as I would prefer, but I'm very happy with this thing.  I can't comment on how long it will last since I've only had it a week or so, but it is sturdy, and seems built to last. query: I'm looking for a baitcasting reel that can handle heavier setups for fishing in the Florida intracoastal and also serve as a lighter option for surf fishing. I want something that casts well with a 9' rod and can easily manage smaller fish like winter bluefish. I'm particularly interested in features like a smooth drag adjustment, good casting distance, and durability after exposure to saltwater. Are there any models similar to the Millionaire Classic that would meet these needs? Also, how do I handle the spool release to avoid straining the anti-reverse mechanism? Any recommendations would be appreciated!
ori_review:
This is the tried and true Millionaire Classic with new colors and carbon fiber drag.

I bought this to fish as a heavier setup for the Florida intracoastal and light setup for the surf. My main surf reels are Daiwa Sealine x30sha but I wanted something lighter to put on a 9' rod to fish the first trough. I have only caught a few winter bluefish between 11" and 18" so far but the reel handled them easily.

The new color scheme is black and it looks great on the all metal body and the gold spool tensioner. Everything is smooth and the drag adjustment turns nicely.

I can cast 73 yards on a 9' rod, 4 oz sinker, stock greased bearings, and with the line leveler in place. It feels very fast though, and if you cleaned the bearings and removed the line leveler I think you could easily cast over 100. I have my Sealines for long casting though so I'm leaving this as is.

The size is comparable to an Abu Garcia 6000 series. You can see the comparison to my larger reels in the pictures.

The only issue - and this is for all reels with a bar and/or button release (as opposed to clutch switch) - is that you need to use your thumb to roll the spool back a little before you put it into free spool if you are using heavy rigs. Otherwise, it feels to me like you are putting extra strain on the anti reverse.

I did open it up to add extra grease to the main gears but they were already well greased. Looked clean inside.

I've had it to the beach a few times, and with a fresh water rinse afterwards, it seems to be holding up just fine.

Highly recommend.

query: I'm looking for a pannier set that is suitable for commuting rather than touring. Can anyone provide details on their experience with the Seymour LX panniers, especially regarding their mounting stability, water resistance, and overall usability? I'd also like to know if they have any features for easy access to items like tools or first aid supplies, and if they are better than other models in terms of design and functionality. Additionally, do they come with any external webbing or rain covers?
ori_review:
just to help other people without them having to check the web for the volumes of the various axiom panniers, since i looked them all up i figured i would save you all the trouble:

pannier volumes:
Seymour LX [this set]
1700c" (27.85L) per pair
Seymour DLX 30
1830c" (30L) per pair
Lasalle DLX 45
1830c" (30L) per pair
Cartier DLX 35
2013c" (33L) per pair
Kootenay DLX
2441c" (40L) per pair
Champlain DLX 60
3000c" (49L) per pair

that said, i also own this set and love em. they mount pretty decently to my rear axiom rack as well as my front jim blackburn rack. you have to pull pretty firmly to release the clips, which is good because my last set of panniers kept leaping off.

so far the bottom bungee is holding well. its thinner than the other pannier models bungees, but with repeated removal the bungee like any of them will stretch so you will have to eventually replace it.

the bungee on this model is the same size as the one on the appalachian set, it took a good 3 years of constant removal for those to lose all of their elasticity though but they still hold, they just no longer stretch.

like any non-rubber pannier set these are water RESIS|TANT but by no means water-proof. if you intend on using them in downpours, plan accordingly and either use dry sacks on the inside or buy or make exteriour rain covers.

waterproofing sprays will eventually wear off, which is just a "feature" of waterproofing sprays.

query: I'm looking for a hitch-mounted bike rack that can accommodate various bike sizes without needing constant adjustments. I want something that allows for quick loading and unloading and has a secure locking mechanism. I've considered options like the Thule 917XT, Yakima Holdup, and Saris Cycle On Pro, but I need to ensure it fits my needs for transporting different types of bikes, including mountain and children's bikes. Can you help me find a rack that meets these criteria?
ori_review:
I purchased this rack on Amazon and got the best deal out there for $340 and free shipping. I would have gone with the 916XT, but unfortunately, my car only had a capacity for a class II hitch, so 917XT it was!

I lamented for days over the Thule 917XT, Yakima Holdup and Saris Cycle On Pro. All of the racks have disadvantages and advantages depending on your application. I chose the Thule for a bunch of reasons, but the one which made the biggest difference was being able to load/unload different style bikes in seconds(Mountain, Beach, BMX, Larger Children's bikes) without having to adjust the front wheel mount. The Yakima seemed to be a one size fits all with the flip down tire mount which didn't seem to be what I needed for my application given it would be me and one of my kids bikes which range in all different sizes. I liked the Yakima's compact size when folded up, but I also had concerns should the mount wiggle loose and having it damage my car. The Saris Cycle On has an excellent price point and great hitch lock/tightening feature that I really liked, BUT, if I was carrying anything less than a 26in bike, I had to adjust the front wheel mount by unscrewing bolts and moving the mount to the smaller adjustment to accomodate the smaller tire up to a 20in. This was too much work for what I needed and I would have potentially been changing this every other day.

All three racks have a no touch frame grab bar, that only makes contact with the front tire. This is invalueable if you cherish your bikes finish OR have an expensive bike where you could potentially damage the top tube when using similar racks like the Yakima Stickup or Thule Doubletrack which are about $100 cheaper. I also liked the fact that I could adjust the angle and position of the tire grab bar. The Yakima is identical to the Thule and the Saris is fixed position. I liked that all of the racks had a security locking device and the 917XT came WITH the hitch STL2 hitchlock and locking cylinders for the grab bars. Remember that these are only deterrents and a determined thief can get it if they want it bad enough. A lot of reviewers dinged the rack in the security aspect which I don't believe is fair. If its that important, take extra measures by buying additonal cable locks if you intend on leaving your bikes on the rack unattended for an extended period of time.

The Thule rack is fantastic all around. I load my bike(s) quickly and they don't move. It only takes seconds to load and you are off. The rack tilts up when not in use and will tilt down to access the trunk/liftgate with the bikes still loaded on the rack. It was well worth the money. I did have a beef with how it the package was treated when being shipped as the box was crushed and the end split open. One of the cross bars was chipped, but it wasn't worth sending it back as I would have incurred shipping charges to return it for such a small blemish. Nevertheless, I give this rack 5 stars for its ease of operation and features that fit what I needed. You can go to Youtube and look at a side by side comparison which was VERY helpful for me...looking at a picture is one thing, but watching the pros who sell these things all day long do a demo is priceless in seeing what you are getting.

If not for my different bike size dilemma, I would have purchase the Saris Cycle On Pro as a side note. It had what I was looking for and was $100 cheaper with free shipping on Amazon ($247), I just couldn't justify constantly changing the mount by unbolting it.
