The phone uses GPS to track my movements so I expect it to be more accurate, which it generally is, but I didn't want to spend a whole lot of money, so I bought this very basic, cost effective, pedometer.

When I carry the Neskla 3D Pedometer AND the phone with the app, and compare steps, the steps for the longer walks (5 km/3 mi) are most closely matched, being less than 50 steps different, with the pedometer collecting the lower number.

Based on movements around the house or office, which tend to be shorter spurts of activity, the difference increases because the Neskla is measuring movement in a different manner, not counting if it thinks you took less than 10 steps, etc. I think that as long as you know that, you can get a rough idea of your daily activity even if the step count doesn't precisely match your actual step count.

It comes with a belt clip and a lanyard. I usually wear it around my neck so I don't leave it in a pocket and send it through the wash by accident. One other feature I appreciate is that because it doesn't measure my activity as accurately as the GPS kind of pedometers do, it allows me to let go of my obsessiveness on the subject and just take a general view of my activity throughout the day. Overall, this unit is exactly what I wanted. It's small, it measures steps satisfactorily enough, and it's very affordable.

I've worn it for a grand total of about 12 miles so far, just trying to dial in the fit and the comfort level, so I won't be able to speak to long-term durability yet, but I'm confident I can provide a solid overview of this pack. Inside the pack, even though the fabric is waterproof, the seams aren't taped so I line it with a trash compactor bag. A sleeping bag, clothes bag, sleeping pad, and puffy jacket fit nicely squeezed into the bottom. I usually carry an Ursack inside a waterproof sea to summit ultrasil bag that includes my food and cook kit just above the other stuff in the middle of the pack. For now, the tent is in the pack next to the food bag, but I imagine I'll have to carry it on the outside after a wet night. What you see in the first picture is the bag packed with all of those items and it fits extremely well. The outside zippered pocket includes my toilet kit and my tent stakes. Behind that front pocket is my ditty bag and a polycryo groundsheet for my tent, as can be seen in the picture. One of the side pockets is a little taller than the others, which is probably where I will keep a wet tent, but both side pockets easily hold 1-liter smart water bottles as shown. You can't see it, but my Katadyn BeFree water filter is in the side pocket with one of the water bottles. The Z-seat nicely sits on the top under the strap and my trowel is on a carabiner hanging off a daisy chain on one side. Arranged this way, the pack is as comfortable as any I've ever worn, including my GG Crown2. I've not fully loaded it down with water but I can't imagine those last few pounds would make much of a difference. The only problem I've run into has been the hipbelt slipping down a bit after a couple of miles, where I have to make an adjustment or cinch or pretty tight to keep it from sliding. I'll update the review once I've gotten a hundred or miles on it and revisit the durability but at the moment it seems like one hell of a tough pack. Oh, and one last thing about the hip belt pockets. They are just barely big enough to fit my iPhone XR, but the zippers are sort of closer to the middle of the pouch than the top. It DOES NOT detect heart attacks. Anyhow, I recently used my Kardia 6L to record some PVCs I was having, (Skipped Beats). What I had captured is nearly 30 seconds of Bigeminy PVC's. I am told not to worry about these Bigeminy beats, but it's hard to do! I follow up with an Echocardiogram and Treadmill test in a few days. query: I'm looking for a small, adjustable focus LED flashlight that uses AAA batteries. I want something bright but don't necessarily need multiple brightness settings. I've seen some flashlights that have zoom features, but I’m curious if this one also allows for easy zooming. I’ve read mixed things about the brightness levels and whether they truly change, so I’d like to know more about its performance and if it’s reliable for regular use.
ori_review:
I've got about a dozen LED flashlights - most bought that way and some are retrofits (a Maglite, a Rayovac, and a 1st gen SnakeLight). They vary in brightness from 30 or so lumens up to 800 lumens. My favorite is my EDC (every day carry) Mini MLR2 that's 1/2 inch shorter than my chapstick and has 7 settings, including a high setting of 180 lumens. I'm currently jonesin' for a $120 L3 K40 with 1147 lumens and 700 meter beam distance - that thing is FRIGGIN' AWESOME! Now, I'm no flashaholic . . . ok - scratch that. I guess my point is that even though I didn't need this little adjustable focus, 3 aaa, cree led flashlight, and it doesn't do everything the description says it would do, and it has middle of the road brightness (compared to other led lights), I STILL love it. Just like a $3 bottle of Oak Leaf Pinot Grigio from Walmart, for $9.90 this flashlight was nearly guaranteed to please. Admittedly, as long as it didn't short-circuit and cook my fingers like grilled kielbasa, I was probably going to like it. Using only 3 aaa batteries, this thing throws a beam that will make you wonder why you'd want any flashlight that's more powerful (trust me - you will). It will also zoom out and cast a flood that's very impressive. What it DOESN'T do is strobe or change brightness, even though the description says it will. You know what? I'm giving it 5 stars anyway. I do recommend taking it apart and using some di-electric grease (silicone lubricant) on the rubber o-ring where the head slides to zoom in and out. Doing this will make it easier to work the zoom. Go ahead and put some on the threads, too. Bottom line? If you haven't seen what they're doing with flashlights these days, you will absolutely be amazed by this purchase. In fact, for less than ten bucks, you too can begin a life of searching for more lumens/$ and trying to justify/rationalize your every flashlight purchase to yourself, your friends, and your therapist. Do yourself a favor and buy it, then give your old incandescent flashlights to Goodwill, the Salvation Army, your so-called friends, or your judgmental therapist. Now - I'm off to look at the K40 website. Again.

Edit: I see the description has been changed and no longer says it changes brightness or strobes. This flashlight gets used regularly and is still a 5 star purchase.

Edit to my previous Edit: They're claiming again that this light has three brightness level choices. It does not. There is a single brightness with no change in battery consumption. I love the zoom feature, but changing the zoom function does not equate to changing brightness. To clarify, the zoom is a continuous slide from spot to flood - there is no setting for spot, flood, or area (and what the heck is the difference between area and flood, anyway?!?). This thing still gets 5 stars from me, but I wish they'd get a better translator.

Update: Just received my third one. I bought it as a gift for someone who will be hiking in Peru. This, along with an [[ASIN:B00C1KI8Q0 Olight I3S 80 Lumen Cree XP-G2 LED LED Flashlight (Black Body) with 3 X EdisonBright AAA batteries]] (also uses an AAA battery and can clip to the brim of a hat), should provide versatile lighting that only uses one type of easily obtained battery. I'm ordering 2 more for some nephews who are in Scouting. Since theirs might get used infrequently, I'm also ordering [[ASIN:B00AHKUOPY Energizer Advanced Lithium AAA Batteries 6 Pack - EA92BP4F2]] ($8.74 shipped) to guarantee against leakage. In fact, I'd recommend that battery or Eneloops rather than alkalines, especially if the light sees infrequent use.

query: I'm looking for an electric bike that is suitable for taller riders, ideally one that offers good range and speed. I want something that rides well and has a solid build, as I'm about 6'2" tall and prefer a bike that can handle my height comfortably.
ori_review:
This is the best ebike I’ve ever own and between my wife and I we’ve own 7 so far. It ride fantastic however, I replace the pogo stick they call a “suspension seat post”. Fair warning this is a BIG bike for taller people. I’m 6’2” tall and it’s great. The frame is very long and heavy. I have ridden 34+ miles on a single charge and I’m guessing it could have gone to 50 miles. I was riding in peddle assist at lower speeds (about 12/hour).

Big negative is the stupid way they program the peddle assist. If you set it for true peddle assist the motor will only run while you are peddling. While the throttle does work it is limited to the assist number you are in at the time. So if you need to make a quick acceleration forget it. You can also set it to throttle assist which is simply a modification of the other peddle assist except the throttle is alway live a available. The draw back is it too is limited to what ever assist level is chosen. So if you power up the bike you must choose a power level. If you want full power available to you you need to press the up arrow 5 times. Then the throttle will work normally. Very strange.

If you need service you are basically calling some guy that I think is actually in China. Not to say this is bad but his response to my problem was to take it to a local bike shop and they could fix my problem. Duh! Option 2 was a Parks Tool Company video that he sent me a link to. While this may not sound like great service I can tell you it’s a lot better then the service I got from the people I bought my wife’s new ebike from.

Bottom line …. if your a taller person this is a very nice bike with good range and speed (25 to 28 MPH on a full pack). I’ve had it for about a month and just got my first 100 miles on it. Would have more but I split my riding time with 2 other bike still. But because of how well it handles and rides I’m now thinking of selling my other bikes.

query: I'm looking for a weighted vest that can help me maintain my strength while walking, especially since I can't go to the gym. ori_review: It's been 3 months now since the gyms closed due to the pandemic. Needing to compensate for weight lifting in the gym, I purchased this product. After 3 months, I have no complaints. I walk with the weighted vest 2 miles every day. It has allowed me to maintain the strength I developed in the gym. Earlier, I was walking with a backpack filled with bricks. The problem with this strategy is that too much weight lies solely on the back.  The vest distributes the weight equally. If you start with the full 80 pounds, your trapezius muscles will pain quickly. I would suggest that you start with a lower weight until these muscles can adapt and develop strength. I would also suggest that you get the shoulder pads. I am comfortable with the full 80 pounds now, so I will begin to add more weight using 5,10, and 20 pound ankle and wrist weights. My only modification was to put duct tape on the parts of the vest that touch my body. I was concerned that my sweat (acidic) would slowly eat away at the material. As is, the material is of strengthened quality. It would be great if RUNFast  would develop a vest that can hold more weight. Maybe 100-110 pounds. Highly satisfied.

query: I'm looking for a bike trainer that provides a workout similar to outdoor riding. I've set it up in my unheated garage and want to know how to best install it, especially regarding the rear axle since my quick-release handle can be tricky. Also, I would appreciate better instructions or an assembly video for guidance. I've noticed that the tensioner doesn't seem effective, and I prefer adjusting difficulty through my bike's gears. Overall, I'm curious about the durability of this trainer after a good initial experience. Can anyone share their thoughts or experiences related to these concerns?
ori_review:
Before I write the cons and pros, here's some context: 70 year old, typically ride 45-75 minutes each day around flat streets of neighborhood when weather permits; median speed: 12 +/- 1 mph. Weather here now has too much ice and snow on roads, so I purchased this trainer. Our house is small, so I set up the trainer in our unheated garage.

Bottom Line Up Front (BLUF): while I have no idea of the durability of the product, it provided a terrific workout that simulated a real bike ride far better than I expected. The "pros" described below far outweighed the 'cons".

Cons (starting with the bad stuff first):
1. Changing rear axle: I hated having to change axles; it was necessary because my quick release handle won't allow the stand to latch. When I was pulling the regular axle out and installing theirs, the wheel and chain slipped, so I had to figure out how to get the chain back on properly. Now I'm hoping that I can just leave this axle on when I return to riding outdoors {manufacturer: that's a question to you].
2. Instructions: Instructions are really not good, just as other reviews have said. It took me quite a while to figure out how to position the roller such that I could mount the bike's axle onto their latching system. Then I had to guess how much to tighten the roller screw. The manufacturer should provide an assembly video that is roughly twice as long and shows each step being performed completely.
3. Tensioner: it's basically worthless. There was no difference between 0-8. I'm probably just going to take it off the handlebars and set it on the ground behind the bike stand.

Pros:
1. Great workout: I was surprised at how closely it felt to riding normally. Even the little bit of wobble made it feel like a real ride. It didn't take me long to figure out which gear(s) to ride in.
2. Noise was not a problem: I wore earbuds with active noise isolation and listened to podcasts and music. I really didn't hear any background noise from the roller. Because I wore earbuds with active noise isolation, any noise generated by the product was utterly negligible.
3. Varied difficulty by changing gears: I didn't need the worthless tensioner as I simply changed gears on my bike to change the level of difficulty of pedaling. Again, this made it seem even more like a real ride.
4. Price can't be beat: given everything on the "pro" side, the price was so low that it made it very worthwhile to take the risk.

TBD: durability... I have no clue how long this product will continue to perform as it did so well on the first ride.

ori_review:
I researched this product and read a number of European reviews. Touring bikes with Panniers is very big in Europe and you see a lot of high-quality bike products like rear racks and panniers. This is one of those brands.

The rack is large diameter aluminum tubing that is TIG welded. It is very light and designed well. What I like about it is its adjustability to various bikes with 26" - 29" wheels. It does take a little bit of time to adjust to your bike but that's the beauty of it. You can move it away from your saddle and still keep it parallel to the ground. Most racks allow you to change the position of the arms attaching the rack to the seat tube. But this rack also lets you adjust the rack where it attaches to the rear wheel dropouts. So you can raise the whole rack up and down while maintaining the distance to the seat.

Ibera makes their own panniers, but I use Ortlieb on my bike. I got a front set of panniers on the rear rack. Full size rear panniers are typically 40 Liters or more. Way too much for small trips and around town. The front panniers are 1/2 this size. Very neat looking and they fit perfectly on the Ibera rack.

I'm buying a second rack for another bike.

query: I'm looking for grips that can help alleviate hand numbness during long rides on my hybrid bike. I've tried other grips and gloves, but I still experience discomfort after 30-40 minutes. I've heard that the Ergon GP5 grips have a larger hand rest pad and adjustable positions for added comfort. However, I had some issues with installation because the grips seemed to slip on my handlebar. Can you provide advice on how to install them securely without rotation, and if others have had similar experiences with their grip installation? I want to ensure I get the best comfort while riding.
ori_review:
I have a hybrid/comfort bike for exercising in the evenings and weekends. I already have a pair of large hand grips with extended pad; but, still had hand numbness after 15-20 minutes of riding. I upgraded my gloves to OutdoorMaster Half Finger with Shock-absorbing Gel Pad and that got me up to 30-40 minutes before numbness would start to hit. The Ergon GP5 have a larger hand rest pad to spread the pressure and I like the handles to change your hand position for added comfort without sacrificing control of the bike. I'm still playing with the best handle position for comfort; but, I like them a little higher up than in the near horizontal setting.

The handle bar hole on the Ergon grips seemed to be a touch too big or my handle bar is a touch too small in diameter because the Ergon grips slipped on with not a lot off effort and rotated freely once I put my palms on them. I experimented with double wrapping black electrical tape the length of the grips on the handle bar and using hair spray to lubricate the bar/tape (YouTube trick). The grips went on with some resistance and took some effort once the hair spray started to evaporate after a while to adjust for the most comfortable hand/palm angle. I also had to insert the grips all the way to the end where the handle bar ends were near to the Ergon adjustable hand grip hold attaches with the Allen topped screw. If not, the Ergon handles will come loose/off when riding. Because of this, the supplied decorative end caps were too long to insert; but, no-one will notice. I have no grip rotation when riding and the handles are very secured on the ends. You may not have the same issue with your bike like I did.

I even ordered a 2nd pair for the wife's bike because I like the improvement in comfort so much.

query: I'm looking for a lantern that I can use indoors and need to know if it has any issues with the base falling out, as I've read about that. When using it, how careful do I need to be with the candle placement? Also, is the metal top safe to touch when the lantern is in use, especially around kids? I want to ensure I can move it without causing spills. Lastly, how easy is it to clean up any spills if they occur? I'm considering buying another one, so I want to make sure it meets my needs.
ori_review:
I've used this candle lantern inside the house for at least two weeks now, and I'm pleased with this purchase. I read other reviews about the bottom falling out, but I did not have that problem. You do have to twist the base until it clicks into place, then the base is locked in.

The glass is held in at three friction points, and I did have to tweak the metal pieces that held it into place just a bit. I did this with the glass out of the unit and then slid it back into place. No problems with the glass since then.

It is a candle lantern and if you have kids you should make sure their curiosity doesn't lead them to touch the metal top as it is hot. Holding it by the wire handle poses no problem when moving the lamp. I have not used this outside and I'm not sure how well it would work, as any major movement of the lamp may cause the wax to spill out into the lower compartment. It happened to me once when I moved the lantern quickly. I easily cleaned the small amount of the contained spill the next morning without any issues.

I would recommend using care when inserting the tea candle so you don't bend the metal pieces that hold it into place. Also, when attaching the lantern cover to the base, do so with gentle firmness so that the tea candle doesn't pop out of its cradle. If it does, pop it back in and replace the cover.

I like this lamp and I will be buying another one as well as UCO's original candle lantern.

query: I'm looking for a tactical belt that offers good value for money, ideally around $25. I want something that is well-built and comfortable, but I have some concerns about the molly system being too loose and the Velcro not matching industry standards. Can I expect this belt to hold up well under a load of 15-20 lbs, and will it work well with other magazine pouches I might want to use in the future? Also, how does it compare to more expensive options?
ori_review:
So let me start by saying this a an AMAZING BELT FOR THE MONEY!!! If you're looking for a CHEAP and for the money an amazing deal. Buy with confidence after you read the pros and cons to see if its right for you.

That said a 25 dollar belt is NOT going to stack well against 150-250 belt systems. I will try to get photos of my Ronin Tactical belt and compare it directly to this belt. It doesn't stack up amazingly. But for shooters or airsofters who want a well built belt but are restricted by income this is a great option.

Pros:

Its a tactical belt for 25 bucks! And it doesn't fall apart as soon as you lock it.

Inner belt webbing is comfortable with a soft grip so it won't rotate on you.

Seems to be built extremely well for the money.

Has a Cobra Locking System.

Double or maybe Triple stitched is most areas.

Love to help out an American Veteran anytime I can.

CONS:
Has 2 major ones in my book.

The molly system is too loose from top, middle, and bottom. The molly system is also too soft and not ridged enough. What does this mean? When you web in single magazine pouches there is quite a bit of play side to side. Which feeds to the second issue.

By having loose molly webbing it will cause a weighted magazine pouch to pull the already too loose webbing forward. I believe this over the long term will cause issues. This is my option

Another gripe from me is the Velcro is not industry norm. In the tactical belt or war belt community the outer belt has male Velcro and the inner belt is female Velcro. I have 2 other battle belts, and wanted to try this belt with a inner belt fed through my belt loops. Because the Velcro isn't industry norm it would be female (soft Velcro side) on female.

Finally I wouldn't want more than 15-20LBS on this belt. But this goes for all warbelts that don't have a locking inner belt.

Final Thoughts:

Mission dictates gear. I can't help new shooters with this enough. With the Cons above how am I giving this 5 stars?!? Because I can live with the cons from a 25 dollar warbelt. I had some extra mag pouches and wanted to make a truck belt that if it got stolen I wouldn't cry about it. I can also let friends borrow this when shooting for fun drills. This belt is amazing for the price.

If you are restricted by funds I wouldn't hesitate to recommend this belt. I would recommend buying name brand magazine pouches. So if you do step up from this belt in the future you don't need to purchase higher quality mag pouches.

I will be uploading photos and a video review shortly.

The AB wheel is a simple and convenient way to daily strengthen not only your CORE (abs & lower back) but also your arms, shoulders, legs, glutes, and entire body as well. query: I'm looking for a reliable and user-friendly mini pump that can handle both emergencies and regular inflating. I appreciate pumps with flexible hoses to avoid damaging my inner tube's valve. I also need a compact option that can be mounted on my bike frame without taking up too much space. Additionally, I want something that can efficiently inflate a 26x1.95 MTB tube to around 30psi. However, I'm concerned about the durability of the hose connection to the pump body, especially if the threads are plastic. Can you recommend a pump that meets these criteria?
ori_review:
Absolutely fantastic mini pump. One of the most obvious advantages of this pump is the flexible hose that comes with it. One of the biggest drawbacks of most mini pumps is that they don't have hoses like full size pumps, and therefore have a tendency to damage the valve on your inner tube. The excellent hose on this pump overcomes that.

At around 7.5 inches in overall length, this won't fit in most saddle bags. Fortunately, the pump comes with an excellent holder that mounts on the bottle holder screw holes. It actually sandwiches between the bottle holder and the bike frame, so you can attach both the pump and the bottle holder onto the same pair of holes.

Although it seems small, it took only a minute of pumping to get a completely uninflated 26x1.95 MTB tube to around 30psi, which was more than sufficent to ride on. All of the connections are sealed with O-Rings, which don't exhibit any signs of falling off in the future.

The only thing I have against this pump is that the female threads on the main body of the pump (onto which the hose screws) are plastic, and not metal. They seem durable and don't appear to be prone to stripping, but I would have preferred the extra peace of mind.

What I liked the most about this cot is, it's comfortable. I'm a big lady (5'6 175lbs) and can still sleep comfortably on it. Last week we took a road trip and brought along just the mattress from this cot. I was able to fit it in the back of my mini van and my son took a nap very comfortably on it. The mattress is thin but made well from foam and it alone is worth the whole price of the cot.

It's now been over a year since we bought this cot so I thought I would update this review. The Mattrissa did not make it a year. The whole was put in the mattress through wear and tear. Then silly me put it in the washing machine after it got dirty and it just kind of fell apart. I believe that that was my fault but I thought I would mention do not wash the mattress in a machine. I guess I should've gotten out the simple green and wipped it down that way. I still believe it's a great bye and I will definitely be buying another one when camping season starts.

Field Tip for scooters in general:
Just a little something extra to consider.
I did notice that units like these are a lot rougher on my knees in rougher surfaced areas like cobble stones and really old patchwork pavement, these units can be murder on the knees. Faster should mean larger wheels also, The faster the unit can go then the larger the wheels should be. The larger the wheel are governs the center of gravity which affects over all stability. query: I'm looking for a reflective vest that provides excellent visibility for biking and running, especially at night. I want to ensure that I can be seen by drivers from a distance. I've heard some vests only work if car headlights are on, so I'm considering adding a blinking light for extra safety. Additionally, I'm curious about the fit of this vest. I'm 5'6" and 131 lbs, but I'm concerned if it will be too snug for taller or larger individuals. Does this vest come in different sizes, or is the "one size fits all" option truly adjustable for various body types? I want something comfortable to wear over both t-shirts and thicker clothing. Can you provide more information on its fit and visibility features?
ori_review:
This is a well designed, light weight vest that allows vehicles to safely see you well in advance due to the high quality of the neon green & silver reflective material. In order to assess the reflectiveness of this vest, I had my boyfriend wear the vest as I drove my car several blocks behind him. This allowed me to see first hand how clear & bright the vest reflected the car's lights. The result is I now feel much safer biking & running during nighttime (& daytime) hours.

Although there's no doubt about the high efficacy of this vest's reflectiveness, it's important to remember that ALL reflective vests will only work if there's an external light that reflects off of it. While I have no doubt that drivers can easily see this vest's reflection well in advance of their car approaching me if their car lights are on, undoubtably some drivers forget to turn on their headlights. For this reason only, I also chose to strap on a small blinking light to the rear crossing shoulder straps in the middle of the back in order to help further ensure my safety in the event a car hasn't turned on it's headlights. And since the vest's shoulder straps cross & are sewn together in the middle of the back, it's very easy to securely attach a small blinking light (I use a Nathan Strobe Light sold here on Amazon) that you won't even feel is there. Although I believe the Tuvizo reflective vest would be more than effective in keeping you visible to oncoming cars, it's just my personal preference to also include a safety option in case a car doesn't have it's lights on (which it's critical for the efficacy of any reflective material).

This Tuvizo vest comes in one size ("one size fits all") and was very easy to adjust, as it has allows for 4 separate adjustments: one on each shoulder strap, as well as a separate waist adjustment on both sides of the anterior clip-on that's located in the middle of the torso.

Since this vest is a clip-on, instead of an over-the-head application, it's extremely easy to put on & off even when wearing bulky clothes. I found the fit was comfortable when worn over t-shirts, as well as thicker sweatshirts.

POSSIBLE CONCERN:

I believe more people would benefit if Tuvizo had additional sizes other than their current "one size fits all" option. Although the vest is perfect for my size (5'6", 131lbs w/ 30" waist), I think people who are taller and/or have a larger mid-section might find this vest a bit snug. When I wore this vest w/ just a t-shirt, I had approximately 2.75" of extra "adjustment" room on both sides of my torso & approximately 4" of extra adjustment on each of my shoulder straps. While I was able to loosely wear my reflective vest at waist level (my own preference), I think most men (or anyone over 5'10") will find that the vest will rise well above their waist. Additionally when I wore this reflective vest over a couple of sweatshirts, the fit was a lot snugger around my waist. While this was fine for my height & size/proportions, I think most men (& taller/larger women) would benefit from a larger size. But if you don't mind a snug fit around the chest (instead of the waist), then this "one size fits all" may feel fine with you. I just would be concerned about the fit if your height was > 5'10" - 5'11" and/or if your torso girth was > than 40".

Overall, this Tuvizo reflective vest is extremely user-friendly, is reasonably priced, & has the best reflectiveness of any of the previous 8 vests I've purchased over the years.

query: I'm looking for a jig rod that combines stiffness with flexibility, preferably with spinning guides for better performance with spinning reels. Can anyone share their experiences with rods like this? How do they perform with different types of fish?
ori_review: I like the Gold better than Buck's regular jig rod. The Gold is stiffer (but not too stiff) and has spinning guides. I use spinning reels on mine and the spinning guides work better for my use than the smaller jigging guides. The workmanship looks much better on this rod than it does on their standard rod. This is a good looking rod. I don't use these light, long rods just for panfish. I have caught large Rainbow on them and they handle large fish nicely. Fighting these long, flexable rods tires a fish out quicker for some reason, and light line holds up to large fish better than on a shorter rod. query: I'm looking for a high-quality leather lifting belt that will last a long time but is also reasonably priced, ideally under $50. I've done a lot of research and found that a 4" non-tapered belt is recommended. I'm curious if this belt comes with a warranty, as I've seen some similar options offer a lifetime warranty. Also, I want to know if the belt provides good support and comfort during heavy lifts, especially for squats and deadlifts. Can anyone share their experiences with this product regarding its fit and performance?
ori_review:
This review is for the ProFitness leatherlifting belt in small. I am in no way affiliated with this company or vendor, and I was not provided anything in exchange for this review.

Before buying this belt, I did extensive research on lifting belts. I wanted a leather belt that would last for life, but I also didn't want to pay over $50. The Inzer Forever Belts, while really nice, were just a tad out of my price range. Perusing Reddit and fitness forums, folks seemed to suggest a 4" non-tapered leather belt, so that was my goal.

After all my research, it came down to this belt and the Dark Iron Fitness leather lifting belt. From what I can tell from pictures, the two seem nearly identical apart from price (the ProFitness was a few dollars cheaper and had free same-day shipping) and the fact that the Dark Iron Fitness includes a lifetime warranty. I don't see any mention of a warranty on the ProFitness belt, and since I didn't notice the warranty on the Dark Iron Fitness until after purchasing this belt, I hope I don't regret my decision. I'm going to ask the vendor to clarify whether the ProFitness belt includes a warranty.

MATERIAL - The leather is very thick yet pliable. It feels much more expensive than it actually cost and has a nice quality suede backing.

STYLING - The logo is a tad large but is simple enough. I actually kind of like it. The red contrasting stitching looks really great against the black leather and won't show dirt quite like white stitching would (part of why I chose the red).

BUCKLE - I'm glad that I opted for a double buckle. The buckle is very sturdy without being too heavy or bulky. It feels nice on and doesn't pinch, even when I'm carrying a little extra fluff around the midsection. I feel like I could like a ton of weight and the buckle would never fail on me. I do wish there were a small leather flap under the buckle like I've seen with a few other leather lifting belts, which would prevent the inevitable cold shock when the metal buckle touches bare skin in the case of my shirt riding up.

FIT - Measured at navel level, my true waist measures 30.5" without cinching the tape measurer, so I decided on a small. This was the right choice. During lifts, I cinch the belt to the third set of holes from the end, which seems to serve a nice balance between not being able to breathe and having enough abdominal pressure. If I wear the belt over a thicker top or coat, the second set of holes works nicely.

PERFORMANCE - I definitely saw an immediate improvement in my lifts, particularly squats. The belt allowed for exceptional intrabdominal pressure, and it kept my form tight. I instantly added weight to all my lifts. So far, I've used the belt for squats, deadlifts, and overhead press, and my form feels a lot more solid during max sets. I initially experienced some slight pinching during deadlifts, but I played with the position of the belt a bit, and it doesn't seem to be a problem now.

All in all, this is a very solid, well-made leather lifting belt. I expect this to last for a long time and will hopefully update my review as a use this throughout the next few years.

EDIT: I talked with Troy, the lovely gentleman who sells these belts, and it does come with a lifetime warranty. Highly recommend this product based on customer service alone - his responses were prompt and very friendly. Five stars.

query: I'm looking for an adjustable weight set that includes a stand and allows for quick adjustments between weights. Are there options that are user-friendly, especially for someone doing a program like P90X? Also, how sturdy is the rack and what should I know about assembling it? Any recommendations or tips for ensuring I get the right fit without feeling like I overspent? Additionally, do the weights adjust in smaller increments, and how do they compare to similar products on the market?
ori_review:
So in looking for an "adjustable" weight set to use while doing P90X I thought the Bowflex weights were the only game in town. I was fully prepared to drop the $$ to get the 552 set AND pay the additional $130 or so for the stand that was, of course, sold separately. Then, purely by accident I ran into these and was immediately interested them not only for their function, which was different from the Bowflex in that instead of turning the ends into position to set the desired weight, you would turn the handle (something I felt seemed like a more natural function since that's where you'd hold them from 99% of the time) but also due to the fact that they were the same price as the Bowflex but INCLUDED THE STAND!! That was huge! So, it's been a week since I've had them and I am extremely happy with my purchase. I don't drop this kind of money for something lightly and I find nothing more annoying when I do so than to be dissatisfied by the quality of the product and while the end caps are made of a seemingly sturdy plastic material, they don't feel "cheap" in any way. Also, I love the way I can rack and re-adjust the weights to what I need for the next exercise without missing a beat and losing precious time between exercises. The rack is strong and sturdy and does not wobble (you can actually use it for certain exercises such as Dips). The weights are definitely longer that "regular" dumbbells but that seems to be expected with weights of this type. If anything, getting used to them will just help you build more strength and endurance since you might have to hold them slightly different than normal weights which also helps with control. Also, each dumbbell adjusts in 5lb increments (15-20-25...etc all the way up to 50lbs) unlike the BF which adjusts from 5 to 52.5 pounds in 2.5-pound increments up to the first 25 pounds. This may be something to consider depending on your strength levels and goals but I personally found it a small price to pay in exchange for the rack as previously mentioned.

Now, there is ONE thing which I want to mention that hopefully many will find helpful ( I know I would have if it had been mentioned in the instruction manual!!) When you open up the boxes with the weights you will find dark grey hard plastic brackets which the weights can fit on perfectly. The instructions tell you to secure these brackets to the rack with the included screws (8 on each side). However, on first glance the holes on the underside of the brackets are too big for the size of the screws so it's wasn't readily apparent (and not mentioned) that you have to UNSCREW THE 8 SCREWS ON THE BOTTOM OF THE BRACKETS IN ORDER TO SEPARATE THE TOP FROM THE BOTTOM AND BE ABLE TO THEN SET THAT TOP PART ON TOP OF THE RACK ARMS WHICH YOU WILL THEN SECURE TO SAID RACK ARMS WITH THE 8 SCREWS PREVIOUSLY MENTIONED (NOT THE ONES YOU UNSCREWED BUT THE ONES IN THE PLASTIC PARTS CASE). In addition, the bracket has fragile plastic posts (I broke two of them by accident but Crazy Glue seemed to do the trick) that extend slightly from the bottom corresponding to where the screws will secure it to the rack. I mention this so you don't panic and think you somehow got the wrong parts in the shipment. Once secured however, the brackets are sturdy and I've not had a problem with them while racking and re-racking the weights.

The set also comes with a pretty cool menu and shopping list inside and 3 workout discs for the included program. I watched the first disc and while it definitely seems like a slicked up studio production (the girl especially is a little "stiff") some of the exercises were pretty decent and showed you how you could utilize the weights for the different workouts. If you actually want to see their slick infomercial type video go to their website...it may be worth a look if only to see the different things they use the weights for.

All in all I'm very pleased with the purchase so far but will definitely post a followup in a few months to see if they continue to hold up. If you are interested an adjustable weight set that comes WITH a rack (thereby saving you $130) and is pretty effortless to use you really can't go wrong with these.

query: I've been using Osprey packs for years, and I'm curious about the new Exos 38. How does it compare in comfort and weight to the previous model, especially for summer backpacking trips? Are the improvements in the top lid and side pockets worth it? Also, I’ve had issues with hydration tube routing—does this model have a better setup for that? Lastly, how does the padding in the shoulder straps and hip belt feel during long treks? I'd appreciate any insights on whether this pack is a good choice for 2-3 day weekend trips.
ori_review:
Let me begin by stating I'm been using Osprey packs of various types for a long time and I own and regularly use the previous model of this pack the Exos 46L. Even with that in mind I'm still objective in my assessments and if function is not up to par or quality is lacking somewhere I will point it out.

Here are my observations:
This pack is extremely light. Ok, maybe like the old model its still not up to UL purists standards but I believe one would be hard pressed to match the load capactiy and overall comfort this pack offers. It has a lot more features and comfort bulit-in from the old model and still manages to weigh less.
There are significant improvements with the top lid/pouch. Often times I find I just don't need the top lid/pouch and I remove it to save weight and streamline my pack, this is a nice feature and carry-over from the old model. But, I believe the top lid is now easier to detach and reattach from the old model. This alone is a great feature of these packs. My favorite new feature of the lid design though is that the new model incorporates a sewn in flap with the Osprey logo so that if you do remove the top lid, you still have a functional flap that uses the same fasteners to cover the top of your pack. Way to go Osprey on this one.
The pouches on the hip belt are roomy and no longer mesh. I do not like the fact that the mesh on my old model allows dirt and debris into those pockets, this issue has now been addressed.
The expanding mesh pockets on the sides of the pack have been addressed as well. The mesh is now a finer weave less prone to snagging and ripping and also I feel more easily expandable. Those mesh side pockets on the old model are practically useless with a full pack. One may force a Nalgene bottle in there, but with a full pack and a tight fit there is no way you will get the bottle out while wearing your pack. Also, every time you force a bottle or something in there there is a good chance you will tear the mesh. The new mesh is much improved. Still not an easy task to get a bottle in and out of there but much, much, better.
The new padding incorporated in the the shoulder straps and hip belt is oh so cushy. I can't believe how comfortable the suspension is on this pack. My old 46L is super comfortable too up to about 26-27lbs for me, but this new padding blows away the old model and still somehow manages to be lighter in construction. I can load this pack if I want to the gills, but the straps still won't dig into my shoulders or hips like the old model will start to do under heavy (for the pack) loads. I don't overload my packs for actual treks, but on occasion for training hikes will do so to test me and the pack.
Like the old model, lots of straps and attachment points for various equipment. Weight savers will want to remove these but the little bit of extra weight on an already light and comfortable platform does not bother me and I tend to use these lashing straps.
Now for a minor complaint. The pouches sewn into the shoulder straps are not easy for me to access while wearing the pack and of course they are also small. Think carefully about uses for these pouches as I feel one is pretty limited in what you can put in there. My suggestions would be small travel size bottles of sunscreen or insect repellent and lip balm.
There is no D-ring for routing of the hydration tube on the shoulder strap. The loop sewn into the strap is really tight for this so do yourself a favor and get the magnetic clip that attaches to your drinking tube. Great invention and totally worth it if you regularly use a hydration sleeve with your pack. [[ASIN:B007TJ5X8E Source Tactical Gear Magnetic Tube Clip (Black)]]

Final thought: I bought this pack for the warm months where my Exos 46L is too much pack for what I do. For my summertime treks the new Exos 38 is the answer. I can't believe the comfort of this pack given it's weight. Even fully loaded it's like it's not even there. For me Osprey packs just fit. I realize this is not the case for everyone but it's like my Exos 38 and 46 were custom made for me. It's also hard to beat the "Almighty Guarantee," but I have not had reason to use it yet. If you are in the market for a pack specifically for summertime weekend long 2-3 day backpacking treks then give this pack a hard look. For two days in most cases I can go without the top lid/pouch and three days treks are a breeze with the lid added.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable and lightweight hammock that comes with an integrated mosquito net. It would be great if the hammock is easy to set up and can be used without the netting as well. Can you recommend something that fits these needs?
ori_review:
I originally purchased one of these from Woot, but my wife and I kept arguing over who got to use it so I had to buy a second one. For those that tend to be mosquito bite prone, this thing is a godsend. The first time we brought it with us on vacation, we were staying in a small cabin with no AC and I got a bad cold. It was way too hot in the cabin to rest, and the mosquitos were terrible outside. However, I laid a blanket down in the bottom of the hammock (to prevent mosquitos from biting through the bottom), zipped up the netting, and was able to get the extra sleep I needed without a single bit.

The hammock is comfortable, strong, lightweight, and packs up really small in the integrated stuff sack. It's easy to hang, although it doesn't come with any straps or rope (I use a couple of old nylon webbing belts that I can stuff inside the sack, but you can get fancier straps on Amazon). The netting is held up by can elastic cord that runs through two parallel rows of loops, so you end up with more room inside the mosquito net than in other netted hammocks that only use a single string throw one row of loops. The hammock is designed to be used between two trees, where the width of the trunk separates the two elastic lines that support the net, but you can easily use a short stick to separate them if you're hanging it from a poll or hook. The black netting provides plenty of visibility and airflow, and seems to keep the bugs out. The netting is permanently attached, but if you don't want to use it you can turn the hammock upside down so that the netting hangs below it.

Now that EEE, West Nile, zika, chikungunya, and other mosquito-borne viruses are becoming a larger threat, this hammock is a great way to enjoy the great outdoors without worry.

query: I'm looking for a backpack that can comfortably fit all my gear for a three-day hiking trip. ori_review: I got this backpack after weeks of researching all the different kinds.  I went on a three day, 28 mile hike at Myakka River State Park, in Sarasota, Florida.  This was my first hike, so I didn't want to spend a lot of money on a pack.  The pack has plenty of room in it. I packed way to much because of it.  In one of the side pockets I put all of my smaller stuff, mp3 player, fire starter, lighter, headlamp, and digital camera. And in the other I managed to fit 1.5 lbs of trail mix and a large package of beef jerky.  In the top there are two pockets one on the outside and one on the inside.  On the outside pocket I put my poncho, and first aid kit, and a pack of cigs.  It has two mesh pockets on the side they are plenty big I put a 1 liter water bottle in each.  They held fine and didn't fall out at all.  The sleeping bag compartment is small but you can fit regular sleeping bag in it.  I don't know if you could fit one of the winter bags.  It is a tight fit but if you push, pull and zip enough you can get it in there.  The zippers appear to be of high quality.  The main part is very large, I fit 5 liters of water, two large cans of beef stew, and three days worth of clothes.  I attached my tent and fold up stool on the bottom loops on the outside of the sleeping bag pouch.  My pack weighed about 45 lbs when it was all packed.  It was my first trip and I learned a lot like, don't wear boots, and don't pack to heavy. The only thing I have to say negative about this pack is the shoulder straps don't really have the padding I would prefer.  My friend had a Coleman Hiking pack, his shoulder straps had/ a lot more cushioning on it. And the things holding on the chest straps are always falling off and I had to slide the chest connector up the shoulder straps every time I took my pack off.  I can think of nothing else negative to say about it.  Overall excellent pack, for a steal of a price.

query: I'm curious if the KardiaMobile 6L will work with my non-compatible phone. I have a Oneplus One and installed the Kardia app without issues, but I'm concerned about its performance and compatibility. Is it easy to use for taking EKGs, and can I save and share the results effectively? Also, does the app require specific settings to function properly, and how long does it keep the recorded EKGs?
ori_review:
I was hesitant to buy the KardiMobile 6L because neither my phone brand nor model were on the list of compatible devices. Before purchasing, I had installed the Kardia app on my phone without trouble. Inquisitiveness won out, so I bought the 6L, and it appears to work fine on my old Oneplus One with Bluetooth 4.0 running crDroid 3.8.3 (Android 7.1.2). I did, however, have to go into my phone's Bluetooth setup menu and tap on the Kardia6L available device before the Kardia app would pair with the 6L.
The 6L is easy to use. You need to be still while taking the EKG, otherwise you will introduce a lot of noise into the EKG. That's the price of the convenience of measuring from your extremities (fingers, leg) instead of with chest sensors.
Immediately after the reading, the Kardia app asks if it was for you or for a guest. Sadly, no option exists for other specific family members.
Once the EKG is finished, click the Share button at top, then three menu choices pop up: Clinician review; Email PDF; View PDF. I chose the latter, skipped the password, and selected one of my installed apps that can read PDFs. That app, Moon+ Reader, saves the PDF for future reference. From there I can easily copy the PDF to my laptop or desktop. Produced PDFs are about 350KB (4 pages) for 6-lead and 70KB (1 page) for single lead, and include the date and time in the file name (e.g., ecg-20210409-070714.pdf).
After recording several EKGs, under Health Diary, the app lets you view recorded EKGs by date. I don't know how long it keeps the EKGs.
The Kardia app would not install on a old Motorola DROID MAXX (XT-1080M) running Android 4.4.4 - no great surprise there.
The Kardai app requires having High Accuracy Location turned on; it will refuse to take a reading if your phone is set for Device Only Location. This annoys me. It makes me wonder if it will stop working while I travel to an "unapproved" country.

query: I'm looking for comfortable knee pads that stay in place during long mountain biking rides. I've tried the original Pro-X and Pro-X2 models, but the sizing and fit were inconsistent. The Pro-Rugged seems to have an adjustable strap and better coverage, but how do they compare in terms of warmth and bulkiness during hot rides? Will they conform to my legs over time, and do they maintain comfort throughout extended use?
ori_review:
Over the years, I've owned 3 pair of the original Pro-X, one pair of Pro-X2 and now these Pro-Rugged kneepads.
I'm a Colorado Frontrange based mountain biker, and go between chill afternoon rides with friends to more aggressive back country multi-hour adventures (@iRideDumb, if you're into that type of thing)...
I continue choosing the G-Form kneepads, because I choose to ALWAYS trail ride with kneepads, and the G-Form pads have been comfortable enough and stay in place, so that I barely notice them on my rides.

The original Pro-X seemed to fit small. I choose the XL in order to retain feeling in my legs... They didn't slip, they didn't stretch, and for me they held up really well.

The Pro-X2 seemed to fit larger than the Pro-X. I did one ride with a pair of XL, and while the coverage was better, they slipped down and just didn't fit right for me.

Now to the Pro-Rugged... I ordered size L because of my experience with the Pro-X2, and because these have an adjustable strap at the top.

Sizing-wise, this was the right choice for me! They fit well on my legs, and the strap helps keep 'em in place.
The padding section on the front of the knee is wider and stiffer than the Pro-X... which makes it flare out a little wider than my knee, vs confirming around my knee like the older versions. After 4 rides, they have started loosening up, and I think this will conform more to my leg as they continue to break-in.

Heat-wise, these are slightly warmer in that padding section then the originals. The back of the knee is a mesh fabric, which is lighter than the original, and more breathable... so long hot days, you'll notice 'em more, but only just.

Weight/bulk-wise, these are a little heavier/bulkier than the original... but not super noticeable once you have them on.

All in all, these are a great upgrade from the original Pro-X and Pro-X2. They provide better coverage over the knee, and remain comfortable enough to keep them on the entire time during long warm rides!

query: I'm preparing for a 6-week trip where I'll encounter snow and heavy rain, and I've just applied a waterproofing wax to my leather walking shoes. How can I ensure the wax application is effective for different weather conditions, and what tips do you have for maintaining the waterproofing while on the road?
ori_review:
I haven’t worn my black leather walking shoes in wet weather yet, but the application was EASY and I can’t believe it won’t work. Since my New Balance shoes have lots of seams and a separate tongue, the best they’ll be good for is slush, heavy rain and shallow puddles, but that’s OK.

I’m about to take a 6 week trip, there will be snow showers at high elevations the first 4 days, so this should do fine, both then and if there are heavy rains or polar vortex mischief later in the trip.

I heated the oven to 170 - it won’t heat below that, put each shoe in for 5 minutes, until it was a bit warm, and worked on it. Much more importantly, I put the tube of wax in a tall glass, poured boiling water over it and left it there until I was ready to work on each shoe. Be sure to turn the tube over midway through, so the entire tube has the same consistency.

Basically, I liquified the wax, which made it very easy to apply. Each shoe got 3 solid coats. I then “detailed” the seams with cotton swabs, which forced the excess into the seams while removing what was left, which would have looked whitish. After the wax dried, I buffed each shoe with a shoe shine cloth. No residue and the shoes look great.

For an ultralight packer (carryon for 6 weeks), this seems like the optimal solution. And,if I’m concerned, I can throw the 100gm tube into my TSA “liquids” pouch and apply more while traveling if needed.

I will try to update after I’ve field tested their waterproofing - but, with this much wax, I can’t see how they won’t work pretty well.

query: I'm looking for a golf simulator that offers great value and a variety of features without breaking the bank. I've tried different in-home swing trainers, and I'm particularly interested in options that provide training, driving ranges, and the ability to play on different courses. I want something that offers good graphics and smooth performance, especially compared to other software options. Additionally, I'm curious about the design and functionality of the swing stick and sensor, particularly regarding noise levels during use. Finally, I'm interested in any updates or improvements for compatibility with Apple TV for a better viewing experience. Can you help me find the best option that meets these needs?
ori_review:
Best in category. I tried all of the in home swing trainers and all have there pros and cons, but Phigolf is the winner for me. I started out testing Phigolf, Tittle x, and Trugolfs home swing studio. Both the tittle x and trugolf run off of the e6 software which honestly looks pretty bad running on an iPad Pro. Phigolf has 2 options, it’s proprietary software that offers various training, driving ranges, and several courses to play. All look much better, and play stutter free compared to what e6 was offering. They also offer several tournaments against real life players that offer amazon gift cards to the winners and a random entrant, which adds a little bit of excitement to playing. Add in the WGT software at an amazing price of only 1.99 a month and you have plenty of variety to play with.

I must give props to Phigolf for there design of the swing stick and sensor. The swing stick has a great look and a fairly decent grip. The best part is the feedback you get with a double click on where the contact takes place and when you stop your swing. Compared to the other 2, it’s quiet enough that I can play early in the morning or late at night and not wake up my family with a loud click.

Finally the accuracy of the sensor. Phigolf has done a great job of developing this sensor and it shows. On both the tittle and trugolf, I would get some random drives that would fly 350 yards, while phigolf has been pretty consistent with what I hit in real life (275 max). The putting actually works.

My only real gripe is not really a gripe, But the Apple TV app was not fully functioning as of this writing. They did announce that an update is coming in the near future, but once it comes it will be great to get a full screen experience without the small sidebars when I airplay to my tv.

Well done Phigolf. Recommending this to all of my golfing friends and looking forward to keeping my swing going in the cold winter months. And especially now with being quarantined.

Catch it early and strengthen it before it gets bad. Sleeves are cheap. Surgery is really, really expensive.

query: I'm looking for a compact and durable stove that can handle cooking tasks during power outages, especially in harsh winter conditions. How well does this type of stove perform in terms of cooking efficiency and smoke management, particularly when used alongside a fireplace?
ori_review:
During the big snow in the East in November/December 2009 my Appalachian Winter came on instantly...and caught most of us off-guard. The snow was wet and heavy, soon the power was out and temperatures were dropping. I had my fireplace, wood and after searching found this stove tucked away for a time like this.

It handled simple cooking chores fairly easily...the key is to cut your wood into pretty thin strips to feed into the stove. The side-door will stay open a lot but with slower burning fuel (coal, for instance) or hardwood it allows for a slower-burning stove. Four prongs on the top are where your pot or pan sits. On my stove one was bent a bit. A hammer or pliers may be needed for "perfection".

It looks like it was built for the French army by the Chinese Army. The is no room for nonsense. It is a clever mini-stove that will boil water, fry a fish or an egg but it is small. You have to pre-prepare fuel and "feed" it to keep the heat up, otherwise, it saved me and though I had a Sterno stove with fuel I found afterwards it mattered not. With my stove on the hearth near the fire the smoke went up the chimney...worth every penny in such a situation. It served me for TWO WEEKS without any other heating method save the fireplace. Pretty good, huh?

query: I'm looking for tips on how to successfully use a refillable hand warmer, specifically regarding the lighting process. I've noticed some negative reviews about difficulty in getting the burner to light properly. How can I ensure that I’m following the correct steps and giving it enough time to work effectively? Any advice on the initial lighting and how to maintain it would be greatly appreciated!
ori_review:
I see a lot of negative reviews for this thing. The problem I think is their lack of patience with a new burner. I purchased this and a spare burner, because they do eventually go out (though it takes a long while) and having a backup for when that happens is nice. My first thought about why so many negative reviews exist for this thing is lack of patience and not heeding the instructions. After pouring the lighter fluid inside the little tank WITHOUT the burner on, replace the burner and the cap and let it sit upright for about two minutes. This lets the fluid vapor finish soaking through the cotton and padding and allow the fumes to lightly saturate the catalyst in the burner. The burner isn't going light right if you don't give it a few minutes EVERY. TIME. YOU FILL IT.

And yet still, on first light (maybe even the second light) with a brand new burner, the burner doesn't play nice. You have to apply that flame for a good 10 or more seconds like the instructions say. (If you're doing it at night or in the dark, the orange glow from the catalyst shows it's lit. If you're lighting during the day time, find a dark corner or cup your hand round the cap and look through the holes, you should see something that resembles an ember despite the daylight) After the burner has gone through roughly an hour of burning (and perhaps even less than that) from then on the catalyst lights very quickly and stays hot for the full 12 hours that it should. You just gotta break the little fella in; I have two now.

query: I'm looking for a compact tire pump that can easily fit in my motorcycle tank bag and work well with tight spaces around the valve stem. I noticed the gauge may not be very accurate, but I want to ensure it can still inflate my motorcycle tires effectively without the hassle of using a larger compressor. Also, how does the locking mechanism work? I want to avoid any confusion when using it during my trips.
ori_review:
You will think you are missing parts, I ordered a 2nd one thinking I was. You're not, just configure the head to how the cardboard sleeve shows. If you're using it on tires you will need to switch the inside part around.
On the lip (locking mechanism on head) UP is Locked, DOWN is Unlocked. So flip the lip DOWN, put the head over your valve stem, flip lip UP once it's on to lock it in place. Yes this is prob opposite of every tire infiltrator you have ever used. This product happens to be reversed. When you are done airing your tire, flip the lip DOWN and wiggle it off the valve stem.
It doesn't feel like it's going to go on at first, just flip the lip Down and wiggle it on, the rubber will stretch around your valve stem I promise.

Yes the gauge is inaccurate, I'm still giving this pump 5 stars for the simple reason that 10 pumps will inflate my motorcycle tire 3-4 pounds! That's pretty incredible.
A lot of folks are criticizing the gauge is hard to read/inaccurate. But I always over fill my tire and use this gauge [[ASIN:B0022ZR3O2 Accugage Dial Tire Gauge with Hose RRA60X]] to let air out to desired level.
Compare your pen drive gauge you got from the gas station to the one above and you will see a 3-4 pound difference, if not more. That's not a big deal in a car or bicycle, but not acceptable on a motorcycle in my opinion (unless in a pinch).

I took this pump on a 1300mi motorcycle trip to the Ozarks. It fit in my tank bag, but I used the included zip-ties and mounted it to the undertail of my sports bike. I'm leaving it on as it's easier to use this then to get out my B&D portable air compressor. No rolling up cords with this pump when I'm done. Also I know this works with my rims. There isn't a lot of space between my valve stem and rim on my Honda CBR and I have issues with some gas station pumps not fitting. Which is frustrating when it's the only thing available. Now I'm a little more self efficient.

query: I'm looking for an exercise bike that offers great value for money. I want something that is easy to assemble, sturdy enough to support my weight of around 200 lbs, and has a reasonable noise level since I plan to use it in my garage. I don't need a lot of fancy features, just a basic display to track time and a comfortable seat. How does the resistance adjustment work, and is it suitable for workouts that require changing resistance levels frequently? Also, how reliable is this bike over time? Any insights would be appreciated!
ori_review: All things considered this is a great value exercise bike. So far, I have been using it for around 4 months normally 2 or 3 times per week and I do not have any major complaints. The assembly was quick and easy. It has an overall fairly sturdy/heavy feel to it and the noise level is reasonable. I’m around 5’9” and 200 LBS and the bike is a good fit and is sturdy enough for me. There are not many bells and whistles on this bike but honestly that’s part of the reason that I purchased it; to me that just means that there are fewer things that can break. The display is very basic and I don’t try to use it for anything other than keeping track of the time. I’ve tried the heartrate sensors a few times but I don’t think they are accurate; but I don’t care about this since I can just get accurate heartrate info from my smartwatch. I think the seat is comfortable enough it’s about how it should be for an exercise bike. There are much more expensive bikes that can be purchased for 5+ times the cost but for the money I think this is a great deal. I currently have this bike setup in my garage and normally I have a fan and a TV going while riding. Having a fan and a TV going creates enough white noise that I don’t really notice any of the minor squeaks and creaks noises from the bike. I think if it was in a completely quiet room then it might be more noticeable / annoying. The resistance adjustment knob doesn’t seem to be very precise so I just have it dialed in to a middle of the road setting and I don’t really try to change it too much. Keep this in mind if trying to do a spin class workout that has you changing resistance levels constantly, I don’t think that this would work very well. But for getting a decent workout without paying a lot for the equipment, so far this bike has been great. Time will tell how good the reliability is and I’ll update this review accordingly if there are any problems with the product quality in the future. So far, I’d say 5 stars considering what you get for the low price.

query: I'm looking for a fitness tracker that accurately monitors sleep and heart rate, especially for my 12-year-old daughter who has started playing sports. I want to know if this tracker can effectively track total sleep time, and how reliable it is for monitoring different sleep stages like deep and REM sleep. ori_review:
Daughter has started playing sports and like many pre-teens doesn't have the best sleep habits. One of the great things about this tracker is the aftermarket bands available, i.e. huge color variety, which are important to her fashion sense, lol. The orange one was on sale, so I got that and she immediately swapped it out for an aftermarket white band (came in a bag of 20 different colors for about 10 bucks!)
Anyways, I was skeptical that the sleep tracking would work, but it does seem to fairly accurately track her total sleep time. We've turned it into a little game where every day we compare who got more sleep. That said, I am skeptical of the sleep details, just as I am skeptical of the sleep details on my fitbit--by that I mean the deep vs. light vs rem sleep...I just have doubts that any of the trackers are really accurate with that, but I think they can get a good ballpark on total sleep time.
The bpm and blood ox seem ok, but seem to read a little slow. She has thin wrists (almost to the last hole on the strap) and likes to wear it a little loose, so maybe that affects it. We go jogging and my fitbit instantly has my bpm but hers needs a few seconds to read. (I think she may have an app setting that only checks every 1 minute)
The app has a ton, ton of tweaks and settings the user can play with to change how it works, a lot of them oriented towards battery life versus data capture. She had no problem figuring out the settings, getting texts to show on the watch, and changing the face graphics to her liking.
I am still getting life out of my 3 or 4 year old fitbit inspire HR, but if/when it dies I'll go with this or whatever its latest version is at the time. Fitbit has gotten too greedy moving premium features to subscription, I really like this band as you buy once, and nothing is paywalled.

query: I'm looking for a quality Baitrunner that offers good performance without breaking the bank. Also, how does the size of the Maelstrom compare to other models, particularly for use with a custom rod? I'm considering the 2000 size to match my setup better.
ori_review:
I'm a huge Baitrunner fan, I've been using the Shimano Baitrunners since the B Models. I've recently moved to the Southwest Florida and have taken to the Inshore Saltwater fishing. I purchased a Shimano OC4000 but then bought a custom built rod 6'10' MH Inshore built (Sewell) and the 4000oc was too big for it. As Shimano don't do a smaller saltwater Baitrunner I hunted around a got an Okuma Avenger ABF B3000 as I read good things about them but the quality wasn't there and I wanted a better reel.

After reading a ton more reviews on the competition I came across the Maelstrom, I decided to take the gamble and ordered the 3000. The quality is really impressive and for the price it blows away the competition. It's smooth, comes with an extra spool and has a high quality drag and casts really well. I've landed Snook and Redfish at around the 2ft size with ease and countless snapper with it.

The things that irritate me about it:

1) When the Baitrunner is set to freeline the click is almost silent.

2) The Baitrunner lever maybe the cheapest part of the reel so we'll see how it stands up to being used at least a couple of trips of times a week.

3) The 3000 size is almost as close to size of the Shimano 4000OC and dwarfs the Okuma ABF 3000 B. I've actually ordered 2000 today (9/1/15) as the 3000 is mismatched on the rod I'm using.

I'm currently using 3000 Maelstrom on a Tackle No8 Hellbent Inshore 7'6' MH or a Star Seagis 7 ft MH. Once the 2000 comes in I will use that on the Sewell rod. I'm now looking at the Maelstrom 5000 size to pair with an Extra Heavy inshore as I'm not sure I'll buy another Shimano Baitrunner again.

If you're looking for a low cost good quality Baitrunner I would recommend the Ecooda Maelstrom without hesitation.

query: I'm looking for a versatile tarp that can handle light rain and strong winds, especially for car camping and backyard use. How easy is it to set up by myself, and are there any tips to ensure it stays secure and doesn't damage the fabric while packing it away? Also, does it provide good ventilation and shade during hot days? Any experiences or recommendations would be appreciated!
ori_review:
Super easy to set up once you have done it a few times. Some reviews here have said that it's difficult without two people but if you follow the instructions which say to stake down the back two corners and then the front two corners you're solid. Do not attempt to put back pole up inside of the tent - it will tear through the tent fabric -- Instructions/pictures are not clear about having the back pole on the exterior of the back mesh wall. Another thing to ensure that it taught enough ...is ensuring the measurement and placement of front corners.

Super easy to set up. I have only used it in my backyard a few times but it held up perfectly through a few light rain showers and some solid wind gusts. It worked well in keeping sun out -- living in South Carolina we get some hot days even in February -- it worked will in that regard especially with the mesh bottom portions of the side walls that also have the vents on both sides, and the entire side triangular back wall is mesh allowing a maximized flow of air.

There is one tiny con, but it's more of a user error. It's important to fold it back small and tight and ensure you don't snag the bag zipper on the tent fabric because it will catch on the fabric if not super delicate when packing back up -- so don't speed through packing up. I will say a good strategy to avoid this is packing the tent/tarp first then placing the stake/guy line/pole bags on top of the tent so when you zip if it catches on any fabric it will be the fabric of the light weight bag enclosed to hold the poles.

I would highly recommend for any type of light daily use in parks, sporting events, tailgating (although you must have enough space since it is rather large), car camping, or even in the backyard for the kids to have a little shade while running around the neighborhood during a sunny day.

query: I'm looking for a waste treatment product that can effectively manage odors during camping trips. ori_review: We did a 5-day self-supported touring kayak trip in Lake Powell with 10 people and used this as part of our toilet system in conjunction with a Playberg folding toilet seat and Cleanwaste wag bags. I used a plastic bag from the wag bag system over the seat and tied a corner--just like setting up a garbage bag in a garbage can.  The wag bags come with a similar desiccant pre-packaged in the bottom, but I set up a lid on the toilet so the group could use the same bag more than once. I had people add powder as they went. I changed the bag out about every night.  It does not have any type of deodorizing scent, with the lid on the toilet and being away from camp odor remained low--not sure how it would do in really close quarters unless you had a pretty tight fitting lid.  I then transferred the used wag bags into tight Ziploc bags (that come with the wag bags) and into a sealed canister that I had. I had asked people to try not to urinate into the bag to avoid too much liquid.  When I transferred the bags back out later I did not get any liquid or leakage of any kind. The powder did it's job. other people have mentioned similar products you can find at RV supply stores I'm not sure if there is a cheaper more generic bulk product that might be less expensive if you use this regularly, but for my trip this package was more than enough I could have probably used half given the wag bags already started with some in them. More for next time!

Just recently i got bit by the blade bug (it was quite painful), and I've been building a small collection of what i would like to call my "survival/home defense kit".

Gerber has been around for some time now and even though they have factories in China (still awesome Gerber knives made in China), Their high-end made knives are manufactured in Oregon. They've been making knives for the US Army since the 1960's..

I have a few Gerber pocket knives all in which are made in China, but that doesn't necessarily make them bad, they are actually all damn good with very sharp blades..

This one, called the Prodigy is made superbly, it feels wicked in the hand, the steel and just overall build quality and feel is pretty damn great! The tanto point with serrated edge is really nice and really makes it look sexy!
The blade is sharp, but not ultra sharp. it definitely needs to get professionally re-edged!
The edge of the blade out of the box was perfect, not chipped or rounded, straight lines all the way through!

It's full tang all the way down to the butt of the handle and even that looks like it would mess somebody's day up real bad.

The grip/handle is good but not great! I have the Strong Arm Gerber knife and the grip on that beast beats this one leaps and bounds!
The Tac-Hide material feels a bit thin, not crappy thin, just thin. It's strong to a point, just don't abuse it.
The butt end of this knife where the grip material ends seems like its peeling, it's just a hair bit, but i wont mess with it and it should stay on.
The plastic mold is solid, it does look like a 2 piece mold though.

The sheath is super ultra tight with knife inserted, hopefully it weakens overtime. Great to know it wont fall out by accident or force!
Sheath is bi-directional, so you can insert it point in with blade left or right.

It's really just so affordable, not cheap!

Update**, i bought another one! So i now have 2 Prodigy Tanto's!

Picture i uploaded is of the Gerber Prodigy Tanto, Gerber Strong Arm Spear Point, and Bear Grylls Compact Fixed Blade.

UPDATE: I'm in peru and have completed all my hikes at Machu Picchu (including wayna picchu) and I wouldn't have been able to complete this steep, slippery hike without this pole -- just used one for this hike. The material is heavier and more durable than I expected from a $35 pack. The zippers seem a bit cheap, so use care opening and closing and don’t overload them, but mine held up to the task. I used the bottom straps of the bag to secure my 2person tent, and they held up nicely. I used two adjustable bungee cords and the side straps on the bag to attach it to my frame and it was very secure. I’m unsure if the bag alone would have held up to the large amount of supplies I packed inside, but I would recommend this bag to anyone looking for a large rucksack to attach to an old-fashioned external frame. Especially if you have the type of frame with a hinged “shelf” at the bottom for extra support, which are also available on Amazon for under $100.

If cables is an issue, the Trion is the light to own. The other manufacturers do not make any lights this powerful that are self-contained with batteries inside the main housing. Before I purchased the Trion, I bought the Triden X 600. The unit came with a stem mount, and all the essentials to mount the battery to the frame. One problem ... my stem length of 100mm was too short to mount the battery. (Units with higher outputs have larger batteries than those that have 350 lumens or less.) Attaching the unit to my high-end carbon frame didn't make sense. It was never an option being that I have an $8000+ professional road bike. Somehow attaching a battery to such a high-end bike was nothing more than a classless act.

The Trion is very well made. I find it durable and suitable for extreme weather conditions. The documentation could be written better, but all the essential information is enclosed. Exceeding speeds above 25mph, the Trion with its 600 lumens generates enough light to give me plenty of warning to avoid any potholes, glass or any other obstacle that may be hazardous.

I ride my road bike in harsh conditions. The Trion has performed well in temperatures ranging from 5 to 40 degrees. There has been no problems with the battery life in these conditions. This light has exceeded my expectations. It comes highly recommended.

query: I'm looking for a heart rate monitor that provides reliable heart rate tracking for both running and strength training, without the extra features like step counting or sleep tracking that I don't need.
