ori_review:
I purchased the Polar FT4 Heart Rate Monitor Watch about a year ago after doing a lot of research on the countless fitness trackers out there on the market, and I rely heavily on Amazon reviews. I typically do not write reviews myself, but I have been so happy with this purchase I was compelled to share my support for this as well.

The ratings and reviews on this monitor are spot on. When I was looking for a fitness tracker I was taking a few things into consideration: truly reliable heart rate monitoring (running & lifting weights), calorie tracker, workout timer, and price. I was not concerned about a step counter, sleep tracker, and or a fancy app tracker to go along with it. Don't get me wrong, those Fitbit watches are slick, but I personally didn't really need all of that. Plus, I didn't want a fitness watch to wear all day; I prefer to wear my other daily watches. Last thing about Fitbit, while they do have a good track record of accurate heart rate monitoring while walking/running, I've read that their watches do not track heart rate as well when doing strength training/lifting, which was personally a deal breaker for me.

My goal was to monitor my daily calorie intake to lose weight, so I paired this watch which tracks calories burned during workouts and the free Under Armour calorie counter app which tells you exactly how many calories are in the food/meals you eat. They worked amazing together. To date, I'm down 23 lbs. and I seriously don't think I could have done it without this watch. It is so simple to use, and it provides instant gratification at the end of the workout to know exactly how many calories you've burned. One thing I've always struggled with while running/working out was the guessing game of how many calories I burned, did I really push myself as hard as I could, and constantly looking at the clock on the wall to figure out my rest time. This watch takes care of all of that.

The workout timer is also amazing because I like to do a lot of circuit training, so whenever I am done with a lift, I know exactly how much time I have to rest until the next set. Such a simple concept for a fitness watch, but Polar just makes it so easy, it’s amazing. No issues with batteries, malfunctioning, or anything like that either.

I could go on, but in all, I couldn't be happier with this purchase. If you are looking for an easy to use, reliable, and functional heart rate monitor, then I can tell you this is it. Awesome job Polar, I think you've made a lifelong customer because of it. Good luck everyone!

The sleep monitor is eye-opening (sorry!) LOL but it is. It shows where you're getting light sleep, REM sleep, deep sleep, etc. It shows if you wake up at night too. Again, I have no idea how accurate it is, but it gives you a nightly score, and my score tracks with my subjective perception of how good a night's sleep I got.

It also calculates calories burned, but sad to say, it's not accurate at all. Today, it tells me I've walked 1.95 miles (true) and burned 350 calories (nope). Impossible. That amount of walking burns at most 200 calories. At most.

I also found a curious bug -- you can change the info in your profile, your name, your birthdate, and your height, but you can't change your starting weight. So be careful when entering your weight!

Overall, I'm very satisfied. It's excellent value for its price and what it offers.

The only thing that surprised me was how darn big the bag is even in the stuff sack. It’s not a problem, and I think is necessary since it’s so well insulated and doesn’t compress as much as a lighter bag, but it’s something to keep in mind for space/packing. query: I'm new to stand-up paddling and just bought an inflatable board that I was concerned might be flimsy or break easily. After using it for a few days, I'm pleased with its performance. I found inflating it a bit challenging, especially getting to 15psi—would an electric pump make it easier? I'm also curious about its stability; I weigh 155lbs and noticed it flexed a little but felt stable overall. I even took it down some rapids and it held up well. Is it common for boards to flex a bit under weight, and how does this one compare to others? Any tips for a beginner like me on improving my stability while paddling? Thanks!
ori_review:
I am new to stand-up paddling, and so I've never tried any other board so that makes it a bit hard to write a review. My big concern when I bought this particular Z-Ray board was that it was going to be flimsy or break and I kept wondering if I needed to pay more to get a higher quality product and so now that I've had a few days of use out of mine, I can say that I'm very pleased.

I unpacked it and was able to pump it up pretty easily - although I never made it to 15psi and stopped around 13psi. I would recommend an electric pump for myself and anyone else. The box says "ready in 5-10 minutes" but I think you need to be an Olympic athlete to be able to pump this thing up in 5 minutes to 15psi. It goes fast enough in the beginning but near the end it gets really hard and you don't make any appreciable progress despite pumping really hard. Once it's pumped up, it is very firm. The fin is easily attached and has a little pin to hold it. It looked a little flimsy but I had no problems with it and it's still looking good after two days of use. I grabbed the paddle - which is workable, if a little bit flimsy and headed out.

I had never actually done SUP before at all, but I didn't fall over and never actually got wet. It's not super stable, but it's pretty stable. I'm 155lbs. and the board didn't significantly flex when I got on it. It flexed a bit, but not enough to be a problem - plus I could have gone up a couple more PSI when I was pumping and the water was cold (and probably knocked it down 1-2psi). It feels light in the water and I made good time paddling across the lake. Every once in a while I'd wobble a bit, but I found my balance every time. I like it.

Once I'd done some SUP for a day and a half, yesterday I had the bright idea of taking it down from the reservoir down the class II rapids below the lake back to my car instead of carrying it. I'm not bad in a kayak and so it seemed like a reasonable enough idea. I put it in, strapped my stuff down with the nice elastic bands that are included - which was my only bright idea of this scheme - and put in and it went well for about 3 minutes until I hit the first rapid. But this review isn't about my lack of skill in taking a SUP down rapids, what I wanted to say is that despite rolling over several rocks and once wrapping it around a rock, the Z-Ray held up fine. When I put it in the car, no punctures, no marks, no nothing. And I learned that the Z-Ray is pretty tough, and that I might be ok in a kayak but I suck rafting on a SUP.

I paid full price for mine, I didn't get anything free or anything.

query: I'm looking for an electric scooter that is easy to charge and has a good braking system. I want to make sure it can handle slight bumps and has a decent speed, ideally around 15 mph. Also, how easy is it to fold and carry? I want something durable with a good battery life that I can use for commuting. Any tips on adjusting the brakes or maintaining the scooter would be appreciated!
ori_review:
I started rising bird scooters about a year ago and always thought about how convient they are. Fast forward and I no longer have a company car but a train near home that takes me close enough for a 50 minute walk to work. Tried it and didn’t like it. Looked into getting a scooter or bike. Ordered a kick scooter and after 30 min uphill returned it the same day.

Moving into electric scooters, i researched them for a good two weeks. Segway, exooter and all the popular ones and not so popular ones. Then after ten YouTube videos i saw this one and thought I’d give it a try. A $500 scooter for $300 was not a bad deal. I’ve used it 2 times so far and have this to say:

Charging: very simple plug and wait. Led turns red then green when charged. You can order more chargers from the manufacturer for $20. Take a couple hours but it’s a big battery

Brakes: the electromagnetic brake requires 30 seconds of riding before it kicks in fully. A disclaimer if it doesn’t work instantly. Back brake required some adjustment. It’s a very easy system to under stand. One side of the pad stays put and the other squeezes down. To adjust just unscrew the two top bolts slightly, elevate scooter, spin back wheel and move the brake pad around until it spins freely. Easy i tell you! Don’t return if the back wheel makes noise or doesn’t spin, check the brake first.

Wheels: air filled wheels make it easy to go over slight bumps but going between side walks i caution slowing down when crossing the street or you’ll be slamming the front and will break it. The manufacturer also has replacement and honey comb hybrid wheels that flex but don’t require air. Very smooth ride

Speed: fully charged got up to 18mph. Weigh 180lbs. Speed 1 got me to 13 mph. When you have used 1/4 of the battery the speed goes to 15 mph.

Headlight: bright enough to be seen, not a search beam so don’t know why people complain, it’s a scooter not a patrol car

Folding: easy enough, the commercials and ads won’t include the fact that there’s a safety bolt that needs to be screwed in when unfolded so it doesn’t collapse. You don’t just unfold and scoot. Unfold, secure bolt (5 second install), scoot. While folded it’s easy to move it around on one wheel though.

Over happy with it and a lot of people ask about it since it’s so easy to use. The weight of the scooter is not bad, it’s a metal scooter with a big battery, it’s got some weight.

Will update if i have issues in the future but so far it’s working well for me

query: I'm looking for trekking poles that are suitable for both urban exerstriding and wilderness hiking. I've experienced issues with the tips wearing out quickly on concrete, and I need to find good quality walking paws that fit securely. I've also been using these poles frequently and would like to know if there are any alternatives to the 12mm size that can handle more demanding terrains. Additionally, I'm curious about the durability of the locking mechanisms and the comfort of cork handles compared to rubber or foam. Lastly, how reliable is the customer service if I encounter any issues with the product?
ori_review:
I use these 60/40 for exerstriding (concrete/asphalt) and wilderness hiking. The tips that come with them are fine for hiking, not so much for urban exerstriding (or Nordic walking). The metal tip wore through the rubber tip in less than a week. That didn't bother me, as those rubber tips were not designed for hard use on concrete and asphalt, but it was all I had while I searched for some proper walking paws. The TrailBuddy pole tips are 11mm. I could not find good, high quality walking paws in that size. The ones made for the higher end poles are mostly 12mm. So, I went with a 12mm Swix walking paw, figured if the fit was too sloppy, I'd just use a bit of tape to secure them. To my surprise, they fit fine and work great! They don't slip or shift out of position. I currently have 50 miles of urban exerstriding on those paws and they've got at least another 50 miles left on them. So, the 12mm walking paws work but if I were using a different paw in that size in more demanding terrain (mud, thick undergrowth, rocky surfaces) where they'd likely be pulled or sunk, I'd definitely add tape for additional security.

The poles themselves have been stable and sturdy. The locking mechanisms are easily understood and set up. The instructions included as well as those emailed by the company rep prior to their arrival are crystal clear on how to properly set them. My poles have been in use 5-6 days a week, for a minimum of 5 miles a day, and they have stayed exactly where I originally set them; no slippage or collapsing. I make sure to heavily lean all my weight on them prior to engaging in the activity, every time, to ensure if there is any issue it will reveal itself before starting out. Never had a problem. I find the cork handles much more comfortable than rubber/foam handles which tend to get slick/slimy with sweaty hands. They're a perfect assist in taking some stress off of a bum knee and aiding balance on uneven ground. I love 'em, wouldn't go on a walk/hike without them. I do wish they were designed to take the 12mm paws, but that's a small quibble and one that could be overcome, when necessary, with good old fashioned duct tape.

EDIT 12/3/19: After using the poles for 3.5 months (approx 175 miles of urban trekking), the plastic tab the hand strap threads through broke out on one of the poles. I notified Trailbuddy via email on 11/28 (Thanksgiving day) and received a response the same day. A replacement set of poles was shipped out on Friday 11/29 and received on Monday, December 2, perfect condition and ready to go. Excellent company, amazing customer service!

query: I'm looking for an easy and cost-effective way to regrip my golf clubs. I've had my clubs for around 10 years, and the grips are in bad shape. Can you guide me on how to use a grip kit effectively, including what additional supplies I might need, like solvent, and any tips for the regripping process? I want to ensure I do it right and have a good experience when playing with the new grips.
ori_review:
I'm not one of those golfers that buy a new set of clubs every year or so, and, after 10 years, the grips on my clubs were in bad shape. I purchased the Golf Pride kit and was able to completely re-grip my set of clubs in a couple of hours. The kit contains 13 grips (you need a different kind of grip for your putter), grip tape and a rubber vice grip (so you won't scratch your club when placing it in a vice). It does not include the grip solvent, which I purchased at a local golf shop earlier when I re-gripped my putter. The instructions tell you about other solvents you can use that can be purchased in a hardware store.

The process is easy:
- Remove the old grip and tape (I used a utility knife but be careful not to scratch the shaft) - be sure all the old tape is removed;
- Place the rubber vice grip on the shaft and place the club in the vice;
- Remove the plastic label from the new grip;
- Apply the tape to the end of the shaft, leaving about 1/4 inch or so overlap on the end (it makes it easier to start the grip on the shaft). The tape is double-sided, so you peel off one side, apply it to the shaft, and then peel off the other side;
- Apply the solvent to the tape - I just applied it to the top and used a finger to spread it out. This makes the tape slippery, activating the glue. Use plenty of solvent so the tape is very slippery.
- Place some solvent inside the grip itself and be sure the inside is coated;
- Finally, with the grip's label where you want it, slide the grip on the tape until it's completely on the club. You have a few seconds to position the logo as you want it.
- Set the club on the floor grip down to drain any solvent that might be remaining.

That's all there is to it. I played a round the next day with new grips and it felt great.

query: I'm really happy I chose this desk bike over cheaper options. After years of using lower-priced models, I finally decided to invest in a higher-end one, and it has made a huge difference in my energy levels and motivation to exercise. I’m curious if others have found it easy to use, especially in tight spaces under desks, and if they’ve experienced any issues with noise during intense workouts. Also, how accurate is the calorie burn calculator? I'm looking for ways to maximize my exercise routine with this machine, so any tips or experiences would be appreciated!
ori_review:
To be honest, I've been eyeing this machine for a while, but put off by the "brand name" presentation, assuming that the price had a lot to do with the exclusivity of branding... which I resented in principle. I've been using desk bikes for a good 4-5 years now, being an office profession who got to be very heavy and struggled with maintaining energy levels and exercise motivation. I started out with much cheaper models, paying $15-30 for each one. I've had probably 6 over the course of the years, having never been able to justify the price of these higher end options, or not being able to afford it.

This time, I decided to splurge. I'd already lost over 100lbs using these types of things, and after breaking my last cheap model, I thought it was about time to really invest in my office activity. I held my breath, hoping that I would not regret it... AND I LOVE IT!!!!

This machine is approved emphatically by my bariatrics physiotherapist, for one thing. Having a ready-to-use activity plan at my toe-tip is a way to eliminate the excuses. I love being able to track my distances; it gives a challenge for me to beat :) I also really appreciate the fact that the makers of this cycle recognize that the default calorie burn is not a universal fit, and that they have made efforts to try and create a calculator so you can try to obtain more accurate numbers on their website if you so choose.

This machine is very heavy, and much bigger than I anticipated, despite having the specs before it arrived. It only barely fits under my desk. I'm 6'1" and very long-legged, but am perfectly able to pedal this bike underneath my desk without hitting my knees. I pedal in a downward recumbent fashion, which is the habit I've built up over time. Following the recommended angling for your knees at full extension helps, and then pointing your toes, are two big parts of the trick. I've read a number of people griping about the "clacking" that happens, which I have noticed on a couple of occasions, but it seems to occur due to overheating when I'm pedaling at a pace of over 20mph for an extended period, which I will say probably means that you need to be slowing down or using a higher resistance. Me, I saw it as a reason to up my game, and raising my resistance slowed me down, toned me up, and *poof* goes the clacking. I'm pretty sure that the machine is not intended for intensive use for 4+ hours a day, as some of the people talking about it making noise have reported using it for...

It's a great tool to have. Using a few minutes of pedals for a quick pick-me-up rather than having a soda, or using it to warm up when you get cold, are perfect short stints and reasons to use it. I like that the timer is automatically turned on and off by use, so it accumulates your activity time throughout the day. I'm so very happy with the purchase, more so than I expected.

query: I'm looking for a tactical sling bag that is durable, has ample storage space, and is comfortable to wear, especially with weight. Can you provide insights on the bag's presentation, storage options, and overall comfort during use? I'm also interested in how well it holds up under different conditions and if it can accommodate hydration packs. Thanks!
ori_review:
This is my review of the Tactical Sling Bag Pack made by Reebow Tactical.

PRESENTATION:
When the item arrived it came in a clear bag inside of a box. Nothing too fancy but that’s fine for this product. I ordered mine in black and the color is deep and saturated into the material. I do not see the color fading anytime soon unless left in the sun for an extended period of time. It also comes with an American Flag patch on the front. The patch attaches itself with velcro and stays on very securely.

MOLLE/PALS:
The velcro section of the bag can hold up to 4 regular sized patches. The velcro section is just like the Molle webbing on the front but the top two rows have velcro over the molle straps. This means if you don’t want patches on your bag then you can still use them as regular Molle/PALS webbing. In addition, there is also 4 rows of Molle webbing on both sides of the bag.

STORAGE:
There are 2 pockets on the front of the bag. The top pocket has a good amount of room to hold something like a medkit, spare mags, some snacks, etc. This pocket is the one containing the velcro Molle webbing. There are two rows of webbing on this pouch. On the bottom of the front, there is a bigger compartment with a front pocket as well. This pocket has over double the space of the top pocket and can hold just about anything you need. The main compartment is way bigger than it looks. This could hold many MRE’s, spare mags, or anything you could fit in there. On the back of the bag, there is a snap button that opens up yet another pocket. This one is for a hydration pouch. It can comfortably fit a 2L pack, but I am sure it could hold a 3L or maybe even 4L pack.

COMFORT:
The shoulder strap is padded and is comfortable on the shoulder even with weight on it. This has plastic D-Rings that can be used for routing the hydration tube. It is connected to the backpack with a plastic side release buckle. The other side of the buckle leads down to a detachable point on the bag where you can take off the bottom half of the strap if you want. There is also a second safety/security buckle that comes up from the left side when you have the bag on. This would ensure the security of the fit and make sure you get a proper and secure fit. The bag only has one strap and goes across your chest. When you put it on you put it on over your right arm and over your head. Once you adjust everything the way you want it is very comfortable even with weight.

DURABILITY:
I have not tested this product’s durability to the extreme but with the tests I have done this bag has proven to be durable. From drops with weight in it to minor abrasions on rough surfaces this bag handled it all.

FINAL DECISION:

In all this bag is a very solid choice for someone who wants a small bag to carry around with them when a larger bag isn’t an option. This would fit your everyday items like a tablet, phone, netbook or other small laptop, pens, paper, or just for transporting small goods. Hope you found this review helpful! This review will be edited with specific measurements for each pocket and overall size of the bag. Stay tuned for the updates.

query: I'm looking for a solid and affordable barbell for my workouts. I need something that's about 5 feet long and can fit standard 1-inch plates. I want to make sure it's durable, but I've noticed some reviews mention rough spots. Are those small imperfections a concern during use? Also, I've read that the spinlock collars can loosen during exercises like bicep curls. Is there a way to keep them secure or any tips for using it effectively? Lastly, how does this bar perform for heavier lifts like bench pressing? Would it be suitable for around 150-200 pounds?
ori_review:
This bar is exactly what it says. 5' long, 1" wide (fits standard plates, NOT 2" OLYMPIC PLATE). Weighed about 12lbs on my scale. Really, I can't imagine getting a better value on this. Went to a few local stores, Walmart, Academy, etc, and couldn't find a place that beat the price. And this is a solid piece of metal, so no one could beat the quality either.

There are a few small things. There were small rough spots on the bar, like other people mentioned, but nothing that felt like it could be a problem during a workout. It looks like it could really comfortable fit 4-6 plates, but given that it claims a max of 250, you probably won't need more than 3.

The spinlock collars do slip a bit, and you'l have to re-tighten them as you exercise. I like doing bicep curls with it, so the swaying motion causes the plates to spin and the collars to start loosening. To address that, I added a small rubber washer before I put the plates on to help keep them more secure, and to add some tension to prevent loosening. I'll be adding photos of that later. This isn't 100% necessary, but the collars spin on so easily that it makes sense they loosen easily too.

FOR EXERCISES:
Seems a little short for bench pressing, so if you're looking to get into serious chest exercises (200lbs+), you might want to look for an 6' Olympic bar instead. But for lighter presses (~150lbs) it should be perfect. It's my favorite to use for bicep curls. Overhead presses for the shoulders are great here too. The only thing I don't 100% recommend: I like doing hip thrusts when I'm working my glutes, but at 1" thin, it does dig into you a bit if you've got it loaded with weights. Otherwise, really versatile given its size.

query: I'm looking for a deep storage box with adjustable compartments that is durable enough to store heavy and sharp objects. How well does it hold up against wear and tear, especially the lid and hinges? I'm also interested in whether it's suitable for storing items with oversized bases, as I need to fit my collection comfortably and safely. Can you confirm if this box is indeed as tough and functional as advertised?
ori_review:
The Plano 3630 is exactly what it is advertised as: a deep depth multiple bin storage box with adjustable compartments.

The superiority of this box is due to several features:

1) The box is molded from a 'soft' thermoplastic -- instead of cracking or fracturing the box may scratch or dent, but stay intact and whole. Many cheaper boxes are made from harder plastics with lower elasticity and hence lifespans. This is particularly useful if you are using the box to store heavy/sharp/metal objects.

2) The box-top clamps (aka the yellow things) are made from a tougher, harder wearing plastic than the box itself.. it is unlikely that the lid clamps will wear out sooner than the box. The clips to which the clamps hold are fairly large and deep and should also stand up well to wear. Again, cheaper boxes will wear out quickly in this area.

The unit appears to be of reasonable quality, although I haven't used it very much yet to see how it does over the long haul (provided I don't lose it!). Best features: 1) The fiberglass ribs - I expect these to hold up better than the typical lightweight and highly bendable ribs that are found in drugstore umbrellas. 2) The Up/Down button - I normally expect an umbrella to have button or switch that opens it. Over the years, between a couple of moves and loaning things out, my once complete weight set purchased in the mid 80s, has dwindled down to a few bits and pieces. And while I still have the curling and dumbbell bars as well as some of the plates, the straight barbell bar necessary for many other types of exercises went missing some years ago. As I have not done any lifting for some time, other than some light dumbbell exercises, this wasn't an issue until I recently decided to start in again to help tone up an aging physique.

This Sunny Health & Fitness 60 inch bar fits my needs perfectly. The fact that it is shorter than a typical 6 or 7 foot weight bar is actually a plus for me, as I am using it indoors in my "man-cave" where I have my TV, stereo equipment, and a number of bookcases filled with CDs and DVDs. I purposely wanted a shorter bar so there might be less chance of unintentionally banging into things about the place. And since my days of being able to bench 300 plus pounds are but a distant memory, any amount of weight I will be using will fit quite easily and safely onto this shorter bar (which I believe has a 250 pound limit). The threaded star locks do need to be re-tightened every so often to keep the plates snug, but I feel this is an acceptable trade-off for the security of having the plates held on by at least several inches of threaded rod, rather than just a clamp. An extra plus is that the star locks from my old curling bar fit this new bar as well, should I wish to double up. Of course, spinning the lock collars off and on is a bit more time consuming as well, but since I do not change weights frequently, this presents no problem for me. With approximately a 37 inch span between the inner plate stops, I am able to adjust my grip width to pretty much whatever I need.

This is a solid one piece weight bar for use with 1 inch plates (NOT 2 inch Olympic plates). It seems to be of good quality, and priced fairly in these days of soaring costs for exercise equipment. It arrived well packed and shrink wrapped inside a long rectangular package, with no assembly required, other than spinning the star locks off, adding some weights, and spinning the locks back on. And you're ready to go. I'm certain there are probably better bars out there. But if you are looking for a good value in something safe and solid to utilize with a moderate amount of weight, this is an ideal choice. Recommended.

Some reviews and other information on the web comment on the inaccuracy of heart rate monitors for workouts. Let's say you did a one hour workout and burned 600 calories according to the watch. So if you typically burn 100 calories an hour 600-100 = 500 extra calories from working out.

query: I'm looking for an inflatable stand-up paddleboard that is durable and easy to transport, especially on my motorcycle. I want something that offers good stability and has a comfortable standing area. I've read that there are many options out there with varying prices and qualities, and I want to make sure I choose one that will hold up well in real-world conditions, especially on rocky or muddy terrain. Can you recommend a board that fits these needs and has a good reputation based on user reviews?
ori_review:
I was first introduced to stand up paddle boarding about a year ago. I enjoyed the boating aspect but also like the requirement for good balance. Having spent time kayaking and canoeing, SUP seemed like a nice change up. A few months later, while camping with some friend, I had a chance to use their paddle boards. I hadn’t realized that their SUP boards were inflatable. The boards were so rigid and stiff, it didn’t seem like what I would have envisioned as something inflatable. ISUPs struck me as an excellent idea. So I began researching something I could get for my camper for trips by the water. I also envisioned throwing the ISUP on the back of my motorcycle. A double adventure: riding and paddling – something I thought I would never be able to do.

There are so many boards out there. The prices range from low to high. I really didn’t know what to expect comparing a very expensive board (>$1000) to something inexpensive(<$300). After pouring through numerous websites – some useful, some little more than a random aggregation of a robot’s search of paddleboards – and tons of Amazon reviews I came down to selecting the ROC ISUP. The reviews were pretty good. The price was reasonable. And it was available. So many of the Amazon selections were unavailable or back-ordered for several weeks. I like the multi-layer design of the board as durability was high on my list of requirements. And I like how it was lighter than a lot of other comparable boards.

The board came quickly and was packaged as advertised. I did a quick test run in our little pond. It wasn’t too bad to pump up and assemble. I like that the package had everything I needed and it all fit in the one bag. Encouraged I scheduled a trip to take the board out on some tidal estuaries I like to visit. And I planned to do it on my motorcycle.

Everything fit easily in the supplied ROC travel bag. It isn’t terribly heavy, but I am not sure how long I would want to carry it on my back - say for a hike to some remote lake. As to putting it on the back of my motorcycle, it fit pretty nicely across my passenger seat and didn’t seem to affect the balance. The bag appears durable enough. And it survived my trip without incident.

I arrived at my destination some 300 miles later and unpacked everything. Real world conditions can be much rougher and I would be seeing how well (durability) the board held up. I didn’t baby it, but I did try to be careful. I rolled it out and pumped it up in a gravel parking lot. No issues and it didn’t seem to be bothered by the rocks. During my outing on the water I avoided oyster and clam beds as those would be sure to tear up the board. Fortunately there are not many of those in this particular area. However, there was plenty of opportunity to drag it through tidal mud banks and it didn’t seem to have any problems. My biggest fear was it getting damaged and leaking leaving me to slog back to the boat dock. I am happy to say that it didn’t happen and I feel pretty confident it would take some serious abuse to cause a leak.

I like the top area where you stand. It gives nice traction. But on the down side, it will capture dirt and hold on to it. Tidal mud flats have very fine mud and even after hosing off the board there is still a little staining (see picture of board in the grass.) That doesn’t bother me. I intend to use the board and that is just going to happen.

I like the multiple D rings and the bungee hold down in front. Useful for holding my pack and ropes and gear. The paddle works fine and seem sturdy. I like how it breaks down for storage and transport. The little dry bag is useful for small stuff and kept the items dry. Reading some of the older reviews, it looked like the pump to board interface might be problematic. But it looks like ROC listened to the reviews and redesigned the connection. It was a simple twist on connection just like the cover for the inflation port. Very easy to use.

I am happy with the purchase. Time will tell how well everything holds up but I am encouraged after 1 outing. I will try to get back to this review in a year or so and give an update.

ori_review:
First off, this jump rope is great and terraFIT has the best customer service evar! They actually take customer feedback into account when designing/re-designing products!

Anyway, everything about this thing is small/svelte. The handles are small in diamter and very light, and the rope is a thin cable that is coated in plastic. The handles are an outer black plastic piece, with an inner white plastic piece that rotates and is connected to the rope. There is an adjustment in the handle to change how much movement/"play" there is between the two parts of the handle, and you want to double check that it is set loose enough for the inner white plastic piece to rotate freely.

The rope simply slides through eyelets at the ends of the handles and has two small metal stops that let you adjust the length of the rope, which you WILL need to do (it comes pretty long). They advise that once you have the rope length adjusted that you cut it to suit, so you don't have a bunch of extra rope swinging around.

The carrying case is a really nice touch.

All in all this is a fantastic jump rope that can achieve some crazy speeds because of how thing / light it is, VERY easy to spin it quick enough for double-unders. On the other hand the rope is so light that you pretty much cannot feel it swinging around you. IT IS VERY DIFFERENT THAN A ROPE BASED JUMP ROPE that you may have used in elementary school. A normal thick rope is easy to feel swinging around your body so you can pretty much feel when you should jump. WIth this TerraFit rope you MUST develop a rythym because you cannot tell where the rope is at very well. This is a skill that will take some time to develop if you aren't used to jumping rope a lot.
I read the reviews that said "not for beginners" and didn't understand what they meant, but it's the heft/weight of the rope that makes all the difference in the technique that you have to use. Once you get used to it though it's great!

End of the day this rope is worth buying for 3 reason 1) you can spin it super fast 2) it comes with a spare rope 3) terrafit is an awesome company.

query: I'm looking for an inflatable mattress that is easy to set up and move around, particularly one that can accommodate my guests comfortably. Finally, how important is it to break in the mattress a couple of days before use for optimal performance? Any advice would be greatly appreciated!
ori_review:
I purchased a queen size and a twin size mattress as extra space for guests. I didn't sleep on them myself, but they were very happy with them and we had no trouble with leaks or deflation over a week stay. Setup was easy and the mattresses are also very easy to move around once inflated. Inflation is fast and setup of the mattresses themselves is easy.

Because I was of course worried about a good experience for my guests, I did inflate the mattresses two days before their arrival, which may have helped with 'breaking in' the mattresses so they would perform at their best. Of course, not everyone has space to do this.

The queen mattress is definitely a better value than the twin if you have the space for it. Not only is it only marginally more expensive, with a higher weight capacity, but also it is longer. I bought one of each because I knew I had space constraints. The twin might not be long enough for tall adult guests.

Sheets are kind of an adventure, given that there is no place to tuck in the ends of a sheet other than underneath, and these mattresses are the height of a mattress plus box spring, and on the whole a bit slippery. Fitted sheets basically work but the top sheet is just going to be loose.

Because they're not the durability of a real bed, you probably don't want to set them up in situations where people would want to sit on them or use them other than as a bed. This sounds obvious, but I can see how sitting on an edge might create some of the problems people have had with leaks or failures. Because they are nice and very tall, it's tempting to use them in this way.

I fretted for days trying to figure out what mattresses to buy and was glad these worked out so well. I didn't need the customer service but I did appreciate getting several emails letting me know it was available and reminding me that there was help available if I needed it.

The mask is hard plastic and may limit your visibility, but it can be removed. My buddy doesn't like it so he spars without it and he still loves the headgear. I'm willing to sacrifice the slightly less visibility and the occasional tease from other boxers in the gym to make sure I walk out of the gym without a crooked nose. query: I'm looking for a high-quality poncho liner that is made in the USA, but I'm concerned about the price. I want to know if the quality justifies the cost, especially compared to cheaper options that I've used before. How do the materials, stitching, and durability compare, and would it be worth it for field use despite being overpriced? Also, are there alternatives to buying new that still meet high standards?
ori_review:
This is a genuine, US made poncho liner, and the quality is top notch. However I do feel that it is way overpriced. It should cost no more than $50-$60. That said, I’ll note the differences between this genuine liner (henceforth referred to as “US” liner) and my USGI industries (made in China) liner (henceforth referred to as “China” liner) so that you can decide if it is worth purchasing for the insane price.
1. The stitching - the stitches on the US liner are closer together (I.e. there are more stitches per inch of fabric) and hence it is stronger and will stand more abuse than the China liner.

2.the trim around the liner perimeter - on the China liner, there is a gap where the trim overlaps itself, large enough to fit a finger or pen into it. This can potentially get snagged on something and result in a tear. On the US liner, wherever the trim overlaps itself the overlap is sewn shut, so there is no chance of it snagging. Also, on the US liner, the stitching that connects the trim to the main blanket is stitched higher up from the edge of the trim than on the China liner. This will prevent the fabric of the trim from coming loose easily. The trim stitching on the China liner is very close to the edge of the trim material.

3. The ropes/tie-outs - on US liner, the tie-outs are made of genuine, gutted milspec paracord. The China liner is made of some kind of synthetic rope material that is obviously not as strong and robust as the paracord and looks like it would easily fray/wear out from heavy use. The bartack stitching used to attach the tie outs to the liner is also more robust and better done on the US liner.

4. The Filling - the US liner has noticeably more filling than the China liner

These are the main differences that I’ve noticed. I wanted a liner that I could trust in the field, so I bit the bullet and bought this, but at home I sleep with my China liner. I’ve had the China liner for less than a year and some of the stitching is already beginning to come out. And that is simply from using it as a blanket on my bed. For home use, the China liner is definitely worth it due to its much lower price tag. If you want a genuine US quality liner for harder use, then you have to decide for yourself if it us worth paying double what the liner is worth. Another option is to buy a used one in good condition. You can get them around $40-$50 if you are Lucky. I hope this review was helpful.
In summary, it is top quality, but extremely overpriced

query: I'm looking for a reliable recumbent bike that offers comfort and ease of assembly. I have neck issues, so I need a bike that allows me to maintain a neutral posture. Can you tell me more about the features and assembly process of the Exerpeutic 900XL? Also, how does the console work for tracking different metrics? I'm particularly interested in the seat comfort and resistance options as well. Thanks!
ori_review:
This is my second purchase of an Exerpeutic recumbent bike. (I previously bought a very similar model about 5 years ago, and my spouse and I have both used it every couple of days without any problems.) I purchased this current model, Exerpeutic 900XL, for our second home based on the great experience we had with the one we previously purchased.

In both cases, the assembly process took an hour or two. It can be managed by one moderately strong person, but be aware that when the box initially arrives at your home you'll likely need two people to carry it to the spot where you'll be setting up. There are a LOT of big and little parts, but if you are methodical and read each step carefully and take your time, in the end you'll have a very reliable bike. The instructions are written in easy-to-understand English (with the exception of a couple of words that puzzled me, but nothing that interfered with assembly). Be aware: you'll be using an (included) Allen wrench during assembly, and also a combination wrench/screwdriver device they include. There is nothing that you'll need in order to assemble this bike that isn't included in the box, which I appreciate.

I like that the Exerpeutic 900XL has a little lip on the console where you can rest your tablet (to distract yourself with Netflix if you're so inclined).

The console rotates through different sets of information (elapsed time, heart rate, etc.). If you want it to stay on one rather than rotating, like my preference to keep it on the time setting, just press the "mode" button for about a second and the current screen will become fixed (that is, the screen stops rotating between different sets of info).

My spouse and I both find the seat very comfortable. The seat positioning is easy to adjust. The tension knobs offers many options, from very low resistance (1) to highest (8).

I have neck issues that make it hard for me to use a regular bike or a spin bike. With this recumbent bike, I'm able to maintain a neutral posture that allows me to keep my chin tucked in and puts zero strain on my neck muscles. It's delightful.

If you need to relocate the bike, you just lift the back of the bike (which is not too heavy; most of the weight is at the front) and tip it forward. Then you can use the small wheels on the front of the bike to wheel it around.

For the price, this is a surprisingly excellent piece of equipment. I have no complaints and in fact I'm so happy I bought the same brand a second time!

ori_review:

"The Rolly Thing" sticks incredibly well to a clean car surface; window or metal. Wipe the surface first, do one side at a time (you'll need two hands).

The point is to lift HALF the boat at one time. Set the stern on the ground, lift the bow, lay it on the Rolly Thing, get behind the boat and shove. Rolly Thing keeps the boat on track, keeps it from sliding sideways as you load, makes your shoving it onto the roof easier, and is an all around useful object especially if you find yourself doing this solo.

I suspect it could be an additional support rack ON your roof (I need a block under my front bulkhead) but as with anything on your roof going down the road at 55mph, you need to tie it down/lash it to the boat as well as use the suction.

I got one of these rather than risking questionable quality of similar roller-loaders, because I had used it and KNOW it works. Another review I read compared three, and this one came out on top.

I'll add that the softer (but dense) foam of this roller keeps the boat from slipping and sliding.

ori_review:
Just got this, and it's working out well as a neat, efficient way to store my dumbbell set. I have a set of Fitness Republic neoprene weights in 3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 17.5 lb sizes. On the sides I keep the 10, 12, 15 and 17.5 lb weights. The 17.5 lb weight doesn't really fit properly - it doesn't go all the way in and sit flush against the rack - but it works ok. Probably weights any larger than that wouldn't work in the sides. I keep the 3, 5 and 8 lb weights on the top bar. The 3 lb weights sit lopsided because they are not large enough. I had never encountered a locknut before, so I was a little confused at first, but with a little research and a trip to the hardware store, I was able to get it together. I got a Craftsman socket wrench set and used the 13 mm size socket. This fits over the locknut and holds it in place while you tighten the bolt with the allen wrench. You could probably do it with an adjustable wrench, although I have to say the socket wrench made it very easy. It was pretty easy to hold it steady and I didn't have to apply a lot of pressure to tighten it up. I'm not handy by any stretch, so if I can do this, so can you.

Its a nice little dumbbell rack. Doesn't take up a lot of space. Holds my stuff. Feels very sturdy. Not really "pretty" but pretty enough. It's a smooth black iron - no unfinished or rough spots, and no odor like I've seen mentioned in reviews of other racks. query: I'm looking for a reliable bicycle lock setup that allows me to secure both my front and back wheels effectively. I want something that I can carry easily and use for both short and long-term parking.
ori_review:
The Sheldon Brown method for safely securing your bike is to use a U-lock on the back wheel, threaded through the rear triangle, and a cable to secure the front wheel. I take this a step further, since I know that a cable lock is like warm butter to a set of bolt cutters, with a 2nd U-lock. Having one black lock and one white lock makes it really easy to know which key goes to which lock. I don't know if I could manage with 2 black locks.

In terms of the lock design, this is almost the best lock Kryptonite sells. There is a way to defeat this lock, but it isn't something that anyone but the most elite criminals would do for a bike. The price and weight difference between these U-locks and the highest rated makes this a real bargain. As stated, I carry 2 in my saddle bag and use them whenever I park my ride outside.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable air mattress for camping that feels like a regular bed. It should be easy to inflate and deflate, with a design that prevents sagging and bouncing. I also want to know if it can accommodate sitting up on the edge without bowing. Additionally, I'm interested in the customer service experience for any potential issues. Can you recommend a product that meets these criteria?
ori_review:
Camping should be the art of being comfortable in nature. This mattress lives up to that epigram. It's high enough off the ground to make getting up a breeze (i.e. you're pretty much sitting up). We sleep as well as we do when we're at home. Not a saggy, back-breaking, close-to-home, air mattress, but "holy cow, can you believe we're *camping*" mattress. That is, it's not an air mattress, it's not a camping mattress: it's a mattress that just happens to have air in it that you can bring camping. It doesn't sag, it doesn't bounce, it doesn't do anything other than be comfortable. The pump is super easy to use, the valve design is great, and inflation/deflation and repacking is a breeze.

[Edit: I forgot to add one of the most important things: the sides stay strong. You can roll over and let your arms/legs dangle about or sit up on it with your feet over the side and the edge doesn't sag or bow. ]

For context, we take this to several music festivals a year. The portable, chargeable pump makes that very simple (as does its small footprint when folded). My wife had NEVER camped before we met, and was a little hesitant at making the adventure. But, knowing that I'm a comfort junky (her words), she trusted me to make things go well. And go well it did.

We got our first Soundasleep back in 2015. A curious pooch (who brings a dog to a music festival?!) punctured it badly enough that a repair didn't hold. We didn't need to shop around and research again --- we knew we loved this mattress.

Our second one has been just as awesome with no complaints. And for several years it hasn't just been my wife and I, it's been the two of us and our five/then six/then seven/then eight/ and now nine year old sleeping with us (we don't go over the max weight allowance; when that happens he's getting his own tent).

And topping it all off, what little service/questions we've had have been instantly answered by awesome customer service reps. "Instantly" as in "holy cow, they got back to us already?!"

So, yeah. Great product that hits all the important areas: very, very comfortable; easy to set-up/take-down, and comes with great service. Just keep it away from big dogs!

Open the box and INSPECT EVERYTHING BEFORE starting assembly. Check the welds, lay out the pieces so you know what is what, and DO NOT, repeat, DO NOT just cut the screws and bolts out until you need them (an exacto knife makes easy work of this.) Some folks have complained about welds and mismatched pieces, but I can't say the same for me. In fact, it's probably the most well packaged gizmo I've purchased in a while with every single piece plastic wrapped and then with foam inlays. Form fit and finish are A++

Assembly - Takes about an hour - do yourself a favor in advance and have a 13mm socket wrench, and 13mm box wrench handy. Save your knuckles and frustration levels and skip the lousy wrench that comes with it. The Allen wrench is perfectly fine for the couple of bolts that use it, and the phillips head on the end is fine too. As I mentioned, open the fasteners AS NEEDED. Here's a trick - lock the table flat when you are trying to put the foot bar on. Or have a helper. Way easier than trying to hold it up and get the pins in at the same time. Other than that, it's just a handful of nuts and bolts.

Use - I use mine barefoot in flip flops all the time. It's got foam ankle braces that (should) soften over time, but you can leave them out in the sun to help them soften up too. When you get on this thing, MAKE SURE THE ANKLE BRACES ARE AS TIGHT AS YOU CAN GET THEM. Remember, that's what's holding your entire body weight. Socks and sneakers will probably work for most people, but you have to get used to it. And again - tight as you can get it for safety.

Using an inversion table is not simply strapping in and hanging upside down for an hour. If you've ever had spinal traction, you know start slow, and traction should only be for a minute or 2 at a time. Don't jump right on and go for broke hanging at 90 degrees or you are going to be really sore. 2 minutes up for every 1 minute down to be safe. I usually do this 3x a day.

Happy hanging!

query: I'm looking for an electric scooter that can handle long daily commutes, ideally around 12 miles round trip. It should have a good battery range, perform well in high-speed settings, and manage rough terrains like potholes and road debris smoothly. I'm concerned about safety, especially since I've heard that scooters can be more dangerous than bikes, so I want to know how well it handles obstacles without suspension. Additionally, if I were to consider a seat for it, how would that affect my ride on bumpy roads? Any recommendations or advice based on these needs would be appreciated.
ori_review:
I've been using this scooter for my daily commute for the past week, about 12 miles round trip, and the battery is still more than half full afterwards even on the highest speed setting, so I believe in eco mode (11mph) it could definitely achieve the advertised 40 mile range.

In sport mode (19-20mph) it has smooth acceleration and handling, I have no problem weaving around potholes and road debris. The headlamp and taillight are very useful during night rides, providing adequate lighting.

In drive mode (16mph) the throttle is perfectly smooth for traversing tight spaces and carefully moving around pedestrians and sidewalks, there's no suspension, but it can handle a bumpy ride so long as you bend your knees and prepare for curbs and bumps.

I'm ~185lbs and usually carry more than 20lbs of cargo with me, and this scooter has no problem reaching top speed in windy conditions or accelerating up modest hills.

I considered buying the seat for it as well, but decided against it due to my commute being quite bumpy, with lots of switching between sidewalks and roadways, so standing seems safer and more manageable.

I will update this review if my experience worsens but so far I'd absolutely recommend this scooter to anyone looking for something that can handle a long commute.

EDIT: I broke my leg riding this scooter, due to it having no suspension it does not handle obstacles larger than a small rock. It's my fault for not paying attention but please be careful on vehicles like this, scooters are a lot more dangerous than bikes.

Back story: about a year ago I was diagnosed with metatarsal neuritis, and the podiatrist put a metatarsal pad in my shoe. A couple of months ago the side of my foot started _really_ hurting, especially when getting out of bed in the morning. A (different) podiatrist said that was tendinitis and sent me to PT. Eventually I am planning to try getting rid of the metatarsal pad, and see if my new, improved gait keeps my foot happy without it.

query: I'm looking for a reliable hand warmer that heats up efficiently and lasts for around 12 hours. I've noticed some issues with loose lids on similar products; how can I fix a lid that falls off easily? Also, are there any specific instructions for use that I should be aware of to ensure it operates safely and effectively? Any tips on maximizing heat output would be appreciated!
ori_review:
It heats up a bit slower than a battery but is much better for my purposes. It generates a good amount of heat and all. Nice materials and feel. NO DIRECTIONS THOUGH.

You are supposed to use the included measuring spout/cup and pour a measured amount and then keep it upright for 2 minutes before lighting or else you will light the cat burner on fire which is not supposed to happen and drastically reduces the life of such. There should be no flame and the indication that it is working is that you will feel heat if you put your hand over the top and you may see a red glow in some parts of the cat burner. It came with a loose lid but I fixed it. fluffing the cat burner helped put out more heat and it made it last 10-11 hours roughly instead of 12. The thing burns for a good 12 hours though unmodified.

BONUS NACHOS LOOSE LID FIX: There is a problem with many of these having a lid that falls off easy. I had this in fact if i turned it upside down and moved it a bit, the lid would just fall off. To fix this flex the lid at the mouth slightly and keep doing it till the lid fits snug. The lid is flexible and is very unlikely to break however you should flex it slightly at a time and more and more. Heating up the lid will also help. This is the same technique to fix a loose insert on a zippo lighter and it's the same material and same technique and everything.

1) think of the Y roller like a set of tracks--remember the Autopia ride at Disneyland!? if you get those tracks right under your scapula, you can roll back and forward directing your movement so that you follow one track or another getting after your trouble spots from all directions without having to reposition the roller.

2) when you're after re-alignment of the upper spine and you have the single-track right up against one side of your spine, roll back and forward several times while changing where you put your arms--try "hugging yourself, extending your arms out behind you, in front and to the side until you find the position that works best for you and what your after.

3) the high density foam spines on this roller are not for everyone. consider if you like deep tissue or swedish massage. if you answer the latter, you may be looking for a less aggressive roller--don't purchase this and badmouth it, it's perfect for those of us who are of the mindset that there is no pleasure without pain.

4) it's absolutely the perfect dimension for stowing in your carry on, never leave home without it!

5) reviewers complaining about too small or difficult to balance on when aligning single-track to spine are likely on the larger size. if you're fit and/or average build you'll have no trouble figuring out how to balance over it. consider placing yourself close to a step, chair or other furniture you can reach back to and use for stabilizing the first few times or for particularly precarious 'floats'.

Warmth wise- air temps dipped down into the 20s. We were both wearing multiple layers, albeit me more than my son. (He's 14 and won't always listen, you all understand.) I even slept in my coat. With that said, I was perfectly warm, with the sole exception of my feet, but that's my own fault because I was only wearing one pair of wool socks and my feet are habitually cold anyway. My son said he got a LITTLE cold, but I don't think he wore enough layers. Even more impressive to me is that we were trying to do this trip pretty minimally. My boyfriend is former SF and strung us all up some sort of tarp contraptions about a foot or so off the ground, so none of us were even in a tent. It was pretty much this bag and nothing else between us and the air on the sides of us. Both my son and I had mats under us. His was thermal, mine was not. We both agreed that we felt warm under us. The top of the bags cinch up super tight and my son said he even got a little claustrophobic and was afraid he wouldn't be able to get out. Me, on the other hand, I found that cord and kept it pulled tight because that air was icy. There was snow under us and quite a bit of dew accumulated on us when the sun came up. Still warm and dry. Only thing I'm doing differently next time is bringing extra socks and investing in a lightweight Hyke and Byke tent because, neat as the poncho hooch was, I'm pretty certain I'd like a tent better.

query: I'm looking for a versatile exercise machine that can help me with my fitness journey. After completing a juice cleanse, I want to incorporate more healthy habits, and I recently discovered the LifePro Waver. I appreciate supportive customer service and instructional videos that feature relatable users. I've been experiencing lower back pain, and I'm curious if this machine could help alleviate that discomfort, as I've heard it has worked for others. ori_review:
I had just completed a three-day juice cleanse/detox that left me super energized and invigorated. For me, losing four pounds was nice, but the detox did something much more and inspired me to turn over a new leaf. Never too old, right? When you notice that your clothes have all shrunk, and your wife insists she didn’t do it...it’s all my doing and time to take the bull by the horns, so to speak. LOL
Upon searching for a way to bring “being healthy-minded” to the next level, I was fortunate to stumble upon the Lifepro Waver. First and foremost, kudos to Joel and his support staff. I am so pleased to have made the acquaintance of several members of their team. They all deserve a bonus! Yep, you can quote me on that!! I’m in my 60s (no Spring chicken here) and have only ever come across two companies online that are amazing in every way imaginable. Lifepro has an incredible group of people who mesh extremely well together. They extend that friendship to their customer base 100%. Sadly, oftentimes in business and the medical profession particularly, there is much disconnect, and there shouldn’t be. Big plus — I do not see that with Lifepro! You have an excellent business model and are spot on. I felt part of the family from the get-go. They tackle all questions and concerns and from their experience also foresee where their customers might be coming from and provide a comprehensive website complete with instructional videos. The videos are informative, encouraging and are easy to follow. I also like how the videos have normal people in them which helps me fit into the mindset. What I mean to convey is that if the videos were with professional body builders it would have made me feel that I didn’t fit in and that the Waver wasn’t right for me. Joel and the support staff are professional, very personable and also right there 24/7. I haven’t felt like I was left hanging on a limb when I reached out for help, even for what could be foreseen as a silly question. Keep up the good work!
I am several days into using my Waver, and one thing I liked about it immediately was the realization that it is so versatile. To me it is constructivist in design, you can move at whatever pace you’d like and combine it with other exercise tools such as resistance bands (which I had never tried but really like) and the dumbbells I already use. Important to me is that the maximum weight limit of the Waver allows for my weight and the dumbbells at the same time with many pounds to spare for when I increase the dumbbell poundage. (once very again versatile)
Another immediate benefit is the way it makes me feel. I had been experiencing an ache in my lower back making it uncomfortable to sit. Two uses of my Waver and the ache is completely gone! It seems unbelievable, but it’s true. I am so relieved.
My apologies for being so long winded, but I wanted to write thoughtfully and share the whole picture. Once again, I thank you so much.

1. Bigger kayaks (like my Malibu Two) benefit from balancing the boat on the cart (attaching it near the center).

3. The cart drags a bit in soft sand - that said, I have SOFT sand and a heavy boat.
4. The cart works very well over hard packed dirt & gravel.
5. I haven't really figured out why it needs a kickstand - maybe smaller boats / boards will benefit from this.

As far as function goes, it does a great job of carrying my Malibu Two kayak (12'6" X 36", and 70lbs with gear). The supplied strap was far too short, so I just use a length of my anchor line with a truckers hitch to secure the 'yak to the cart.

One hint for people not used to using these products - place the cart as close to center as you can, to help manage weight, and attached your strap / line to a tie down on the boat to keep the cart in place when rolling over soft sand. I take mine aboard when paddling in the harbor; just remove the wheels, fold the cart, and use a short length of line to secure to the boat.

query: I'm looking for a sleeping pad that is comfortable, lightweight, and packs down small enough to fit into a weekend bag. I’ve used many pads over the years and need one that provides a luxurious sleeping experience without taking up too much space in my pack. I also want something that is easy to inflate and has features like an integrated pump and pillow. Can the Nemo Cosmo meet these needs, and how does it compare to other high-end options in terms of comfort and insulation?
ori_review:
I believe this is the best sleeping pad I've ever seen. Five Stars.
I used to be a rock climbing guide. I guess I was super hard core. LOL. I spent quite a lot of time hiking and camping and sleeping out doors. Because of this I have had the pleasure of owning most of the sleeping pads that have been available since the 1990's. Most of the good ones were the wonderful Therm-A-Rest self-inflating products: thick and thin, short and long, shaped and rectangular. And there are the cheep ones, the cool z-fold ones, and the several varieties of dense closed-cell foam (military grade and nicer REI blue gel-type ones).
Having said that, most all of them are variations of the same theme: they're big, they take a up a lot of valuable real estate, and if you want to have enough insulation that you can tell they're there, they need to be pretty thick. They either just barely fit in a pack (taking up too much valuable real estate), or you have to strap them to the outside of your pack, also taking up valuable real estate - especially if you are carrying both camping and climbing gear....

When I was shopping for this I was primarily looking for a pad that would be comfortable, light and not take up much space. I wanted one that would easily fit INTO a weekend bag for packing light, maybe traveling without a tent. I was envisioning doing some self-contained bicycle packing, and longer multi-day solo trips.

That's what I like about this Nemo Cosmo. It's really neat, it's a little different, and compared to any other pad I'd want to sleep on, it packs down really really small. With no real effort mine packs down to a 5.5" x 10" cylinder. It weighs about the same as the other medium-thick pads, but once it is inflated it is actually VERY thick. Mucho Grande thick. Now, I realize this is not THE LIGHTEST nor the SMALLEST pad out there. But I believe it is one of the THICKEST and most LUXURIOUSLY COMFORTABLE ones. Sometimes life is full of wonderful little compromises, but at 2lbs 4 oz, there's not much compromise here. The Nemo Cosmo comes with its own carry sack and an integrated repair kit. However, after how small it gets, the feature that most sets it apart from its competition it is its integrated 'soft' foot pump. If you get a chance to actually play with a bunch of the different pads out there, this is a really BIG deal. Most of them are a real pain to inflate, they take forever, or they require some special additional apparatus that costs more money..... The Nemo Cosmo has a non-intrusive, integrated pump, and it Freaking Rocks! It takes me about 30-45 seconds of casual foot pumping effort to fully inflate the pad. Using just the pump it is easy to over inflate the pad until it feels too hard -- which is perfect because next to the integrated pillow there is a handy little screw-valve so that once you lay down you can easily let air out and 'fine tune' the pressure to whatever feels right. Yep, there's an integrated pillow too. Not only that, but all the pump mechanism and intake/exhaust valves are down at your feet, so they won't ever bother you while sleeping. They say this Insulated version of the Nemo Cosmo 'has a layer of PrimaLoft." This appears to be a thin layer of fleece laminated to the inside of the top half of the pad. It feels like its about the thickness of your standard fleece sweater, which is not a lot of insulation compared to the expanding foam Therm-A-Rest pads. Then again, without a pad, I almost never feel cold from the ground. I am am much more likely to feel the hardness or the bumpiness: I would prefer to have a more comfortable sleeping pad over a more insulated one. If I was sleeping on snow or somewhere properly frozen I don't know if this Nemo Cosmo would be the best pad for me, but it might me. And the last detail is a minor one, but I like how the baffles of the air chamber run side to side, not lengthwise along the pad. Why? I don't want the pad to 'wrap up' around me as I sink into the middle. The horizontal baffles seem to offer more consistent support than lengthwise ones.

I am a recovering Gear nerd. Before I spent $150 buying yet another sleeping pad, I spent a good bit of time reading up on ALL the pads currently available, then I went to several major retailers of the high-end good ones (places like REI) and spent several hours at each physically fiddled with, inflating and laying on all the interesting ones. I had conversations with the people who sold the various pads. I LOVE smart attention to details. I care a LOT about little things like fit and finish, simplicity in design, about seam strength, and whether or not a product FEELS solid and durable. I care a lot about comfort and aesthetics.
I am kind of shocked to say it, but the Nemo Cosmo exceeds all my expectations, I think it is noticeably better than the other pads out there, and I expect it bless many adventures with a good night's sleep.

query: I'm looking for a workout bench that is easy to assemble and feels solid without wobbling. Can you provide tips on how to avoid issues during assembly, like handling the bolts and washers? Also, what should I do if I can't find the allen wrench needed for assembly? Finally, how can I ensure that I don't accidentally stack washers when putting it together? For my workouts with dumbbells, I need something reliable and durable that fits my budget.
ori_review:
The bench assembled easily and feels solid with no wobbling. My first work out with the new bench went well. I'll only work out with dumbbells, so I don't envision any issues in terms of weight loads.

A few recommendations...

1. Be careful when opening the shipping box. The package that contains the bolts and washers had opened in transit. Had I opened the box in the wrong area, it could have been a bear to find the washers after they spilled out. Fortunately, I opened the shipping box on the living room carpet, so it was easy to corral the runaway washers.

2. Do not tighten any of the bolts until you have all of the bolts in and they've begun to thread. You have to jiggle things a bit to get all holes lined up. If you tighten things down ahead of time, you won't be able to jiggle the pieces enough to get all of the bolts threaded.

3. There is an allen wrench provided in the shipment. (It was the only tool I needed to complete the assembly.) At first, I didn't see it and thought I'd have to head to the store to buy a metric allen wrench to tighten the bolts, but as I rummaged through the packaging material, the allen wrench appeared. I'm not sure if it was in the same package as the bolts and washers and had broken free, or if it was free swimming in the box. Anyway, it is there, so keep an eye out for it.

4. The washers tend to cling to one another, so it is easy to put two washers on a bolt and not notice. I ended up thinking I was two washers short as I was ready to put the last two bolts into place. On closer examination, I noticed two of the partially inserted bolts had two washers on them.

For the price and for my purpose, it fits the bill.

query: I'm looking for a comfortable and adjustable backpack that can handle a lot of gear for a father/son backpacking trip. I want to ensure that it fits well for both me and my son, who is still growing. I'm also interested in how well it performs in wet conditions, as I need something that can keep our gear dry if we get caught in the rain. Can anyone recommend a pack that meets these needs?
ori_review:
My son just turned 10, so I purchased this pack so we could go on our first father/son backpacking excursion. He was carrying a Teton Summit 1500, which was perfect for his size, but which meant that I was carrying most of the major gear in the Teton Scout 3400.

The first thing that impressed me about the Scout were the adjustment options. I'm 6'0" and I was I bit worried that this was more of a junior sized pack, but after I made the torso height adjustment and followed the suggested setup instructions, I found that this pack fit me like a glove. It was very stable and very comfortable, even with gear for two.

Speaking of gear, and as others have pointed out, the second most impressive feature of this pack is just how much gear I could pack/attach. With the aid of a quality compression bag, I was able to pack two 40 degree bags, 2 pillows, tyvek, extra clothes, food, stove, fuel, and a couple of other odds and ends in just the main compartment (with the false bottom removed). The side and top compartments are spacious and easy to get at, and the extra straps, loops, and bungees on the exterior of the pack provided a very secure ride for my hatchet, camp shovel, water bottle, tent, and camping pad.

The third, and most unexpected, impressive feature of the Scout was the effectiveness of the attached rain cover. We wanted to pack as light as possible, so we took a tent that didn't have any extra room for the packs. Instead, we hung them both up on improvised hooks, which may or may not have resembled a tree branch tied to a tree trunk--completely exposed. As the forecast for the evening was looking a bit wet, I put the rain covers on both packs and hoped for the best. 12 hours of heavy precipitation later, we removed the covers and both packs and their contents were bone dry. It was amazing!

The Teton Scout 3400 is 100% quality. Not only will I enjoy this pack for years to come, but I imagine that my son will inherit it when he gets a bit older and is able to handle a "full sized" pack. Also, knowing that I can adjust it to fit him as he grows makes this relatively small investment even that much more of a no-brainer.

query: I'm looking for an affordable bike trainer that is easy to assemble and allows me to attach my bike without too much hassle. I want to know if it includes a front wheel stabilizer and how noisy it is during use. Also, can I make small resistance adjustments while riding? I'm particularly interested in finding a sturdy model that does the job well without breaking the bank, especially for indoor workouts. Any recommendations or insights would be appreciated!
ori_review:
I was somewhat reluctant to purchase this based on some of the product reviews, but I rolled the dice and was NOT disappointed! Let me refute some claims in other reviews:
(A) It is VERY easy to assemble. There is ONE bolt to install the resistance wheel to the trainer frame. The instructions are pictorial only, but every screw, washer, bolt, and tool (included) are labelled. If you can follow "align bolt A with washer B into hole C and tighten with bolt D", you'll be fine. Its not rocket science. After attaching the resistance wheel to the trainer frame, be sure to align the tightening screw (with the big nob) into the bolt on the resistance wheel. Again, its not rocket science.
(B) Attaching your bike to the trainer frame might be a little awkward the first time, especially if you are doing it by yourself, but its not difficult. After you get it right, removing the bike and reattaching it is easy. With some bikes, you may have to replace the axle pin (included), but I did not have to do that. My 25 year old mountain bike attached fine the first time. RECOMMENDATION: Do not rush this step or you may find your bike slipping out of the trainer frame and you flying across room on your moving bike!.
(C) A front wheel stabilizer IS included. Once my bike (with 26" mountain bike tires) was attached in the trainer frame, the front wheel sat 3" above the ground and the real wheel sat about 2" above the ground. I am using this in my basement with 7' ceilings and still have headroom when I ride.
(D) Noise. Its not silent, but I would not describe it as "noisy" either. I would compare the noise to that of a someone using a vacuum cleaner on the floor above you. Its more of a "drone" or a "whir". Pitch varies with speed and - for me - at a low-moderate speed the noise definitely gets more pronounced, but is less so at low, moderate, and higher speeds. My trainer sits on a "commercial" type carpet that you'd find in an office building. To say one needs "noise-cancelling headphones to watch TV while riding" seems way out of whack with what I am experiencing.
(E) An adjustment dial can be attached to your handlebars, nut it does not do much (I'll agree with that!) but - once I set the base resistance using the nob at the back of the resistance wheel (while I am off the bike), I am able to use my front and rear derailleurs to adjust resistance somewhat (its not as pronounced as when you are riding on the road, though). You can then use adjustment dial to make small resistance adjustments within a gear (if that makes any sense). NOTE: I used 2 or 3 small Velcro straps to attach the adjustment cable to the frame. This is not necessary if you plan on using your bike in- and out-doors, or moving the bike between uses...but I plan on keeping it where it is until spring/summer, so the Velcro just keeps things tight and tidy.
(F) The workout: Call me Captain Obvious, but the higher the resistance you set initially will determine how hard you work. I'm still playing with it to find the right setting. What feels "right" at first may be too tough to sustain. My first workout kicked my butt. You will likely find yourself making many small adjustments at first until you find your "sweet spot"
BOTTOM LINE: Looking for a budget bike trainer, this is the one. There is nothing out there less expensive than this. Its sturdy AND it does the job. Are there better, quieter, more feature-rich units out there? Sure...but a 2 or 3 times the cost, or more! If you are looking to buy an inexpensive indoor bike trainer to help lose your COVID-15, this is definitely worth the investment, IMHO
