query: I'm looking for a lightweight sleeping pad that keeps me warm in very cold temperatures, ideally with a high R value. I've had issues with gear malfunctioning in the backcountry before, so I want something reliable. I also need it to be easy to pack away, though I can compromise a bit on that for better performance. Additionally, if I sleep on my back, I want to know if there is a wider version available to accommodate my shoulder width. Are there any tips for inflating it efficiently without losing air? I've heard mixed reviews about the inflation method and would appreciate some advice.
ori_review:
I've only used it for a week in the backcountry so far, but I have to say, this thing has kept me warm! Temperatures dipped into the low teens every night, and not once did I get cold, or feel the sleeping pad was not up to par. Now, I was also using a 0° bag, so that plays a part, and I did not compare this directly to my old Thermarest that has an R value of ~1.5, nor do I plan on doing that comparison, mainly because this thing is lighter than my other pad, even while providing an R value in the high 5s.

Now, it is expensive, but let's put some things in perspective. Most other sleeping pads will still cost you $70-$120. So you spend, at most, $100 more than an alternative sleeping pad. This thing will not let you down in the backcountry. If you've ever had a piece of your gear malfunction, or simply not be up to the task, in the mountains, you'll know that you'd easily give up only $100 right then and there to fix it. This is not a once-a-trip purchase. Remember, this thing is basically your mattress in the wilderness. A mattress is one of those things in real life that you should absolutely not skimp on or short change yourself.

I'm providing a 5 star value based on my positive view on this item. It is very light, and very warm; a great combo.

Some possible negatives for some people:
-If you sleep on your back, you may want to get the wide version. I'm 6'1" with wide shoulders, and if I lay down naturally on my back, my arms fall in such a way that they are not completely on the pad. For me, this isn't a problem, as when I do sleep on my back in the backcountry, I usually cross my arms in front of my chest anyway, or even put them down my pants for that sweet sweet warmth...although they smell the next day :(
-The internal baffling makes it hard to fold in half once you're ready to store it, in comparison to other sleeping pads. It naturally wants to fold open, and it can be frustrating. For me, that's a sacrifice I just make, because to have a pad with an R value of 5.7 or whatever, and weigh less than a pound, I'm willing to be frustrated for 2 minutes while packing up, rather than frustrated for 8 or 10 hours while I lay but cannot sleep because I'm cold.
-The stuff sack includes a hole which you can use in order to blow up the pad. However, it slips off easily without much force, and requires you to be quite gentle. If it does fall off, then you lose a bunch of air/time. I find it easier to just blow it up by mouth. The turtle beats the hare here. If you can do it perfectly, it's quicker with the stuff sack. I've yet to do it perfectly. Blowing it up by mouth is not that difficult, but some people feel the need to rush, and then they get light headed. Simply breath in through your nose as if you were breathing at any other time, then exhale through your mouth into the pad. Takes a tad longer, but you won't get dizzy from breathing in huge breaths, and breathing them out at a fast pace.

This is a great headlamp when I'm out in the dark with the cougars and other beasts lurking around the bend. I have really great visibility.

I enjoy how easy it is to adjust up and down depending if I'm running uphill, down, or flat.

The battery life is amazing. I never need to use the brightest setting, but I do right at twilight and I'll explain why below.

The reactive lighting is a bit of a sham. It totally works, but part of the reason the battery life is so long in reactive mode is because it doesn't use the focused beam. Standard mode uses both.

When I run, I used the middle of the three settings in standard mode so that the focus beam is enabled. I've run in that mode for 90 mins and only used 20% of the battery. Right at twilight when I can see ok w/o the headlamp, but not quite enough, I like to switch to the highest setting in reactive mode. It gives me just the right amount of light to enhance my view and when I'm going in and out of trees, it brightens when I need it.

It wears well, isn't too heavy, and adjusts easily. Easy 5 stars. Very happy I purchased it.

Note: I haven't run for more than a few hours in the dark, so I haven't pushed this to its limit. If you're looking for an 8 hour lamp, hopefully others have reviews on that. Good luck!

query: I'm looking for a sturdy and comfortable cot that I can easily set up on a concrete floor for a trip. ori_review: I purchased this cot to take with me on a trip where I would have to sleep on a concrete floor.  Rather than get an air mattress or a foam pad, I opted for a cot.  This cot was an excellent choice.  It is basically three pieces: the main frame of cot, and to end pieces that keep the cot fixed in the unfolded position..  One person can set this up.  There are two arms that unfold from the middle towards each end.  They swing around 180 degrees to reach their position.  That leaves the cot spread out to full length and folded down the center.  You then spread apart the two sides of the sleeping surface which also spreads out the legs into the "x" shape you see in the picture.  The final step is to place the bars on each end through the sleeping surface which serve to snug up the sleeping surface and keep that cot from being able to fold up.  It is simple and sturdy.  I loved the little pouches on the side that gave me a safe place to store my wallet, glasses, etc at night along with enough space to store my GPS and kindle so I could reference them as need be.  The cot is high enough off the ground to sit on comfortably.  It was very comfortable to sleep on.  I slept on it for a week without any aches or pains.  When it was time to fold up it is equally easy to disassemble.  I didn't have to carry my cot very far, but it would probably get heavy if you were planning to go on a hike with it, but worked perfect for my purposes.

Sun protection is not quite as good as tents that have walls, but you can adjust the tent down to two poles and angle it away from the sun to get better protection early or late in the day when the sun is closer to the horizon.

query: I'm looking for an ergonomic ball chair that can help improve my posture and breathing while I work. I need something durable and aesthetically pleasing, as I work in an open office space and want to avoid anything that looks too much like exercise equipment. I’ve had issues with my previous ball being too squishy and deteriorating over time, so I want one that retains its shape and looks good in an office environment. Also, I’d like to know if anyone else has had trouble with the pump design, as I found it quite difficult to use. Any recommendations or insights?
ori_review:
I bought this as an ergonomic chair for the office, both for better breathing/posture and to help calm my desire to fidget, grind my teeth and go nuts in an office. I used to use a ball for a desk chair at home, which I loved -- really helped eliminate the back/shoulder/neck pain of sitting at a computer for too many hours. But that ball was both too squishy and over time the surface kind of deteriorated, getting porous and sticky. Eventually I threw it out.
Enter the Santulana ball. I just joined a new office after years of working outdoors and from home. It's an open work space, and I doubted my ability/desire to sit still in an enclosed space without driving my coworkers nuts. I'm not the most office-y of people. We have adjustable standing desks, but sometimes I need to sit. So I thought a ball would keep my inner child entertained and keep my outer adult from turning into a mushpie of hunched over deskjockey. I looked at a lot of them - needed to be both anti-burst (staples on the ground) and look good with birch and gray office decor. (Remember, I'm new here. Trying not to raise too many eyebrows with playground-looking equipment.) I'd planned on the Black Mountain one, since their quality is great. But bringing in a giant black rubber ball, or a sad gray? Not helping my mood. The colors were all either drab or too exercisey. Santaluna was the only company I found that had both high quality and great colors.
Okay, the review: I love this ball.
It's a fabulous lime green color (not too mint, not dayglo; perfectly lime green), very thick and durable. After the initial stretching period, it has held its air well, is taut and strong and so very comfortable. It looks great in the office - interesting but not obnoxious. Got the approval of the boss, who says the color is perfect for the space. I got a flat ring base to hold it still if needed, but I use it without the base so I can roll in and out of the desk as needed. Didn't want the bulk of the whole wheeled base thing; seems like it defeats the purpose of the ball. When no one is in the office, I can bounce or rock on it, and lay back on it to open my chest and shoulders - feels great. I'm sitting much straighter, am more energetic, and resent being indoors much less. This ball makes me happy every time I sit on it or see it. Silly, I know, but it's true. Much better quality than the last one I had.
The downside: The pump is a joke. It is -terribly- designed, to the point of being almost unworkable. You have to hold onto an unnecessarily tiny sloped piece with one hand, while pumping the much larger cylinder side with the other hand, so that the sloped piece slides out of your hand with every pump. Not only does the bottom hand keep slipping and/or getting pinched between the two especially as the ball gets more inflated, but the motion of the other hand on the cylinder can be called nothing other than giving the thing a hand job. Or masturbating I suppose, but I'm a woman. At any rate, pumping this ball with this pump is totally inappropriate for work. Do not allow your coworkers to see you do this - unless you have that kind of office. Better idea, Santaluna should redesign this horrible little thing. I can only assume that some jokester designer at their end is laughing it up at the idea of people all across the country using this thing. Very funny guys. Now send out the real one.
Synopsis: Ball gets an A++ for durability, smooth surface and awesome color. Pump gets a D- and a wink.

It takes time and effort to figure out the best technique to cut.  The blade has a tendency to catch and so you need to work the blade in different directions and tensions to free it to resume cutting. When the blade is free you can make long strokes. When it binds, all you can do are short strokes. As with any saw, smooth light sawing gets the job done faster than brute force.  Finally, some reviewers mention uneven cuts of big branches. I had same issue.  Solution is to first cut the branch a foot or two from trunk.  Come back and cut the stub.  Definitely more work, but a professional result.

query: I'm looking for a great elliptical trainer, but I'm concerned about the packaging. I received mine and was overwhelmed by the amount of Styrofoam used, which is difficult to recycle in my area. Has anyone else experienced this issue? Also, during assembly, I found some instructions unclear, and I was missing screws initially but later discovered they were hidden. How can I ensure a smoother assembly process and minimize waste in the future when purchasing fitness equipment?
ori_review:
It a great product. We have had it about 3 weeks, and my husband is using it regularly ... a good idea believe me!

Amazon delivered it quickly, and the truck driver got it just inside our door. Then the fun began!

When I opened the box, I was confronted with a giant piece of 3 by 5 foot Styrofoam, about 14" deep. It has many cutouts, and a similar piece of Styrofoam was at the bottom of the box- basically the entire box is filled with styro. There is nowhere to recycle Styrofoam in our area, so I posted on Craigslist to find someone who wanted it. I was very lucky that worked out.

Assembly took 1 1/2 hours, for 2 highly skilled engineers (us) using power tools where possible. In one place, the directions failed to show a critical part, a 2" long roller type spacer which is inserted into a joint. When we were done, we were missing 6 screws that hold several decorative plastic covers in place.

We called Schwinn/Nautilus to get replacement screws. Two things to keep in mind - you need the serial number to get parts sent to you. The serial number is located on the _underside_ of the unit. And you need to fax or email a purchase receipt. The ENTIRE replacement parts kit arrived a week later, including a second very nice Phillips head screwdriver. Thank you Schwinn!

The following week, as I re-used the several cardboard boxes (found inside the giant styrofoam pieces) for packing presents, I found 6 tiny screws in a tiny bag taped on the inside of the lid of the fan packaging. So they were not missing after all, just very carefully hidden. You have been warned!

Schwinn, I like the product, now can you please find a way to package equipment that does not generate so much landfill debris?

query: I'm considering purchasing a bike rack for my 2012 Toyota Corolla S but saw that it might not fit well due to clearance issues with the trunk and spoiler. Can anyone share their experiences with assembly and whether using foam or other protective measures helped prevent scratches on the paint? I'm also curious if it’s manageable for one or two bikes. Thanks!
ori_review:
The Allen Sport's website says this model does not fit the Corolla S because of the clearance of the rack onto the trunk over the spoiler. I decided to give it a shot anyway as the price was so cheap. Here is my finding..

First, the rack has a warning about the two metal hooks you have to set into place during assembly being a pinch point. Do not ignore this. I wore a glove when setting them and had no issues but I can definitely see how someone could get hurt. Assembly was simple, basically that was the only step.

Second, if you set the bottom pads of the rack against your license plate and the top on the trunk, it clears the spoiler fine. The metal hooks mentioned earlier do rest against the spoiler and can easily cause scratches. I used a piece of foam to separate and it worked out fine.

Third, many reviews mention the hooks that attach to the sides of the trunk scratching the paint. I used a piece of foam with an adhesive side under each hook to keep it off the paint, no issues.

Fourth, an extra bungee comes in handy to keep loose bits like the front tire from moving around too much. Get creative.

Overall, I'm happy with the purchase. The rack is being used for one bike but I don't think a second one would cause an issue with this set up. Again, great price to not at least give it a shot. Glad I did.

So bottom line-- I am thrilled with this product because I can multitask and get work and exercise out of the way at the same time. We purchased these at the beginning of June and have had them out on four different lakes already. Sunday we paddled a good 4 miles and into a narrow cave and it did awesome.

All in all if your nervous about trying out a board and are a beginner on a budget I think they are a great place to start.

query: I'm looking for a folding electric scooter that offers great speed and stopping power, ideally faster than 15.5 mph, and has features like regenerative braking and a good headlight. ori_review:
Recently I had the opportunity to ride one of the new bird scooters in my town. I really loved the convenience and idea of not having to move my car when I went to lunch or get coffee, but I found that ride-share could also be not so convenient when I was in a time crunch, as they are sometimes hard to find. So I decided why rent when I can buy.

Last year I had  purchased a hoverboard from gotrax.com and it worked out great for my son, so when I received an email from them about their new product launch I decided to give the gotrax gxl commuter scooter a shot. Here are my thoughts... Speed, obviously the first thing I noticed is that mine was faster than the advertised speed of 15.5 mph, I had this thing clocking almost 18 in second gear.  With that speed the stopping power was equally as great, they conveniently placed a foot brake on the rear of the deck which controls its rear wheel disk brake which works amazingly... the kid in me had this thing getting sideways on the gravel like I used to do with my kick scooter when I was younger. Overall it just feels like great craftsmanship, it is really sturdy,  well constructed, and folds perfectly to fit in the trunk of my car. Oh ya the headlight is really nice too. Additionally it also has another feature of regenerative disk braking, that is suppose to add power back into the battery system, although I am not quite sure how to test.

I'll have to say I am brilliantly surprised at how great this folding electric scooter is for the price point at which they are selling them, the other e scooters on the market are way higher priced. I will likely buy another for my eldest son as he is getting ready for college and this will be great for helping get across campus and to class on-time. I am now a scooter guy.

An amazing scope built with amazing quality. The magnification adjustments work really well. The mil dot reticle tracks very well to the m5 turrets. The turrets track very well and are extremely repeatable back to zero. Glass clarity out at distance was an extremely noticable increase to my old millet trs 16x scope. At 6.5x magnification the reticle is still a reasonable size. There is very very minimal tunneling at the lowest magnification (that is where there is no change in the field of view when lowering magnifaction, it typically happens around the lower end of the magnification. Schmidt and bender scopes have pretty bad tunneling as an example but are superior in every other respect.)

Anyways for the price point I don't think this scope can be beat unless you want to drop another $600 and go with something tier 1 like a vortex razor hd gen 2 or a nightforce atacr f1 or something.

query: I'm looking for a flint striker that creates a lot of sparks. I've tried a couple of different scrapers, but I've heard that the Super Scraper from Firesteel.com performs better. Can you help me find a striker that is similar in thickness and sharpness to the Super Scraper, but perhaps even lighter and easy to use, or suggest if I should stick with the Super Scraper for optimal performance? I also want to know if ditching the scrapers that come with my current flint is a good idea.
ori_review:
A flint is a flint, it's the striker that makes all the difference.

I have the flint from Firesteel.com and from Coghlan. The only difference between the sparks I create from the two is due
to the striker. The 'Super Scraper' from Firesteel.com makes more sparks and it easier to strike. The Super Scraper is thicker
and has a sharper edge and this makes a whole lot of difference. When I strike my Coghlan flint with the Super Scraper I get the same amount of sparks as I do when I strike it on the Firesteel.com flint. Therefore, it's not the flint but the striker that make the difference.

The opposite side of the sharpen edge of the blade of my Spyderco pocket knife has as similar thick right angle as the Super Scraper and it gives me a similar spark as the Super Scraper. However, the Super Scraper is lighter and attaches to my flint with a lanyard.

Ditch the scrapers that come from the Colghan, Light My Fire, etc. and either get the Super Scraper or use something similar the Super Scraper. BTW the Super Scraper is @2.5mm thick and the edge is a right angle and where the angles meet, it kinda feels 'sharp' but not the kind of sharp that you get from a knife... I hope you understand what I am trying to mean.

query: I'm interested in getting a trike, but I've read that there can be some initial challenges with assembly and setup. Can you provide tips on what to expect during the assembly process? Also, I’ve noticed some reviews mention the color and packaging issues. Is the bike really more of a silvery blue than a darker slate? Lastly, can you suggest any modifications for comfort, especially regarding the seat, since I'm looking for something suitable for longer rides?
ori_review:
I bought this bike after reading every single review, both positive and negative. I even took the step of ordering the bike from Amazon's Warehouse Deals. I paid a very reasonable price. I am a 52 year old woman who does not really have a lot of mechanical experience, but it was a beautiful day when the bike arrived. I got my iced tea and sat on my porch with the box and spent a leisurely afternoon figuring it out. With only a little help from my husband and son (mostly to just confirm I did something correctly) I was able to assemble the bike. I'm glad I did, too, because now, adjustments make more sense to me...I know the parts and understand how they work and fit together.

That said, if you are just hoping for a quick experience putting it together, you may want to get help or pay a bike shop. I rate the bike 5 stars because I love the style and I think it was a GREAT value. It seems to be working well. But for the sake of those who read reviews, here are some notes that might help you.

--The color: I read a lot of reviews that complained that they were hoping for a more BLUE bike. This should be called "Ice Blue" or something like that, not Slate, because the bike is really a silvery blue not a darker color like I would think Slate would be.

--Packaging: I ordered from Amazon Warehouse Deals, which said the item would be repackaged, so I expected that. The large box it came in was not TOO badly roughed up from shipping, but when I opened it, the inner box that was holding all the bike parts was fairly frightening. Torn spots, dents in the cardboard, etc. From reading a lot of reviews about dents, I wonder if shipping is just really hard on this. Mine came basically double boxed. I wonder if someone returned it because of the condition of the original box! The original box did not appear to ever have been opened and resealed? Anyway, I probably got lucky, but my guess is this is a shipping issue and perhaps unavoidable when you have parts, like fenders, that are easily bent out of shape.

--Assembly: Yeah, there were a few head scratching moments where I had to look at the diagram, re-read and THINK, but I figured them out. I saw a YouTube video of a guy who was pretty mechanical and putting this bike together for one of his parents and he had pretty much the same issues I had! I used (after googling!) Vicks VapoRub for grease for the handlebar stem and it is working great. Did have to laugh at the whiff of menthol I got just before my second ride on it, when I adjusted the handlebars. Vaseline would work too if you don't have a tube of grease that they call for. I confirmed with a mechanical friend that this will be no problem, we're not dealing with high temperatures or huge amounts of friction. I had to really work to get fenders lined up to the holes for the bolts that hold them on, then I had to bend them into shape a little to keep them from rubbing. This is no big deal to me, but if it is to you, you're forewarned. If you can't find the stem for the seat, look inside the hole in the frame, lots of people think they don't have one then find it there! Brakes might take a while to get them adjusted properly. If any of this really doesn't sound like something you want to mess with then definitely find a handier friend or take it to a bike shop for assembly. I didn't mind the tweaking.

--Riding: THIS IS DIFFERENT THAN A TWO WHEEL BIKE! You have to really remember this or you may think something is wrong when it is not. If you learned to ride a two wheel bike, you instinctively *lean* to keep balance. Leaning on this bike is not necessary and may even make your sensation of being off balance WORSE. You *might* even want to lean OUT of a turn (the opposite direction) a tiny bit! I did feel a bit wonky on this trike at first, but I just took a deep breath and tried to remember that this was different. Much better as time goes on! Also, the road where I live is slightly graded to allow rain to runoff so if I'm riding on the road, I realize that it is going to feel off balance. I only take the road for a short while, then I am on the rails-to-trails near our home. That too is ever-so-slightly graded for runoff, but I can work with it better there. If the trail is clear, I just take my spot up the middle and my fellow bikers let me know they are coming with a friendly call or ring of their bell and I move over. :)

--Mount/Dismount: At first, I kept whacking the back of my legs with the back wheels. Just needed to get in the habit of remembering that unlike a 2 wheel bike, I have to watch for them.

--Seat: I'm a middle aged woman with an ample middle aged figure. The seat is just *okay* for me but since I got such a nice price on the bike, I don't feel badly about seeking out a wider, more comfortable seat. Until switching the seat, I only had gone about 3 miles at a time to avoid a sore posterior.

query: I'm looking for a compact and quiet under-desk exercise bike that allows for both forward and backward cycling, and has multiple resistance levels. Excellent buy for the price. Excellent quality. One thing... I ordered the large display and the extension cable & mount to attach it. I sent it back simply because it seems to be totally unneeded and because the extension cable had 2 males ends and the cable it attached to on the DeskCycle also had a male end. Too, I'm working while I'm pedaling so I really don't care to have a monitor on my desk. Heck... I can simply back up a few inches and look down at the monitor that's already on the cycle. Personal thought... save yourself the time and just purchase the DeskCycle itself!

query: I'm looking for a lightweight backpack that can comfortably handle heavy loads, ideally one that has a good suspension system for hiking. I've had experience with various packs over the years, and I appreciate durability, especially in water bottle holders and back panels. I also prefer packs that offer decent ventilation to keep my back dry. Are there any options that are tough yet lightweight, and can accommodate additional gear like raingear or a two-person tent? Lastly, do you have any suggestions for a pack with adjustable features and a good value for someone who might be using it for a long time?
ori_review: I put 7500+ miles on my first Granite Gear Blaze AC 60; I loved the pack so much that when I decided to finally semi-retire her I bought this identical replacement. The suspension on the Blaze is good enough to comfortably handle 40+ pound loads when necessary, but the pack is light enough to still be a legit choice for lightweight trail hiking. I've owned a LOT of different packs over the years, ranging from the seven pound Dana Designs load-monster I carried on my first AT thruhike over two decades ago, to the ultralight  ULA Ohm which was my first Blaze's immediate predecessor. Despite some initial reservations about the durability of the mesh material which makes up the water bottle holders and back panel, the Blaze proved to be as durable as any pack I've ever used, and significantly tougher than any other sub-3lb pack I've tried out. The Air Current design does a respectable job of keeping your back from getting soaked with sweat- vastly better than the ULA did, though not as well as a heavier pack with an arced frame. The water bottle pockets will easily hold two one-liter bottles; the back panel is stretchy enough to hold raingear, or even a two person tent. (On a trip with a friend I was able to get a Big Agnes Copper Spur 2 inside it). The mesh WILL stretch, and I eventually abraded numerous holes in it, but the tears won't grow, and can be easily patched. I also found the compression straps unnecessarily long, and trimmed 2-3oz of excess material off the pack when I first bought it. What else to say? It's comfortable, tough, and a great value. If my knees hold up for another 7500 miles I could easily imagine buying a third Blaze some day.

query: Why should I consider using trekking poles for hiking, especially if I'm not looking to spend a lot? I’ve been hesitant about them but have heard they could really help with my hiking stamina and knee pain. What features should I look for in affordable poles, and how can I ensure I'm using them correctly to avoid issues?
ori_review:
My husband and I have been avid hikers over the past 15 years. But we poo-pood trekking poles. I would see other hikers slide using them and thought they would just get in the way.
This spring we were getting ready to complete the ADK Firetower Challenge. We needed to hike 5 mountains in 6 days. I joined a Facebook group about these hikes. And that is where I realized trekking poles would be beneficial. We didn’t want to spend a lot of money on poles that would only get used 5-10 times a year. Someone in the group recommended these. As soon as I read Ken and Cathy’s review (after laughing so hard), I knew if they liked the poles, so would we.
Well, they are the best! And I will never hike without them again. We have used them on trails that were dry, wet, snow covered, and even ice. Through mud and creeks. I feel they help my cardio stamina going up trails. And oh man, the difference in my knees going down! Worth every penny. Now I did watch a ton of you tube videos on how to measure for best height. And where to position them when going up or down mountains. . Just like when I was learning the best way to kayak, I found just do what works for you. When I had the poles at the height recommended going down mountains, my knees still hurt. When I raised them higher, that was my magic spot! So experiment with height and placement. These poles have kept me from sliding on my tush quite a few times. And at 66, I’m doing all I can to avoid falling.
I love these poles so much, when I saw them at an even cheaper price than I paid for them earlier this year, I bought another pair. Same color.
READ THE DIRECTIONS! I am quite confident that any of the negative reviews were due to user error.
Open the latch before tightening them. Check the latch before each use. I have had to tighten them on occasion. I put my full weight on each pole to test before use, and have never had the pole collapse on me. They fold up nicely to a manageable size when not in use. I love that it comes with extra tip, and accessories for mud, and snow.
There is no need to spend a fortune on trekking poles. We ran into a retired mountain hiking tour guide on one of our hikes. He and his friend both were using these poles. He said in all of his years as a tour guide, he tried several poles, and found the Trail Buddy to be the best.
Do not hesitate to buy these. You won’t regret it.

query: I'm looking for a stable inflatable paddle board that can handle ocean use, especially in choppy water. I want something that's easy to pump up and store, suitable for both my 12-year-old and myself. It should come with good accessories, like a leash and a carrying strap, and I need it to be durable enough for frequent use. Can you recommend a board that matches these needs and has a good reputation for quality?
ori_review:
For reference, I bought this for frequent ocean use. I live on a tropical island and already own to solid boards: one Naish and one Vesl. Both of those boards, the Vesl in particular, are high quality. The boards are primarily used within a lagoon where water is fairly calm, though we also use our SUPs for easy surfing when swells are there. My 12-yr old loves the Vesl but that's also my favorite so I went searching for inflatables as something he can use. After reading a lot of reviews and looking for something with the same dimensions as my Vesl (shorter and wider than the Naish for more stability), I settled on the Roc. I bought it from Amazon Warehouse so it was a bit of a gamble.

Out of the box, it looked unused and all components were present. I used the included pump and timed myself. 5 1/2 minutes continuous, though easy pumping without trying to "race". Definitely broke a sweat but it wasn't difficult to pump up at all. Please note (and this may be obvious already): the gauge will not register psi until the board appears mostly inflated. From there (5 psi), the pumping gets a little more difficult but goes quick. I stopped at 12 psi since I knew this would always be used in the hot sun. After pumping it, I stored it for 4 days to check for any leaks. Still registers at 12 psi after that.

I left this inflated and strapped it to the top of my car, along with one of my solid boards. 15' straps were perfect for this set up. If you were strapping two inflatable SUPs to the top, you'd need 20' straps since the inflatables are thicker than the solids. This is also pretty small once collapsed and stored in the included bag, so it wouldn't be difficult to set it up at the beach.

First impressions in somewhat choppy water with a strong current (both from a distant tropical storm): this board is stable and cuts through the water fairly quick. Had no trouble staying together between this board and the Vesl. It definitely feels a little different...not squishy per se, but just not the same as a solid board. The foam grip pad is great, the handle works well and isn't bothersome, the straps and D-rings are fantastic inclusions for this board. The paddle feels heavy compared to my carbon fiber paddle, but the cool thing is that it adjusts to a lower height than my other one, so my 12-yr old can use this with a proper fit. I also like that it initially floats. It doesn't stay floating, but it doesn't need to--you have enough time to pluck it from the water if you fall off.

I appreciated that this came with everything right out of the box. The leash is of good quality and looks nearly identical to my coiled Dakine leash. There was an included carrying strap for the board, once inflated, in case someone needs to carry it far down a beach or anything. The backpack/duffel is impressively well constructed. The fin is easy to attach and detach, and you get a high quality small dry bag (looks just like my expensive ScubaPro one) for phone, keys, etc. All in all...I am super impressed. Time will tell how it holds up, but I'm surprised what it comes with at this price point. Great board to learn on, nice and stable, would be great for SUP yoga as well.

query: I'm looking for a comparison between different mountain bike pedals, specifically how the Fooker pedals stack up against the Raceface Chester. Can anyone share their experiences with the build quality, bearing design, and overall performance of the Fooker pedals? I'm particularly interested in how the three bearings affect ease of use and assembly, as well as any concerns regarding durability on trails.
ori_review:
I just received my Fooker pedals and I am really impressed. I own both the Raceface Chester and now these. Comparably they are very similar from the outside. Main noticable difference is the distance the fooker pedals is from the base of the crank. Its about 2mm longer then the raceface. I dont know how the polymer will hold up as I haven't been on a trail with them yet. After disassembling both the raceface and these fooker pedals I have to give props to the Fooker. The Fooker pedal uses 3 bearing which is noticeable and easy to assemble and adjust with the internal preload nut. The Raceface only use 1 bearing and a nylon sleeve acting as the other bearing. Both work but I did had alittle more trouble setting up the raceface when a bearing went out. Too much tension will cause the pedal not to swivel freely and when I tighted the fooker all the way down it did not have the same issue. The design may be a knock off but I have to say these look and feel very promising. It's less then half of what the raceface cost and with what I feel is a better internal design. The shafts are different respectfully so as the fooker uses 3 bearings compared to the raceface internals using only 1 bearing.

Fooker pedals
Pros: build is quality. Price, 3 bearings, different colors, easy to repair. Comes with 3 spare pins, smooth, 8mm hex to fasten from inside the crank,

Cons: 2mm gap longer then raceface. [Referring to the space between the crank and the pedal platform.], Design is not their own.

Raceface chester.
Pros: haven't failed yet, trusted brand name, different color.

Cons: 1 bearing design, price is twice as much. Uses a 6mm hex to tighten the pedals

Both can also use a 15mm wrench to tighten to the cranks.

query: I'm looking for a beginner lacrosse package suitable for young girls, ideally for 5th and 3rd graders. I want to ensure that it includes a comfortable eyewear fit and a good backpack. Additionally, I heard that it might be helpful to get a large box of practice balls that are lighter and safer for beginners. Any advice on that would be great!
ori_review:
Bought this as some Xmas presents for two girls. One in 5th grade and the other in 3rd.
These are a great starter pack for the girls. Eye wear fits fine and the backpack is nice.
The pocket, like many lacrosse sticks needs to be broken in. For beginners, i highly recommend loosening some of the straps on the head so it doesnt play like a tennis racket for beginners.
Also buy a large box of practice balls for beginners. This package does not come with any balls. They are less heavy, will cause less bruising if it hits the body for beginners and also has less bounce to them so they wont get away easily.

query: I'm looking for a compact exercise machine that I can easily assemble and use while sitting on my sofa. Are there any tips for preventing it from moving around during use, and how can I ensure I maintain proper foot positioning while pedaling? I'm also curious about the workout intensity at various tension levels. Is it really effective for breaking a sweat?
ori_review: Assembly was very easy.  I use it while sitting on my sofa.  Two things to know:  (1)You need to brace the stand's base  against something at least on one side to keep it from "creeping" and (2)while the straps on the pedals do a great job, you need to sit high enough to keep your heel from hitting the ground.  In other words, you need to keep your feet level while pedaling.  It is easy to knock off 10 miles at level 2 and you will break abit of a sweat.  But it will be a real workout at higher tension levels.  Well made product!
